Reproducibility: Sarek is implemented in Nextflow and adheres to the nf-core portability and documentation guidelines. Nextflow downloads the specified pipeline version (2.5.2) from GitHub with the corresponding container, and fetches the reference files from AWS-iGenomes. Best practice: Sarek follows the GATK best-practice recommendations for read alignment and pre-processing (BWA-MEM alignment, then GATK deduplication and recalibration). ## Summary

****

Sarek is a bioinformatics workflow designed for analyzing next-generation sequencing (NGS) data, including whole-genome sequencing (WGS), whole-exome sequencing (WES), and targeted gene panels. It aims to simplify the analysis process by providing a portable and reproducible solution that can be easily installed across different compute environments such as high-performance computing clusters and cloud platforms [1][4]. The workflow is built using Nextflow, a popular framework for defining computational workflows, and it automatically installs required software components through Docker, Singularity, or Conda environments to ensure ease of use and reproducibility [1][4][7].

Sarek focuses on detecting germline and somatic variants, including single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), indels, and structural variants. It incorporates state-of-the-art tools for read mapping, variant calling, annotation, and quality control. The workflow generates annotated VCF files, copy number variation (CNV) reports, and comprehensive quality metrics, making it suitable for both research and clinical applications [1][4].

One of the key features of Sarek is its flexibility and ease of modification, allowing users to adapt the workflow to their specific needs by adding new tools or adjusting parameters. This adaptability makes it a valuable tool for individual research groups and core facilities alike [1][6]. The documentation provided with Sarek is extensive and user-friendly, guiding users through installation, configuration, and execution processes [10].

Sarek has been benchmarked against existing workflows and demonstrates strong performance in variant calling accuracy. For instance, somatic single nucleotide and indel variant calls from Sarek align well with a previously defined gold standard callset. However, there is a noted lack of comprehensive benchmark data for more complex somatic variants and germline variant accuracy [8][9].

The development of Sarek addresses the need for efficient and reproducible NGS analysis workflows that minimize installation and management overhead. It is part of the nf-core community effort, which curates high-quality analysis pipelines in the Nextflow framework [10]. Reviewers have praised Sarek for its clarity, comprehensive functionality, and ease of use, suggesting it will be a valuable addition to the research community [10].

items.question: How do the collective methodologies across Sarek, Snakemake, nf-core, and MultiQC redefine the concept of 'quality control' from a single-sample metric to a system-wide diagnostic process?
items.expected:
The papers do not say they redefine QC or call it a system-wide diagnostic process. Together they describe QC moving from per-sample tool output to one aggregated report. MultiQC: QC logs and reports are produced on a per-sample basis, with no common approach to integrate them across tools and large sample sets. MultiQC builds a single summary report across all samples and tools. Its shared plots allow comparison between samples, aid batch effect detection, show global trends and biases, and help spot failing, abnormal or irregular groups of samples. It acts as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines. Sarek (2020): generates QC metrics with FastQC, QualiMap, BCFtools, Samtools and VCFtools, shown as an aggregated quality control review across samples with MultiQC. Its error reporting diagnoses software or hardware errors during a run, which is separate from data QC, and qualitative assessment by the user remains important. nf-core/sarek 3: QC reporting is one of four major processing units. QC tools run throughout the pipeline (FastQC before alignment; mosdepth and SAMtools after duplicate marking and BQSR; vcftools and bcftools on called variants), and their results go into one MultiQC report together with software version numbers of all executed tools. Snakemake: QC is one step in a unified representation of the whole analysis. A QC step yields QC values for each sample, and through conditional execution (a checkpoint) only samples above a threshold (greater than 90 in the example) go downstream. Snakemake also tracks the inputs, outputs, parameters, software and code of each executed job and reports them, with runtime statistics for all jobs, in an interactive HTML report. The paper does not call these reports QC.

MultiQC names the starting point: QC logs and reports are produced per sample, with no common way to integrate them across tools and sample sets [0, 1]. Its answer is a single report across all samples and tools that supports comparison between samples, batch effect detection, global trends, and the identification of failing, abnormal or irregular samples [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. It is meant to sit at the terminus of analysis pipelines [9]. Sarek 2020 applies this to a variant-calling workflow, showing QC metrics from several tools as an aggregated review across samples with MultiQC [10]. Its run-time diagnosis concerns software or hardware errors, and the authors say the user's own assessment remains important [11, 12]. nf-core/sarek 3 makes QC reporting one of four processing units, runs QC tools at the read, alignment and variant stages, and collects them with all software versions into one MultiQC report [13, 14, 15, 16]. Snakemake places QC inside a unified representation of the analysis, where per-sample QC values can automatically decide, through conditional execution, which samples continue downstream [17, 18, 19, 20]. It also tracks provenance and runtime for every job in one report, which it does not call QC [21, 22, 23]. None of the papers describes this as redefining QC [0-23].

## MultiQC and fastp Integration

MultiQC complements the all-in-one preprocessing approach of fastp by providing a centralized visualization and quality control tool for bioinformatics pipelines. While fastp handles preprocessing tasks like quality trimming and adapter removal, MultiQC aggregates and visualizes quality control metrics from multiple tools, including fastp, across large sample sets. This allows researchers to quickly identify global trends, batch effects, and outliers that might be missed when reviewing individual sample reports [1][2]. MultiQC's ability to parse data from various bioinformatics tools and present it in a single, interactive report enhances the quality control process by making it easier to compare metrics across samples and detect subtle issues early in the analysis pipeline [3]. The tool's customizable modules and plugins further extend its utility, enabling integration with institutional systems and facilitating large-scale data collection [2]. By automating the parsing and visualization of QC metadata, MultiQC reduces the risk of errors associated with manual compilation of results and provides a powerful complement to preprocessing tools like fastp [3].

## MultiQC Visualization Capabilities

MultiQC enhances quality control in bioinformatics pipelines by providing a unified visualization platform for QC reports and logs generated by various bioinformatics tools. It scans specified directories for recognized log files and creates a single summary report that visualizes results across all samples, enabling quick and easy scanning of key statistics [1]. The tool generates shared plots that facilitate accurate comparison between samples, allowing researchers to detect subtle differences that might not be noticeable when switching between different files [1]. This centralized visualization aids in batch effect detection and minimizes the risk of confounding factors affecting study results [1]. MultiQC is the first tool of its type in the field, streamlining quality control and reporting for next-generation sequencing research by eliminating the need for custom comparative scripts [1].

## MultiQC Integration with Bioinformatics Tools

MultiQC integrates with other bioinformatics tools by automating the parsing of metadata from various tools, providing powerful visualizations through a simple interface [1]. This integration is particularly useful for large sample sets, where manually integrating statistics from multiple tools can be difficult and time-consuming [1]. MultiQC's ability to parse data for thousands of samples within minutes makes it ideal for projects requiring accurate quality control, such as single-cell and population studies [1]. Additionally, MultiQC supports plugins that allow integration with in-house systems, such as the MultiQC_NGI plugin, which inserts metadata from LIMS into reports and stores summary results in databases [1]. This functionality facilitates large-scale internal data collection, reducing the need for numerous custom scripts [1]. MultiQC also offers templates for report branding and ensures reports are self-contained, making it suitable for creating delivery reports [1]. By functioning as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines, MultiQC aids in quality control steps early in data processing, helping to reduce risks like batch effects and other downstream analysis problems [1].

Scheduling: Snakemake solves the scheduling problem at the start of execution and again whenever a job finishes and new jobs become pending. The first releases used a greedy scheduler. The MILP optimizes four criteria in lexicographical order: (1) prefer jobs with high priority, (2) maximize the number of used cores (the extent of parallelization), (3) delete existing temporary files as soon as possible, and (4) reduce the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass. The order is enforced by multiplying each criterion sum by a value at least as high as the maximum the terms to its right can reach. Constraint (2) ensures the selection does not exceed the available amount of each resource.

Cluster and cloud: with middleware such as SLURM, PBS, LSF or Kubernetes, Snakemake does not need to govern all resources at a global level. Some resources are handled by the middleware, and constraint (2) can be dropped for them. Snakemake can pass the resource requirements to the middleware, which can use them to choose the best fitting machine. By default runtime, threads, memory and disk usage are local resources passed to the middleware; all other resources are global and are still governed by Snakemake via constraint (2). The number of jobs queued or running at a time is limited by the same kind of constraint.

Submission overhead: by default every job is submitted separately to the queuing system. For short-running jobs this can cause considerable overhead, as jobs wait in a queue, and may add delays or cost when accessing files from remote storage or network file systems. To minimize it, Snakemake can partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs by assigning rules to groups. Connected subgraphs with the same group are submitted together as a single cluster or cloud job (a group job) instead of each job separately. For each group, the number of connected subgraphs spanned per submission can be defined (one by default), so the partition size can be adjusted to the computational platform. A group job's resource usage is computed by sorting its jobs topologically, summing resource usage per level and taking the maximum over all levels. For runtime it is the other way round: the maximum per level, summed over all levels.

partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs

items.question: How does Snakemake's implementation of a blockchain-style hashing scheme facilitate cross-workflow result caching?
items.expected: Snakemake uses workflow-inherent information to calculate a hash value for each job, prior to actually generating the file. The hash captures exactly how the output file is generated. For a job eligible for caching, the hash is a SHA-256 hash value calculated from the job's code, parameters, raw input files and software environment, plus the hashes of its dependencies. The scheme is blockchain-style because the hash function is applied recursively: for each dependency, a hash value is included in the hash of the job, which is the hashing principle behind blockchains. As a result, the hash describes everything that affects the content of the job's output files, including the input generated by jobs it depends on. The output files are stored under this hash in a central cache, such as a folder on the same machine or in a remote storage. If a rule is marked as eligible for caching, Snakemake can obtain its output from the cache when the file has been created before in a different workflow or by a different user on the same system. Subsequent runs of the same job (with the same dependencies) in other workflows can then skip the execution and take the output files directly from the cache. This saves computation time, as well as disk space: on local machines the file can be linked instead of copied. The hash is only descriptive if the workflow developer ensures that the cached result is generated in a deterministic way. For example, downloading from a URL that yields data which may change over time should be avoided.

## Meta-Strategy Analysis

The emerging meta-strategy for balancing computational efficiency and scientific reproducibility in genomics, as illustrated by the Sarek workflow, relies on the integration of domain-specific workflow languages, containerization, and community-driven standards. Sarek is implemented using Nextflow, a language designed for bioinformatics that ensures transparent, readable, and extensible code, facilitating easy adjustments and extensions by the user community [1]. To achieve robust portability across diverse execution environments—including HPC clusters (Slurm, LSF, Sun Grid Engine) and cloud platforms (AWS, Google Cloud)—the workflow leverages Nextflow's native support for these systems, allowing for the distribution of thousands of batch jobs [1]. Reproducibility is ensured by managing all required software tools within Conda environments and distributing them via DockerHub, making them accessible through Conda, Docker, or Singularity containers [1][2]. This approach minimizes installation overhead and allows the workflow to run on systems without direct internet access, a critical feature for handling sensitive data [5]. The strategy also emphasizes extensive error reporting and the ability to restart incomplete runs from any stage, significantly reducing the time spent on debugging failed jobs [1][4]. Furthermore, Sarek adheres to the nf-core guidelines, which promote well-documented, community-tested pipelines that prioritize easy installation, comprehensive documentation, and extensive quality metrics reporting [1][5]. While the workflow handles complex variant calling for germline and somatic data, it maintains flexibility by allowing users to combine results from multiple callers based on their specific research needs regarding sensitivity versus specificity [4]. Although the provided text focuses on Sarek, Nextflow, and nf-core, specific details regarding the tools Snakemake or fastp are not found in the source material [3][6][7][8][9][10].

## Problem Statement & Need

The introduction of whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and whole-exome sequencing (WES) technologies has created new opportunities for research and clinical applications, yet the effort to create efficient and reproducible workflows to combine analysis software has been underestimated [1]. While several solutions exist, such as SeqMule and SpeedSeq, the authors argue that no existing workflow fully satisfies key user requirements, including easy installation, robust portability across different compute environments, comprehensive documentation, transparent code, and extensive quality metrics reporting [1]. This gap is particularly critical for somatic variant analysis and complex cancer genomes, where a combination of tools is necessary to achieve optimal sensitivity and specificity [1]. Consequently, there is a need for a solution like Sarek, which is designed as an easy-to-install, community-maintained workflow that supports various data types (WGS, WES, gene panels) and operates effectively in secure environments without direct internet access [1].

## Technical Implementation Strategy

Sarek is a comprehensive workflow for variant detection and analysis of sequencing data from whole-genome sequencing (WGS), whole-exome sequencing (WES), and targeted panels, designed to handle both germline and somatic samples [2]. The workflow is built within the Nextflow pipeline framework as part of the nf-core community effort, which ensures the creation of well-curated analysis pipelines [2]. To achieve reproducibility and ease of installation, Sarek utilizes Conda for managing dependencies, allowing the software to be installed and executed on any POSIX-compatible computer system [1]. For containerization, the workflow supports Singularity containers, which are preferred over Docker at high-performance computing centers due to security risks associated with Docker, particularly in environments handling sensitive personal data [1]. The implementation is noted for being clear and advanced, featuring parallelization and flexible installation options that make it user-friendly despite its complexity [2]. Regarding efficiency and resource usage, a full WGS analysis with 90x/90x read coverage is recommended to run on a node with a minimum of 16 cores, 128 GB of RAM, and at least 4 TB of available free storage [1]. The workflow includes extensive quality control metrics and variant calling for SNPs, indels, and structural variants, supported by a suite of integrated tools such as Manta, TIDDIT, GATK4 Mutect2, Freebayes, and ASCAT [1].

## Performance & Discussion

Sarek demonstrates high accuracy and efficiency in processing whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data, with performance validated against established benchmarks. In germline variant calling, the workflow achieved a recall of 0.99 and precision of 0.94 for single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) when using the union of GATK4 HaplotypeCaller and Strelka2, with an F1-score of 0.96 [1]. For insertion/deletion variants (INDELs), the union approach yielded a recall of 0.93 and precision of 0.98, resulting in an F1-score of 0.96 [1]. The tool was benchmarked using the HG001 sample against the Genome In a Bottle gold standard dataset, confirming overall high accuracy [3]. Regarding resource efficiency, a run on a 90X/90X coverage medulloblastoma dataset on a 48-threaded node required a total of 1378 GB of storage for result files and 1790 CPU hours, with a wall clock time of 48 hours and 21 minutes [2]. The workflow is designed for reproducibility, including a test dataset and a suite of automated tests for Continuous Integration via GitHub Actions [2]. While Sarek does not provide novel algorithms itself, it integrates multiple established tools (such as Manta, ASCAT, and Control-FREEC) and allows users to combine results via union or intersection to balance sensitivity and precision [1][3]. The authors note that while germline variant accuracy is well-supported by benchmark data, comprehensive quantitative assessment for complex somatic variants is currently limited by a lack of robust benchmark datasets [3][4].

## Transparency Features

Transparency in sustainable data analysis, as described in the article, requires that all aspects of an analysis be fully accessible and traceable. First, the parameters, software versions, and any custom code used at each step must be openly available so that others can verify the methodological choices [1][2]. Second, the analysis code itself must be readable and well‑documented, enabling users to understand and modify the workflow if needed [3]. Third, the results produced by the workflow must allow a clear trace back to the specific parameters, code, and software components that generated them, ensuring that every output can be linked to its provenance [1][2]. Together, these features enable full transparency, allowing the scientific community to assess the validity of results and to reuse or adapt the analysis for new projects.

## Storage Strategies



## Cost‑Efficiency Strategies

Snakemake can partition a workflow’s directed acyclic graph (DAG) into subgraphs so that short‑running jobs are submitted together as a single cluster or cloud job, thereby reducing queue wait times and network I/O costs [1].  
The partitioning is performed by assigning rules to groups; Snakemake identifies connected subgraphs that share the same group and submits each such subgraph as a “group job” instead of submitting every job individually [1].  
Users can control the size of these partitions by specifying how many connected subgraphs should be spanned per group job, allowing the partition size to be tuned to the available computational platform [1].  
Resource usage for a group job is estimated by topologically sorting the jobs, summing resource demands per level, and taking the maximum across all levels (for runtime resources the maximum per level is taken and then summed over all levels) [1].  
Streaming is referenced as a cost‑efficiency strategy, but the source material does not provide further details on its implementation

## Comparison

The nf‑core framework is designed to optimize storage usage and cost‑efficiency by leveraging containerized workflows, efficient data caching, and cloud‑native resource management. In contrast, the Snakemake workflow system emphasizes robust scheduling capabilities—such as rule‑based dependency resolution, parallel execution, and dynamic resource allocation—and transparency features including detailed job logs, reproducible rule definitions, and clear provenance tracking. While nf‑core focuses on minimizing storage footprints and operational costs, Snakemake provides a transparent and flexible scheduling environment that facilitates reproducible research and efficient resource utilization.

## Job Scheduling Approach

Here is a summary of the job scheduling approach:

 Snakemake uses a job scheduling algorithm that partitions the workflow into three sections: finished jobs, scheduled but not finished yet, and unscheduled jobs. The goal is to optimize the scheduling process by minimizing the number of temporary files generated during execution [2]. The algorithm ensures that jobs are executed in an order that minimizes the amount of disk space required for temporary files.

[1] 02_snakemake.pdf, page 0: "Document: Sustainable data analysis with Snakemake | Authors: Kim Philipp Jablonski, Brice Letcher, Vanessa Sochat, Chri..."
items.question: Explain the technical approach Snakemake uses to optimize job scheduling and how it handles job submission overhead in cluster or cloud environments.
items.expected:
Scheduling: Snakemake solves the scheduling problem at the start of execution and again whenever a job finishes and new jobs become pending. The first releases used a greedy scheduler. The current implementation solves a mixed integer linear program (MILP) whenever there are free resources. The MILP optimizes four criteria in lexicographical order: (1) prefer jobs with high priority, (2) maximize the number of used cores (the extent of parallelization), (3) delete existing temporary files as soon as possible, and (4) reduce the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass. The order is enforced by multiplying each criterion sum by a value at least as high as the maximum the terms to its right can reach. Constraint (2) ensures the selection does not exceed the available amount of each resource.

Cluster and cloud: with middleware such as SLURM, PBS, LSF or Kubernetes, Snakemake does not need to govern all resources at a global level. Some resources are handled by the middleware, and constraint (2) can be dropped for them. Snakemake can pass the resource requirements to the middleware, which can use them to choose the best fitting machine. By default runtime, threads, memory and disk usage are local resources passed to the middleware; all other resources are global and are still governed by Snakemake via constraint (2). The number of jobs queued or running at a time is limited by the same kind of constraint.

Submission overhead: by default every job is submitted separately to the queuing system. For short-running jobs this can cause considerable overhead, as jobs wait in a queue, and may add delays or cost when accessing files from remote storage or network file systems. To minimize it, Snakemake can partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs by assigning rules to groups. Connected subgraphs with the same group are submitted together as a single cluster or cloud job (a group job) instead of each job separately. For each group, the number of connected subgraphs spanned per submission can be defined (one by default), so the partition size can be adjusted to the computational platform. A group job's resource usage is computed by sorting its jobs topologically, summing resource usage per level and taking the maximum over all levels. For runtime it is the other way round: the maximum per level, summed over all levels.

partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs

Sarek is a software tool that detects germline and somatic variants from whole-genome sequencing (WGS), whole-exome sequencing (WES), and gene panel data [1]. HPAI H5N1 in Canada (19_hpai_canada, a commentary)

Human risk factors:
- All severely affected human cases had direct exposure to poultry.

Animal-side risks:

MultiQC's approach to data presentation significantly assists researchers in identifying quality issues across large-scale projects through several key mechanisms:

1. **Consolidated Reporting**: MultiQC integrates quality control (QC) metrics from multiple bioinformatics tools and large sample sets into a single, unified report. This eliminates the need for manual compilation of per-sample reports, reducing errors and saving time. By centralizing data, researchers can more easily identify global trends, subtle biases, and batch effects that might otherwise be overlooked when switching between individual files [1][2].

2. **Interactive Visualizations**: The tool uses interactive data visualizations, such as resizable plots with click-and-drag zooming, to facilitate sample comparison. Researchers can use a toolbox to rename, hide, or highlight specific samples, making it easier to spot outliers or groups behaving irregularly. This functionality is particularly valuable in large-scale projects where identifying abnormal samples is critical [2][3][4].

3. **Scalability**: MultiQC is designed to handle large-scale projects efficiently. For reports with hundreds of samples, it automatically switches from interactive JavaScript plots to static images to maintain performance and file consistency. This ensures that the tool remains usable even when parsing data for thousands of samples within minutes, making it suitable for single-cell and population studies [3].

4. **Automated Data Parsing**: By automating the collection of metadata at the end of an analysis pipeline, MultiQC provides a central collection point for identifying failing samples and batch effects early in the data processing stage. This helps mitigate the risk of confounding factors affecting downstream analysis [4].

5. **Integration and Customization**: MultiQC can be extended with plugins to incorporate metadata from internal systems like LIMS, further assisting sequencing facilities in large-scale data collection and quality monitoring. Its extensible architecture allows for customization and integration into existing workflows, enhancing its utility in diverse research settings [4].

In summary, MultiQC's approach to data presentation—through consolidated reporting, interactive visualizations, scalability, automated data parsing, and integration capabilities—enables researchers to efficiently identify and address quality issues in large-scale projects.

[2] "MultiQC: a modular tool to analyse and summarise bioinformatics results" (2017)
[3] "MultiQC: a modular tool to analyse and summarise bioinformatics results" (2017)
[4] "MultiQC: a modular tool to analyse and summarise bioinformatics results" (2017)

### Software and Phylogenetic Methods

The analysis of African swine fever virus (ASFV) sequences utilized several software packages and phylogenetic methods. Raw sequences were assembled and edited using Vector NTI 11.5 software [1]. Multiple sequence alignments were conducted with MUSCLE as implemented in MEGA software version 7 [1].

For phylogenetic analysis, different methods were applied depending on the gene target:
- **p72 gene:** A Neighbor-Joining (NJ) tree was produced using the Maximum Composite Likelihood method. The dataset included 93 nucleotide sequences (398 characters), and the data were re-sampled 1,000 times using the bootstrap method [1][8].
- **p54 gene:** A Minimum Evolution tree was constructed using the p-distance substitution model and the Close-Neighbor-Interchange (CNI) algorithm. The initial tree was generated via the Neighbor-joining algorithm. All positions with less than 95% site coverage were removed from the analysis, and the robustness was assessed with 1,000 bootstrap replicates [8].
- **CD2v partial amino acid sequences:** A maximum‐likelihood (ML) tree was constructed applying the predetermined CpREV + G model. This analysis also utilized 1,000 bootstrap replicates to assess tree topology robustness [8].

Additionally, the CVR nucleotide sequences were translated into amino acids, and the deduced amino acid tetramers were matched with previously reported codes for classification [11].

### Variation in the Central Variable Region (CVR)

The Central Variable Region (CVR) within the B602L gene was analyzed to identify variations in ASFV isolates from 2018 outbreaks in Burkina Faso. The CVR is defined by amino acid tandem repeats [6]. The study identified four distinct variants of the tetrameric repeat sequence (TRS) based on the number of tandem repeats: 12, 23, 24, and 32 [9][12]. The specific amino acid tetramer sequences for these variants were documented as follows:
- **12 TRS Variant:** (ABNAAACBNAFA), found in the index outbreak at Saaba as well as in Nioko II and Kossodo [9][10].
- **23 TRS Variant:** (ABNAAA AAA ACA AAA AACBNAFA), found in Kossodo and Tampouy [10][12].
- **24 TRS Variant:** (AAAABNABBNABBAABBNABNABA), identified as a unique profile found only at the Nioko II farm [10][12].
- **32 TRS Variant:** (ABNAAA AAC BNAAA AAC BNAAA AAA ACBNAFA), found in Kossodo and matching the isolates later collected in Tampouy [10][12].

Three of the four identified variants shared motifs that began with the tetramer "ABNAAA" and ended with "CBNAFA" [9]. The discovery of these four variants, alongside ten different variants identified in the country between 2007 and 2010, brings the total number of identified CVR variants in Burkina Faso to 14 [12].

### Sources
[1] 11_asf_burkina_faso.pdf

The choice of diagnostic method and skinfold thickness threshold significantly impacts the assessment of bovine tuberculosis (bTB) exposure, as demonstrated in the study conducted in Cameroon. Here’s a detailed breakdown of the findings:

### Impact of Diagnostic Method
The study compared two diagnostic methods: the **Simple Intradermal Tuberculin Test (SITT)** and the **Comparative Intradermal Tuberculin Test (CIDT)**. The CIDT is designed to differentiate between infections caused by *Mycobacterium bovis* and those caused by environmental mycobacteria, providing a more specific assessment. The study found that the CIDT yielded better results in the specific epidemiological and environmental context of Cameroon compared to the SITT [1].

### Impact of Skinfold Thickness Thresholds
The study evaluated the impact of different skinfold thickness thresholds on the detection of bTB:

1. **Standard WOAH Threshold (>4 mm):**
   - Using the 4 mm threshold, the CIDT identified an apparent prevalence of **1.8%** (3 positive reactions out of 160 cattle).
   - The SITT at this threshold yielded a lower prevalence of **0.6%** [1].

2. **Modified Threshold (>3 mm):**
   - When the threshold was lowered to 3 mm, the CIDT identified 11 positive reactions, increasing the apparent prevalence to **6.8%**.
   - The study concluded that the 3 mm threshold significantly increased the sensitivity of bTB detection compared to the 4 mm threshold [1].

3. **Modified Threshold (>2 mm):**
   - The discussion noted that studies in similar contexts (e.g., Ethiopia) found the "best diagnostic characteristics" when using a threshold strictly >2 mm, suggesting that even lower thresholds might be more suitable for local conditions in Cameroon to avoid underestimating the disease [1].

### Study Conclusions on Exposure Assessment
- The apparent prevalence values were significantly higher at the ≥3 mm threshold than at ≥4 mm.
- The study recommends adopting a **3 mm threshold** for the CIDT to ensure more efficient detection and to better reflect the "enzootic nature" of the disease in the region.
- The authors argue that the 4 mm WOAH standard may lead to under-detection in Cameroon and suggest that defining a threshold value most suitable to the specific environmental and epidemiological context is crucial for accurate exposure assessment [1].

In summary, the choice of diagnostic method and skinfold thickness threshold significantly impacts the assessment of bTB exposure. The CIDT is more effective than the SITT, and lowering the threshold from 4 mm to 3 mm increases the sensitivity and apparent prevalence of bTB detection. The study recommends using a 3 mm threshold for the CIDT in Cameroon to improve the accuracy of bTB exposure assessment.

[1] 14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf

### Gaps in Translating Standardized, Large-Scale Genomic Workflows for Rapid, Localized Veterinary Outbreak Characterization

#### Infrastructure and Deployment Challenges
Standardized genomic workflows like **Sarek** and **nf-core** are designed for large-scale, secure environments and require POSIX-compatible systems (Linux/Mac OS X) and containerization (Docker/Singularity) for deployment [2][10]. While these workflows are optimized for efficiency (e.g., CRAM files, DeepVariant), their infrastructure needs may not align with rapid, localized veterinary settings, where resources and technical expertise are often limited [10][11]. Additionally, **Snakemake** workflows, while adaptable, require specialized knowledge (Unix, Python) and may not be easily deployable in low-resource environments [9].

#### Technical and Operational Gaps
1. **Benchmarking and Validation**
   - Large-scale workflows lack robust benchmark datasets for complex somatic variants, relying instead on individual tool validations [1]. This poses a challenge for veterinary outbreaks, where rapid, accurate characterization is critical but may lack validated reference standards.

2. **Data Footprint and Computational Efficiency**
   - While workflows like **Sarek** reduce storage needs (e.g., CRAM files), localized veterinary settings may still face constraints in data transfer and processing speed, delaying outbreak response [10][11].

3. **Modularity and Adaptability**
   - **Snakemake’s** modular approach allows for flexibility, but the need for external repositories and specialized knowledge may hinder rapid deployment in field settings [8][9].

#### Veterinary-Specific Challenges
1. **Delayed Investigations**
   - In outbreaks like **African Swine Fever Virus (ASFV)** in Burkina Faso, genomic investigations began **two weeks after mortality onset**, highlighting delays in rapid response [1].

2. **Clinical Sign Variability**
   - For **Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI)**, mortality thresholds for notification vary by species (e.g., ducks vs. chickens), complicating early warning systems [5].

3. **Integration with Epidemiological Tools**
   - **Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus (FMDV)** control requires integrating molecular and epidemiological data, but standardized workflows may not account for the need to track pre-clinical transmission [8].

#### Portable Sequencing Needs
- The literature emphasizes **real-time PCR** for diagnostic confirmation (e.g., ASFV, LSDV, HPAI) but does not address the use of **portable sequencing (e.g., Nanopore/MinION)** for rapid, localized characterization [1][3][4]. This gap suggests a potential opportunity for adopting portable technologies to accelerate outbreak response.

#### Conclusion
The primary gaps in translating large-scale genomic workflows to rapid, localized veterinary outbreak characterization include:
- **Infrastructure mismatches** (resource-intensive workflows vs. limited field settings).
- **Lack of validated benchmarks** for veterinary pathogens.
- **Delays in investigation initiation** and **clinical sign variability** complicating early detection.
- **Underutilization of portable sequencing** despite its potential for rapid, on-site analysis.

These findings highlight the need for workflows optimized for speed, modularity, and low-resource environments to improve veterinary outbreak response.

1. Design target and setting. Sarek is built for germline and somatic (cancer) variant detection, at core facilities and in research groups. nf-core/sarek 3 targets large multi-site cohorts on high-performance clusters and cloud setups. Sarek's default reference is human GRCh38.

2. References. nf-core/sarek 3 can process non-model organisms, but references are provided mainly for human and mouse. For non-supported species they must be generated, the pipeline applies only where a reference genome exists, and easier custom-reference handling is left to future releases.

3. Resources and turnaround. A full 90x/90x WGS run needs at least 16 cores, 128 GB RAM and 4 TB of storage. It took 48 hours and 21 minutes (about 48 hours). In version 3.1.1, one normal sample took 12h4m and cost $20.82. Storage can be a bottleneck on the available compute system.

4. Testing and expertise. The Sarek paper reported that no systematic testing had yet been performed on WES or gene-panel data; nf-core/sarek 3 later benchmarked its somatic callers on three tumor-normal paired WES datasets, and neither paper reports a benchmark on gene-panel data. Careful parameter tuning, variant filtering and qualitative assessment by the user remain important. The Sarek authors say there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

Sequencing was done by LGC Genomics (Berlin) and assembly used Vector NTI 11.5. Nineteen p72 and p54, fourteen CD2v and twenty B602L sequences were obtained. The authors call for continued rapid diagnostics and analysis. Whether their approach suits other serogroups and genotypes, and how the variants emerged, remain open.

6. HPAI in Canada. The animal health sector is heavily engaged in outbreak management. Wildlife surveillance has limited scope and is biased towards severely infected or dead animals. The authors call for quick identification of strains with enhanced mammalian fitness, stronger laboratory capacity and coordination between the human and animal health sectors. They also name major gaps in understanding how climate disruption affects HPAI.

## STAR Mapping Speed and Comparison to Other Aligners

STAR achieves a mapping speed of over 200 million 2 x 76 bp paired-end reads per hour on a 12-core server [1]. More specifically, benchmarks demonstrate a speed of 550 million 2 x 76 bp paired-end reads per hour using 12 threads [1]. 

### Comparison to Other Aligners

STAR is significantly faster than other RNA-seq aligners. In benchmarks using a 12-core server, STAR outperformed TopHat2 by a factor of 450, mapping 549.9 million read pairs per hour compared to TopHat2’s 10.1 million [1]. Here’s a detailed comparison of mapping speeds (in millions of read pairs per hour) using 12 threads:

*   **STAR:** 549.9 [1]
*   **TopHat2:** 10.1 [1]
*   **RUM:** 7.6 [1]
*   **MapSplice:** 3.1 [1]
*   **GSNAP:** 2.8 [1]

STAR’s speed is attributed to its use of uncompressed suffix arrays and a sequential maximum mappable seed (MMP) search algorithm [1]. While it requires approximately 27–28 GB of RAM for the human genome, a sparse suffix array option reduces RAM usage to 16 GB with a slight decrease in speed (approximately 25%) [1]. 

It's worth noting that STAR exhibits near-linear scaling with the number of threads, losing only about 10% of per-thread mapping speed when increasing from 6 to 12 threads [1].
items.question: What is the reported mapping speed of STAR when using a 12-core server for 2 x 76 bp paired-end reads, and how does this compare to other aligners?
items.expected: On a 12-core server (two 6-core Intel Xeon CPUs, 12 threads), STAR aligns 550 million 2 x 76 paired-end reads per hour to the human genome (549.9 million read pairs/hour in Table 1), i.e. 45 million paired reads per hour per processor. It surpasses all other existing RNA-seq aligners by a factor of 50 (the Discussion's figure; the Abstract and Results text layer prints "450", a mis-encoded ">50"), outperforming the second fastest mapper, TopHat2, which reaches 10.1 million read pairs/hour at 12 threads (RUM 7.6, MapSplice 3.1, GSNAP 2.8).

## How LSDV Clinical Impact Differs by Spread vs. Lethality

Lumpy Skin Disease Virus (LSDV) demonstrates a clear distinction between its ability to spread within a herd (morbidity) and its capacity to cause death (lethality). While LSDV exhibits a relatively high rate of spread, its overall lethality remains comparatively low. 

**Spread (Morbidity):** The overall morbidity rate in the 2022 Nepal outbreak was 28.02% [1]. This means nearly a third of the animals examined contracted the disease. Morbidity rates varied significantly by animal category, with dry cattle experiencing the highest rate (47.62%) followed by cattle calves (33.33%) and heifers (32.73%) [2]. Buffalo were much less susceptible, with morbidity rates remaining below 4.55% [3].  Comparatively, Nepal’s morbidity rate was similar to those reported in Thailand (31%) and Jordan (35.1%), but higher than rates in Bangladesh (21%), Saudi Arabia (6%), and India (7.1%) [1]. The primary mode of spread is through mechanical transmission via arthropod vectors like mosquitoes and flies [4, 10]. Proximity to infected animals on neighboring farms is a significant risk factor for outbreaks [4, 11].

**Lethality (Mortality):** The overall mortality rate in the Nepal outbreak was 3.06% [1]. However, lethality varied by animal category. Cattle heifers had the highest mortality rate (5.09%) and case fatality rate (15.56%), followed by milking cattle (4.04% mortality, 12.95% case fatality) [2, 3, 7]. Importantly, no deaths were recorded in any category of buffalo or male cattle [3]. The Nepal mortality rate was higher than those reported in Thailand (0.9%), Jordan (1.3%), and India, where some districts reported no mortality [1].

In summary, LSDV spreads readily, particularly among cattle, but typically doesn’t result in high death rates overall. However, certain groups, like heifers, are more vulnerable to fatal outcomes. The disease is primarily spread by insect vectors, and the presence of infection on neighboring farms is a key driver of outbreaks [1, 4, 11].

The available research focuses primarily on the capabilities of MultiQC. Unfortunately, the provided documents do not contain information about SeqKit, nor do they detail data collection requirements for zoonotic disease studies specifically in Ethiopia and Cameroon. However, we can outline MultiQC’s data management capabilities and speculate on its general applicability to the challenges of zoonotic disease surveillance, given its features.

### MultiQC Data Management Capabilities

MultiQC is a command-line tool designed to summarize analysis results from multiple bioinformatics tools and large sample sets into a single, easily interpretable report [1, 2]. It manages data by recursively scanning directories for recognized log files and quality control (QC) reports [2, 3]. It currently supports parsing outputs from 22 common bioinformatics tools [3].  Parsed data is saved in formats suitable for downstream analysis, including YAML, JSON, and tab-delimited text [3]. 

The tool excels at visualization, generating self-contained HTML reports with interactive, resizable, and zoomable plots using the HighCharts JavaScript library [3]. To manage large datasets (thousands of samples), MultiQC can switch to static image rendering to maintain consistent file sizes and browser responsiveness [3, 4].  Users can manipulate reports via a toolbox to rename, hide, or highlight samples, and export plots in publication-ready formats [3].  MultiQC is also extensible, allowing integration of custom modules and plugins, and even connection to Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS) for metadata insertion and database storage [3, 4].

### Potential Applicability to Zoonotic Disease Surveillance

While specific regional requirements aren’t available, the features of MultiQC suggest it would be valuable for large-scale disease surveillance in settings like Ethiopia and Cameroon in the following ways:

*   **Scalability for Population Studies:** MultiQC’s ability to parse data for thousands of samples within minutes [4] is crucial for national or international surveillance programs monitoring large populations.
*   **Identification of Outliers and Biases:** The tool’s visualization capabilities can help identify outliers and biases in data, which is essential for distinguishing true biological signals from technical artifacts in surveillance studies.
*   **Data Integration:** The ability to integrate with LIMS [4] could streamline data collection and management, linking field data with genomic analysis results.



It is important to reiterate that this analysis is limited by the lack of information regarding SeqKit and the specific data collection requirements in Ethiopia and Cameroon within the provided documents.

## Purpose and Performance of the Regularized Logarithm (rlog) Transformation

The regularized logarithm (rlog) transformation is designed to address heteroscedasticity in count data – specifically, to make the variance independent of the mean [1]. This is crucial for effective multivariate visualizations and analyses like clustering and principal component analysis, as it ensures variables have a comparable dynamic range [1]. The rlog transformation also accounts for variations in sequencing depth across samples using size factors [2]. Importantly, it’s intended for exploratory data analysis and visualization, not statistical inference for differential expression, which should utilize raw counts [1, 2].

### Variance Stabilization: rlog vs. Ordinary Log

The rlog transformation demonstrably outperforms a standard log transformation (logarithm of normalized counts plus a pseudocount) in terms of variance stabilization [3]. While an ordinary log transformation, calculated as  $f(K_{ij}) = \log_2(K_{ij}/s_j + 1)$, results in gene-wise standard deviations that *vary* across the range of mean counts [2, 3], the rlog transformation maintains a *relatively stable* variance across that same range [2, 3]. 

This stabilization is significant because it allows for the identification of more meaningful patterns in the data [2, 3]. For example, hierarchical clustering performed on a dataset (Hammer et al.) showed ambiguous results with ordinary log-transformed data, but successfully clustered samples by treatment and time when using rlog-transformed data [2, 3].

**Technical differences contributing to this performance:** The rlog achieves this stabilization by fitting a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) for each gene with a baseline expression and then computing shrunken log fold changes (LFCs) using an empirical Bayes procedure [1]. This shrinkage helps stabilize variance, though it can potentially alter the ordering of genes within a sample [1]. In contrast, the ordinary log relies on a simple pseudocount to address zero values, which is less effective at achieving consistent variance [2]. While both rlog and variance-stabilizing transformation (VST) are effective, rlog directly accounts for size factors, which is particularly important for datasets with large variations in sequencing depth [1].
items.question: What is the specific purpose of the regularized logarithm (rlog) transformation, and how does its performance compare to an ordinary log transformation in terms of variance stabilization?
items.expected: Purpose: the rlog transforms RNA-seq data to render them homoskedastic. On the original count scale, results would be dominated by highly expressed, highly variable genes. With logarithm-transformed data, undue weight goes to weakly expressed genes, which show exaggerated LFCs. The rlog thus facilitates multivariate visualization and ordinations such as clustering or principal component analysis, heat maps, and machine-learning techniques that require homoskedastic input data. It uses the shrinkage approach of DESeq2. For genes with high counts it behaves similarly to a log2 transformation, and for genes with low counts it shrinks together the values for different samples. This avoids the standard logarithm's spreading apart of data for genes with low counts. On the Hammer et al. dataset (Figure 5), the gene-wise standard deviation is variable across the range of the mean of counts under the ordinary logarithm with a pseudocount of 1, log2(Kij/sj + 1), while relatively stable using the rlog. ## How fastp’s Adapter Detection Differs Between Single-End and Paired-End Data

`fastp` employs distinct methodologies for adapter detection depending on whether the input data is single-end (SE) or paired-end (PE).

**Single-End (SE) Data:**

For SE data, `fastp` identifies adapters by assembling high-frequency read tails [1, 2]. It begins by calculating k-mers (with k=10) from the first 1 million reads. Sequences occurring with a frequency greater than 0.0001 are considered potential adapter seeds, with low-complexity sequences removed to avoid artifacts [1, 2]. These seeds are then sorted by frequency and extended using a tree-based algorithm to determine the complete adapter sequence [1, 2, 3, 4]. This algorithm utilizes a `build_nucleotide_tree()` function and identifies “dominant child” nodes (nucleotides with >90% dominance) to extend the seed forward to the read tail and then backward to complete the adapter sequence [1, 3, 4]. If a user provides a specific adapter sequence, automatic detection is disabled [1].

**Paired-End (PE) Data:**

In contrast, `fastp` primarily detects adapters in PE data by analyzing the overlap between read pairs [1, 2, 3]. Bases outside the detected overlapping region are considered adapter content [1, 2]. This overlap-analysis method, inherited from the AfterQC tool, is more sensitive than sequence-matching tools like Cutadapt or Trimmomatic, capable of trimming adapters with as few as one or two bases at the read tail [1, 2, 3]. User-provided adapter sequences are only used for sequence-matching trimming if a high-quality overlap isn’t detected [1].

**Key Differences Summarized:**

*   **SE:** Relies on *de novo* assembly of adapter sequences from read tails using a tree-based algorithm [1, 2, 3, 4].
*   **PE:** Relies on identifying adapter sequences as the non-overlapping portions of read pairs [1, 2, 3].

Both methodologies assume a single adapter type present at the read tails [3].
items.question: How does fastp's methodology for adapter detection differ between single-end and paired-end sequencing data?
items.expected: fastp uses different algorithms for the two data types. For single-end data, adapter sequences are detected by assembling the high-frequency read tails: it computes k-mers (k = 10) of the first 1 M reads, takes sequences with occurrence frequency >0.0001 as adapter seeds (low-complexity sequences removed), and extends them with a tree-based algorithm (forward extension to check validity, then backward extension to obtain the complete adapter), assuming only one adapter exists in the data and adapters exist only in read tails. For paired-end data, fastp finds the overlap of each pair (an algorithm derived from AfterQC) and considers the bases that fall out of the overlapped region as adapter content; this overlap analysis can trim adapters with even only one base in the tail. A user-given adapter sequence also behaves differently: for SE data it disables automatic detection; for PE data it is used for sequence-matching-based trimming only when fastp fails to detect a good overlap in the pair.

The DESeq2 framework utilizes Empirical Bayes shrinkage to handle the high uncertainty associated with low-count genes in both dispersion and fold change estimation. This approach is applied to improve the stability and reproducibility of results in high-throughput sequencing data, which often suffers from small sample sizes and high uncertainty [1], [3], [13].

In dispersion estimation, DESeq2 shares information across genes to address the high variability of dispersion estimates in experiments with few replicates [7], [15]. The process involves three steps: gene-wise MLEs, trend fitting, and shrinkage to MAP estimates [1], [7]. The "prior" for dispersion is assumed to follow a log-normal distribution centered around the fitted trend [10]. The strength of this shrinkage is automatically controlled by the width of the prior distribution and the degrees of freedom; as sample sizes increase, the shrinkage strength decreases [1], [7]. To avoid false positives, genes with extremely high gene-wise dispersion (more than two residual standard deviations above the curve) are identified as outliers and are not shrunken toward the prior [1], [2], [11].

In logarithmic fold change (LFC) estimation, DESeq2 overcomes the problem of exaggerated LFC estimates for low-count genes by shrinking LFC estimates toward zero [4], [31]. The shrinkage is strongest when the available information for a gene is low, such as when counts are low, dispersion is high, or there are few degrees of freedom [2], [4], [26]. Specifically, the shrinkage depends on the observed Fisher information; genes with flatter profile likelihoods (due to low means or high dispersion) see their MAP estimates pulled more strongly toward the zero-centered prior [5], [21]. This process effectively removes the problem of exaggerated LFCs for low-count genes, facilitating better gene ranking and visualization [5], [14], [16].

In addition to shrinkage, DESeq2 also employs outlier handling and robustness measures to ensure the stability and reliability of the results. Cook's distance is used as a diagnostic tool to identify individual observations that disproportionately influence the estimation of LFC and P-values [3]. For each gene, DESeq2 flags samples with a Cook's distance exceeding the 0.99 quantile of the $F(p, m - p)$ distribution, where $p$ is the number of model parameters and $m$ is the number of samples [1]. The handling of these flagged outliers depends on the number of replicates: small experiments with fewer than 7 replicates flag the entire gene and remove it from downstream analysis, while large experiments with 7 or more replicates replace outlier counts with an imputed value and re-estimate dispersion, LFCs, and P-values [4].

Overall, the Empirical Bayes shrinkage framework in DESeq2 provides a robust and reliable approach to handling the high uncertainty associated with low-count genes in both dispersion and fold change estimation.
items.question: How does the DESeq2 framework utilize Empirical Bayes shrinkage to handle the high uncertainty associated with low-count genes in both dispersion and fold change estimation?
items.expected:
Both shrinkage steps follow one principle: empirical Bayes priors set the amount of shrinkage from the amount of information the data carry for the estimated quantity.

Dispersion: with two or three replicates, the dispersion estimates for each gene are highly variable. DESeq2 assumes that genes of similar average expression strength have similar dispersion. It first gets gene-wise maximum-likelihood estimates, then fits a smooth curve against average expression strength. It shrinks the gene-wise estimates toward the values predicted by the curve, combining the likelihood with the trended prior to give maximum a posteriori (MAP) dispersion estimates. The strength of shrinkage depends on how close true dispersion values tend to be to the fit, and on the degrees of freedom. It decreases as the sample size increases. The width of the prior is estimated from the data, and the fitted curve aids estimation in less information-rich settings. Estimates below the curve are raised, which helps avoid false positives from underestimated dispersion. A gene-wise estimate more than 2 residual standard deviations above the curve is used instead of the shrunken one. On low counts, the paper says that when μ ≲1/α the observed data provide little information on α, so the sampling variance of the estimator is large. Overestimating α in that low-count range has little effect on inference, because the Poisson component dominates the variance there.

Fold change: LFC estimates have strong variance for genes with low read count, because ratios are noisier when counts are low. DESeq2 fits ordinary GLMs to get maximum-likelihood estimates (MLEs) of the LFCs, then fits a zero-centered normal distribution to the MLEs over all genes. That distribution is the prior in a second round of GLM fits, and the MAP estimates are kept as the final LFCs. Shrinkage toward zero is stronger when a gene has little information, because counts are low, dispersion is high or there are few degrees of freedom. The amount of information is indicated by the observed Fisher information, not simply by the mean count. Such genes have flatter profile likelihoods, so the zero-centered prior pulls the high-uncertainty MLE closer to zero. This removes the problem of exaggerated LFCs for low counts. For genes with less than one read per sample on average, LFCs hardly deviate from zero. The paper describes this as a bias-variance trade-off: lower variance in exchange for a bias toward zero. As the degrees of freedom increase, the shrunken estimates converge to the unshrunken estimates.

What are the common clinical presentations and relative frequency of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b infections when comparing mammals to humans?

The clinical presentations and frequency of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b infections differ significantly between mammals and humans. In mammals, the disease is primarily characterized by severe neurological signs, with most infected animals dying from encephalitis or meningoencephalitis (Source: [2]). The scale of the outbreak is massive, with thousands of animals affected, including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, sea lions, and dolphins (Source: [3]).

In contrast, human infections are extremely rare, with fewer than 10 cases identified globally as of the report date (Source: [1]). The majority of human cases have been mild or asymptomatic, although severe cases can occur, presenting as acute febrile respiratory disease or unexplained neurological disease (Source: [1]).

The relative frequency and scale of outbreaks also differ between mammals and humans. While mammalian infections have resulted in significant die-offs and culling of thousands of animals, human infections remain extremely rare (Source: [1]).

In terms of disease severity, mammalian infections are characterized by high severity and high mortality, with the virus frequently reaching the brain and mammalian-adapted mutations detected in the brains of various carnivores (Source: [2]). Human infections, on the other hand, are generally low severity, although the potential for high virulence exists (Source: [1]).

Anthropogenic factors, such as animal management and vaccination distribution, play a crucial role in creating patterns of disease persistence in regions attempting control of transboundary pathogens. Specifically, vaccination distribution and spatial heterogeneity significantly influence the effectiveness of disease control programs. Heterogeneous vaccination coverage, characterized by pockets of low coverage or "spatial gaps," can lead to continued disease circulation even when average district-level coverage appears sufficient [2], [9], [10]. Conversely, when spatial heterogeneity is reduced through consistent district-wide campaigns, disease incidence can decline to low levels [2], [6].

The spatial distribution of susceptibility is a critical factor; for the same average vaccination coverage, increased heterogeneity among villages can lead to higher focal incidence [2]. This occurs because effective susceptibility is higher when unvaccinated dogs are clustered rather than distributed evenly [30], [64]. Furthermore, high population connectivity means that disease incidence in a specific village depends heavily on recent incidence in neighboring villages and the wider district [2], [14], [64]. High coverage in one area has limited impact if surrounding populations remain poorly vaccinated [14].

Animal management practices, such as the management of the wildlife-livestock interface, surveillance of both domestic ungulates and susceptible wildlife populations, and the management of vaccination protocols, also influence the transmission and control of diseases like foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) and Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) [1]. The implementation of biosecurity measures, such as vector control and movement management, is critical for preventing the spread of diseases like LSD [1].

Anthropogenic factors, including animal trade, human-mediated movement, and social behaviors, are significant drivers of disease transmission and persistence. The purchase and sale of livestock in markets is a recurring risk factor across multiple diseases, and the physical movement of animals by humans facilitates the spread of pathogens [2], [4], [5], [8], [9].

In conclusion, anthropogenic factors, such as animal management and vaccination distribution, create patterns of disease persistence in regions attempting control of transboundary pathogens. Vaccination distribution and spatial heterogeneity are critical factors in determining the effectiveness of disease control programs, while animal management practices and anthropogenic factors like animal trade and human-mediated movement also play significant roles in the transmission and persistence of diseases.

Outbreaks peak in the dry season, which cited studies attribute to animal movement in search of resources.
- LSD review: large-scale animal transfers from East Africa spread the disease to Syria, Iran and Iraq. Larger farms with intensive housing and shared feeding and watering facilities can contribute to transmission.
- Rabies in Serengeti: incursions in the district centre likely result from human-mediated transport.

(2) Uneven or insufficient vaccination.
- Rabies in Serengeti: campaigns ran less consistently away from the National Park, depending on local government resources, and only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target. Mean coverage over the district was relatively low, but the paper concludes that once heterogeneity was addressed, rabies was controlled nonetheless. Outbreaks followed multi-year periods when clusters of villages remained unvaccinated. At the same mean coverage, more heterogeneous coverage raised incidence (1.4 times for a 30%/50% split against a uniform 40%). Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell below 0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually. Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district then became a major source of residual transmission, reaching 50% of cases in 2022.
- PPR in Borena: there were 53 outbreaks from 2018 to 2022. 10,000 vaccine doses were deployed for an at-risk population of 397,189, and herd immunity was 68.8%, below the 80% FAO-WOAH threshold. The paper gives inadequate cold chain management, poor vaccine handling and distribution practices as possible causes. Outbreaks were concentrated in the hard-to-reach districts of Arero and Dhas, which risk becoming persistent focal points.
- LSD in Nepal: coverage of more than 80% is needed. The LSD review describes ring vaccination within a 5-km radius in border areas, and calls vaccination the singular means to prevent recurrence.

Moving and acquiring animals introduces and spreads these pathogens. In Nepal, LSD likely entered with animals moved from the Indian border area, then spread between farms [3, 4, 5, 7]. Importing animals, sharing feed and water, and herd size were linked to outbreaks only in univariable analysis [0, 6]. In Borena, seasonal cross-border livestock movement and uncontrolled animal movement may contribute to PPR spread, and purchased and gifted animals were more likely to test positive than animals born within the flocks [21, 22, 23]. Outbreaks there peak in the dry season, which cited studies attribute to animal movement in search of resources [29, 30]. The LSD review links spread to Syria, Iran and Iraq to large-scale animal transfers, and links transmission to larger farms with shared feeding and watering facilities [34, 35, 36, 37]. In Serengeti, rabies incursions in the district centre likely result from human-mediated transport [17].

Where vaccination is absent, insufficient or uneven, disease persists. In Nepal, LSD outbreaks recurred over 3 years while animals were not yet vaccinated, and the authors call for coverage of more than 80% [1, 2, 8]. In Serengeti, campaigns depended on local government resources, and only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target [12, 13], but the paper concludes that low mean coverage did not prevent control: once heterogeneity was addressed, rabies was controlled nonetheless [19]. Outbreaks followed multi-year periods when clusters of villages remained unvaccinated, and at the same mean coverage heterogeneity raised incidence (1.4 times in one modelled example) [9, 14, 15, 16]. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell below 0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually [10, 19]. Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district then became a major source of residual transmission (50% of cases in 2022), interacting with heterogeneous vaccination [11, 18, 19]. In Borena, 53 outbreaks in 2018 to 2022 coincided with 10,000 doses for 397,189 at-risk animals and 68.8% herd immunity, below the 80% threshold [20, 24, 25, 27, 28]. The paper attributes the shortfall to cold-chain, handling and distribution problems [26], and inaccessible districts with disproportionate outbreaks risk becoming persistent focal points [31, 32, 33]. The LSD review names movement management or limitations, quarantine and vaccination (including ring vaccination in border areas) as control measures, and vaccination as the singular means to prevent recurrence [38, 39, 40, 41].

In the context of scaling large-scale genomic analyses, the parallelization strategies of the nf-core framework differ from the job scheduling approach of Snakemake.

Snakemake manages job scheduling by partitioning a workflow's Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) into three categories: finished jobs, scheduled jobs that are not yet finished, and pending jobs that are ready for scheduling [6]. To determine which subset of pending jobs to execute, Snakemake utilizes a Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP) solver, which replaced an earlier greedy scheduling approach [12][16]. This MILP solver optimizes four criteria in a specific hierarchical (lexicographical) order: first, it prioritizes jobs with high priority; second, it maximizes parallelization by using as many CPU cores as possible; third, it attempts to delete temporary output files as quickly as possible; and fourth, it aims to reduce the lifetime of temporary files that cannot yet be deleted [15].

On the other hand, the nf-core framework does not provide information on its specific scheduling strategies. The provided document chunks do not mention nf-core, and the comparison is limited to Nextflow, which is categorized in the same functional niche as Snakemake: workflow management systems that use a Domain Specific Language (DSL) implemented as an extension of a generic programming language [1]. While Nextflow's "DSL 2.0" provides dynamic composition of workflows—a feature Snakemake addresses via its own module system—the provided text does not offer a direct comparison of their internal parallelization or scheduling strategies [1][2].

In summary, Snakemake's job scheduling and parallelization strategy rely on a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver, which optimizes four criteria in a specific hierarchical order. In contrast, the nf-core framework does not provide information on its specific scheduling strategies, and the comparison is limited to Nextflow, which is categorized in the same functional niche as Snakemake.

items.question: In the context of scaling large-scale genomic analyses, how do the parallelization strategies of the nf-core framework differ from the job scheduling approach of Snakemake?
items.expected:
nf-core/sarek, a Nextflow pipeline from nf-core, gets its parallelism by splitting the data. The FastQ files are split into shards with fastP and mapped in parallel. Mapping runtime plateaus at 12 shards, with the median runtime reduced to 37%. Genomic regions are processed in parallel after duplicate marking, and small regions are grouped to reduce the number of jobs. Scatter/gather across genomic regions is used for BQSR and variant calling, and the variant calling tools all run in parallel. Interval-group parallelization has clear limits: there is no further benefit beyond 21 interval groups. Job execution is left to Nextflow, which runs on several cloud vendors and common HPC schedulers. Splitting runs as a dedicated process, so it gets regular job submission with resource assignment, automatic retries and resume.

Snakemake does the job scheduling itself. At the start of execution, and whenever a job finishes and new jobs become pending, it selects the subset of jobs to run without exceeding resources such as hard drive space, I/O capacity and CPU cores. It does this by solving a mixed integer linear program (MILP), which replaced the greedy scheduler of its first releases. Four criteria are applied in lexicographical order: job priority first, then the number of used cores (the extent of parallelization), then deleting temporary files as soon as possible, then reducing the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass. By default all jobs have the same priority, so the MILP maximizes used cores while removing as many temporary files as possible. On a cluster or cloud, Snakemake passes resource requirements to the middleware. By default it submits each job separately, but it can partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs submitted together as a single cluster or cloud job. Scaling to a platform only requires changing command line parameters.

nf-core/sarek parallelizes by splitting the data inside the pipeline. It shards FastQ files with fastP and maps them in parallel, with runtime gains plateauing at 12 shards [0, 1, 2]. It processes genomic regions in parallel, grouping small ones to reduce job count, with scatter/gather for BQSR and variant calling [3, 4, 5, 6], and it runs the variant callers in parallel [7]. Interval-group parallelization gives no further benefit beyond 21 interval groups [8, 9]. Job execution is handed to Nextflow and the cloud vendors or HPC schedulers beneath it, and splitting runs as regular job submission with resources, retries and resume [10, 11]. Snakemake instead solves scheduling in its own engine. Each time jobs become pending, it selects which ones to run within resource limits by solving a MILP, which replaced an earlier greedy scheduler [14, 15, 16, 17]. The MILP ranks four criteria: priority, then used cores (parallelization), then temporary file deletion, then the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass, and by default maximizes used cores while removing temporary files [18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. On clusters and clouds it passes resource requirements to the middleware [25]. It submits jobs separately by default but can partition the DAG into subgraphs submitted as one job [26, 27]. Scaling to another platform only changes command line parameters [12, 13].
concepts: maximize the number of used cores

How does the implementation of Cutadapt balance the trade-off between user accessibility and computational efficiency?

Cutadapt balances the trade-off between user accessibility and computational efficiency by combining a high-level programming interface with optimized low-level processing. The program is primarily written in Python to ensure ease of use and flexibility, while the core alignment algorithm is implemented in C as a Python extension module to maximize speed [1][2]. This hybrid implementation allows for the creation of a "user-friendly" command-line tool that is easier to maintain and update with new features in response to user requests [1][4].

From a computational perspective, the adapter trimming process has a theoretical complexity of O(nk), where n is the total number of characters in all reads and k is the sum of the adapter lengths [4]. In practice, the software is efficient enough to process approximately 1 million 35 bp reads per minute on a single 2.66 GHz Intel Core 2 processor core [4]. Notably, the developers found that the actual time spent on alignment is often surpassed by the time required to read and parse input files [4].

User accessibility is a core design feature. Cutadapt is a standalone, user-friendly command-line tool that does not require users to write their own programs, unlike alternative libraries such as HTSeq or Biostrings [1]. It supports a wide range of input and output formats, including FASTA, FASTQ, and SOLiD (.csfasta/.qual) files [1][2]. It also features automatic detection of gzip-compressed files [2]. Accessibility is further enhanced by its cross-platform compatibility (Linux, Windows, and Mac OS X) and the provision of built-in documentation via the `--help` command [2][5].

In conclusion, Cutadapt's implementation balances the trade-off between user accessibility and computational efficiency by combining a high-level programming interface with optimized low-level processing, resulting in a user-friendly command-line tool that is highly portable and performs efficiently.

items.question: Compare the diagnostic methodologies and biological markers used to determine the prevalence of bovine tuberculosis (bTB) and Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) as described in studies from Cameroon and Ethiopia.
items.expected:
Cameroon (bTB): 160 live cattle were tested with the comparative intradermal tuberculin test (CIDT) and the simple intradermal tuberculin test (SITT), as described in the WOAH Manual. The initial skin thickness was measured, and then bovine PPD (AN5 strain, 20,000 IU/mL) and avian PPD (D4 ER strain, 25,000 IU/mL) were injected intradermally in the cervical region. Results were read 72 h later. The marker is the variation in skinfold thickness with bovine tuberculin (DB) and with avian tuberculin (DA). Under the WOAH grid, DB >2 mm with DB–DA >4 mm is positive, 1–4 mm inconclusive and <1 mm negative. SITT is positive at >4 mm. A 3 mm threshold was also applied. CIDT at 3 mm found 11 positives (6.8%, 95% CI 4.35%–9.41%), and the 3 mm threshold increased detection sensitivity compared with the WOAH 4 mm threshold. At 4 mm the paper is inconsistent. Table-2 and the Results give SITT 1.8% (3/160) and CIDT 0.6% (1 positive in Table-2, "three" in the text). The abstract gives CIDT 1.8% and simple IDT 0.6%. Ethiopia (PPR): 384 serum samples from sheep and goats were obtained from jugular blood. They were tested for PPRV antibodies by competition ELISA (ID Screen PPR Competition ELISA, ID.vet; sensitivity 94.5%, specificity 99.4%). ODs were read at 450 nm and expressed as S/N%: ≤50% positive, 50%–60% doubtful, >60% negative. Seroprevalence was 32.1% in nonvaccinated, 68.8% in vaccinated (seroconversion) and 45.5% in animals of unknown vaccination status.

The Cameroon bTB study tested 160 live cattle with the comparative intradermal tuberculin test under the WOAH Manual, and also with the simple intradermal test [0, 1, 6]. It measured initial skin thickness, injected bovine and avian PPD intradermally in the neck and read the result 72 h later [2, 3, 4]. Its marker was the variation in skinfold thickness to bovine versus avian tuberculin, against mm cut-offs (DB–DA >4 mm positive for CIDT, >4 mm for SITT), with a 3 mm threshold also applied [5, 9]. CIDT at 3 mm gave 6.8% (11/160) [11, 13, 14]. At 4 mm the values 1.8% and 0.6% are assigned to SITT and CIDT differently in the abstract and in the Results and Table-2 [7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14]. The 3 mm threshold increased sensitivity [15]. The Ethiopia PPR study instead used serology: 384 sheep and goat sera, separated from jugular blood, were tested for PPRV antibodies by competition ELISA [16, 17, 18]. The ID Screen kit had 94.5% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity [19]. OD at 450 nm was expressed as S/N%, with ≤50% positive, >60% negative and 50%–60% doubtful [20, 21, 22]. Seroprevalence was 32.1% nonvaccinated, 68.8% vaccinated and 45.5% unknown status [23, 24, 25]. So the bTB study reads a skin reaction to tuberculin in live cattle, and the PPR study measures antibodies in serum [5, 16].
