## Summary

STAR (Spliced Transcripts Alignment to a Reference) is an ultrafast, universal RNA-seq aligner designed to address key limitations of existing tools—namely, low mapping speed, reduced accuracy, read-length constraints, and alignment biases [7]. Its core algorithm uses a novel two-step approach: first, it performs a sequential search for Maximal Mappable Prefixes (MMPs) using uncompressed suffix arrays (SAs), enabling rapid detection of splice junctions without prior knowledge of their locations or the need for preliminary contiguous alignment [1][5]. The MMP search is implemented via binary search on uncompressed SAs (Manber and Myers, 1993), yielding logarithmic scaling of search time with genome size and allowing efficient identification of all distinct exact genomic matches for each MMP, which improves alignment of multimapping reads [1]. The sequential MMP search is applied only to unmapped portions of the read, distinguishing STAR from tools like Mummer and MAUVE and enabling precise detection of splice junctions—superior to arbitrary split-read methods [5].  

When the MMP search cannot extend across the full read due to mismatches, indels, or splice junctions, STAR uses the identified MMPs as anchors to extend alignments, and if extension fails, it can detect artifacts such as poly-A tails, adapter sequences, or low-quality ends [1]. The search is performed in both forward and reverse directions and can start from user-defined points, enhancing sensitivity for reads with end errors or high sequencing error rates [1]. After seed detection, STAR performs clustering, stitching, and scoring using a local alignment scoring scheme with user-defined penalties, selecting the highest-scoring alignment (or reporting all alignments within a user-defined score range for multimappers) [2]. This enables detection of chimeric alignments—including inter-mate, intra-mate, or fusion transcripts (e.g., BCR-ABL in K562 cells)—even when junctions lie in unsequenced regions [2].  

STAR achieves exceptional speed: 550 million 2×76 bp paired-end reads per hour on a 12-thread server (450× faster than TopHat2), trading RAM usage (~27 GB for human genome) for performance [7]. It supports sparse SAs to reduce RAM to ~516 GB (at ~25% speed cost) [3]. STAR’s algorithm is extensible to long reads (0.5–5 kb), matching or exceeding BLAT’s accuracy while being >100× faster [3], and is compatible with emerging long-read platforms (e.g., Oxford Nanopore) [3]. In benchmarking, STAR shows high precision in novel junction detection: experimental validation of 1,960 novel intergenic splice junctions via Roche 454 sequencing yielded 80–90% success rates [7]. On real data, STAR achieves the lowest pseudo-false-positive rate among tested aligners while maintaining high pseudo-sensitivity [4]. STAR is implemented in C++ as open-source (GPLv3), available at http://code.google.com/p/rna-star/ [7].

## Summary

Sarek is a portable, reproducible, community-maintained bioinformatics workflow for detecting germline and somatic variants from next-generation sequencing (NGS) data, including whole-genome sequencing (WGS), whole-exome sequencing (WES), and targeted gene panels [1][4][5]. Built using the Nextflow domain-specific language, Sarek implements a philosophy of narrow, independent workflows to simplify maintenance at sequencing core facilities and enable easy deployment and modification by individual research groups [1]. It leverages state-of-the-art tools for read mapping, variant calling, annotation, and quality control, and supports installation via Docker, Singularity, or Conda environments, ensuring reproducibility and portability across POSIX-compatible systems—including high-performance computing (HPC) clusters and cloud environments—even in offline or secure data settings [4][6]. For 90×/90× WGS data, Sarek completes analysis in approximately 48 hours; for WES, it takes a few hours; and for gene panels, it operates within minutes (based on in-house, unpublished data) [1].  

Sarek outputs annotated variant call format (VCF) files, copy number variation (CNV) reports, and comprehensive quality metrics for both germline and cancer samples [1]. While it supports multiple variant callers (e.g., FreeBayes is optionally included [6]), it reports variants from all callers used and leaves the decision of how to combine results to the user, acknowledging that optimal sensitivity/specificity trade-offs vary by project [3]. The workflow is designed to minimize installation and management overhead—critical given the high labor and maintenance costs associated with complex NGS pipelines [2][5]—and includes robust error handling: Nextflow reports failed processes and error codes, and Sarek supports resuming failed jobs from the point of failure [3].  

Benchmarking showed that somatic single-nucleotide variant and indel calls from Sarek align well with a gold standard callset; however, no benchmark data was available for more complex somatic variants, and germline variant accuracy was not evaluated [3][7]. Its design prioritizes usability and transparency over unique functionality, with differences from other workflows lying primarily in practical deployment rather than exclusive features [3]. Sarek ensures reproducibility and portability by implementing its workflow in Nextflow, a domain-specific workflow language designed for bioinformatics applications [9]. Nextflow provides transparent, easy-to-read code that supports reproducible execution across diverse compute environments—including high-performance computing (HPC) clusters (e.g., Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF) and cloud platforms (e.g., AWS, Google Cloud)—with native support for AWS Batch [9]. ## Summary

This study analyzed clinical manifestations of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1, H5N8, and H5N6 outbreaks in the Netherlands between 2014 and 2022 across different poultry types (layer-type, meat-type, and ducks) and age groups (juvenile vs. adult) [7]. Outbreaks in ducks decreased from 2014–2018 to 2020–2022, while those in meat-type poultry increased during the same period [7]. Adult duck (breeder) and juvenile chicken (broiler and laying pullet) farms were not diagnosed before 2020 [7].  

Neurological and locomotor signs were frequently observed in ducks and juvenile poultry (both chickens and ducks), while mucosal membrane and skin signs—including cyanosis and hemorrhagic conjunctiva—were more common in chickens (both layer- and meat-type) than in ducks [7][10]. Respiratory signs were more frequently reported in chickens, especially meat-type poultry, than in ducks [4]. Reproductive tract signs, including decreased egg production, were observed in layer-type poultry and in all five breeder duck flocks studied [4][10]. Diarrhea occurred more often in adult chickens and juvenile ducks [10].  

Mortality trends varied by poultry type: in chickens, mortality increased exponentially within four days before notification, whereas in ducks and meat-type poultry, mortality showed a more fluctuating trend with multiple peaks [6][7]. The mortality ratio (MR), defined as daily mortality relative to the previous week’s average, exceeded 3 less frequently in ducks than in chickens [7]. For ducks, policy thresholds were adjusted to include MR > 3, or 0.15% daily mortality for two consecutive days combined with a 5% feed intake reduction [1]. For broiler chickens, a proposed daily mortality threshold of >0.17% (after the first week of production) was estimated to reduce reporting delays by 5 days, compared to 0.13% for layers and 0.3% for ducks [1].

## Evolution of Efficiency

The corpus illustrates a clear evolution in bioinformatics tool development—from localized, single-tool performance optimization to integrated, systemic efficiency across the entire computational workflow stack. Early efforts focused on optimizing individual tools for speed and quality, such as fastp, which was designed as an ultra-fast all-in-one FASTQ preprocessor and shown to be significantly faster than competitors like FASTQC, Cutadapt, Trimmomatic, SOAPnuke, and AfterQC while maintaining or improving data quality [1]. For instance, fastp processes paired-end data ~2.7× faster than umis and ~6.1× faster than UMI-tools, and it has been adopted by the bcbio-nextgen pipeline framework [2]. Similarly, STAR emerged as an ultrafast RNA-seq aligner, achieving 550 million 2×76 bp reads/hour on a 12-core server—450× faster than TopHat2—by leveraging uncompressed suffix arrays and sequential maximum mappable seed search [6]. SeqKit further exemplifies localized optimization, using Go-based parallelization and custom algorithms (e.g., a slice-based reverse complement implementation) to achieve ~20× speedups over map-based approaches and competitive performance against C-based tools like seqtk [7].

Beyond individual tools, the corpus reveals a shift toward systemic efficiency: workflow systems like Snakemake and nf-core frameworks now integrate reproducibility, scalability, portability, and sustainability as core design principles. Snakemake supports full in silico reproducibility via automation, scalability across platforms, and software deployment (e.g., via Conda/Docker), while enabling transparency and adaptability through readable, well-documented workflows [9][11]. nf-core/sarek 3 demonstrates how systemic efficiency is achieved by rewriting pipelines to reduce storage (via CRAM) and runtime (via intra-sample parallelization), yielding a 70% cost reduction in cloud deployments [13]. These systems also promote interoperability—Snakemake can export to CWL and import CWL tool definitions—enabling workflows to run across diverse infrastructures [9]. Thus, the field has evolved from optimizing isolated tools (e.g., fastp, STAR, SeqKit) to building cohesive, scalable, and reproducible computational ecosystems that optimize the entire analysis pipeline [9][11][13].

## Summary

Sarek is a portable, reproducible, community-maintained workflow for germline and somatic variant detection, annotation, and quality control from whole-genome sequencing (WGS), whole-exome sequencing (WES), or gene panel data [2]. It is built using Nextflow and leverages state-of-the-art tools: BWA-MEM for read alignment, GATK for deduplication and recalibration, HaplotypeCaller and Strelka2 for germline SNPs/indels, Manta and TIDDIT for structural variants in germline samples, GATK4 Mutect2 and Strelka2 for somatic single-base mutations and small insertions/deletions, and Manta, ASCAT, and Control-FREEC for somatic structural variants, copy-number variation, ploidy, and sample purity estimation [1]. Variants are annotated using snpEff and VEP [1]. Sarek integrates a comprehensive suite of quality control tools—including FastQC, QualiMap, BCFtools, Samtools, and VCFtools—with results aggregated via MultiQC [1]. The workflow is designed for ease of installation (via Docker or Singularity containers), portability across POSIX-compatible systems (e.g., Linux, macOS), and operation in isolated environments without internet access [2]. In a benchmark run on a 48-thread node with 756 GB RAM and 100 TB storage, a full analysis (preprocessing + germline + somatic calling + annotation) of 90X WGS data completed in 48 hours and 21 minutes, requiring ~3× the storage of input data [3]. Performance evaluation using a “Gold Set” benchmark showed F1 scores of 0.80 for somatic single-base mutations and 0.58 for somatic insertion/deletion mutations when using the intersection of GATK4 Mutect2 and Strelka2 outputs, placing Sarek in the top range of 18 benchmarked somatic callers [3]. Sample purity estimation yielded 100% (vs. 98% previously reported), and the workflow executed fully automatically with no manual intervention [3]. Sarek is part of the nf-core community effort and is open source [8]. Peer reviewers praised its comprehensiveness, usability, documentation, and robust implementation [7][8][9]. The authors note that while Sarek reduces labor and management overhead, users still need to perform parameter tuning, downstream filtering, and qualitative assessments [4]. Ongoing development includes add-on modules for variant ranking, visualization, and extraction of clinically relevant findings [4].

## Quality Control Capabilities

MultiQC is a tool designed to summarize and visualize quality control (QC) results from multiple bioinformatics tools and many samples in a single report, addressing the challenge of manually compiling per-sample QC outputs [1]. It scans analysis directories recursively for log files and QC reports (e.g., from FastQC, Qualimap, RSeQC), parses them, and generates integrated reports with shared plots to enable accurate cross-sample comparison [3]. This helps detect subtle batch effects and outliers that might otherwise be missed during early analysis stages [1]. MultiQC supports rapid parsing of thousands of samples, adapts report output as needed, and allows post-processing and dataset filtering using its parsed data [3]. It is particularly useful for large-scale projects such as single-cell and population studies, as well as high-throughput sequencing facilities, where it helps identify failing samples and irregular sample groups [3]. The tool is extensible—users have contributed new modules and plugins—and integrates with in-house systems (e.g., LIMS and databases) via plugins like MultiQC_NGI [2]. Reports are self-contained, customizable via templates, and suitable for delivery reports [3]. MultiQC is open-source (GNU GPLv3), available on GitHub, the Python Package Index, and Bioconda, with documentation at http://multiqc.info [1].

items.question: Explain the technical approach Snakemake uses to optimize job scheduling and how it handles job submission overhead in cluster or cloud environments.
items.expected:
Scheduling: Snakemake solves the scheduling problem at the start of execution and again whenever a job finishes and new jobs become pending. The first releases used a greedy scheduler. The current implementation solves a mixed integer linear program (MILP) whenever there are free resources. The MILP optimizes four criteria in lexicographical order: (1) prefer jobs with high priority, (2) maximize the number of used cores (the extent of parallelization), (3) delete existing temporary files as soon as possible, and (4) reduce the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass. The order is enforced by multiplying each criterion sum by a value at least as high as the maximum the terms to its right can reach. Constraint (2) ensures the selection does not exceed the available amount of each resource.

Cluster and cloud: with middleware such as SLURM, PBS, LSF or Kubernetes, Snakemake does not need to govern all resources at a global level. Some resources are handled by the middleware, and constraint (2) can be dropped for them. Snakemake can pass the resource requirements to the middleware, which can use them to choose the best fitting machine. By default runtime, threads, memory and disk usage are local resources passed to the middleware; all other resources are global and are still governed by Snakemake via constraint (2). The number of jobs queued or running at a time is limited by the same kind of constraint.

Submission overhead: by default every job is submitted separately to the queuing system. For short-running jobs this can cause considerable overhead, as jobs wait in a queue, and may add delays or cost when accessing files from remote storage or network file systems. To minimize it, Snakemake can partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs by assigning rules to groups. Connected subgraphs with the same group are submitted together as a single cluster or cloud job (a group job) instead of each job separately. For each group, the number of connected subgraphs spanned per submission can be defined (one by default), so the partition size can be adjusted to the computational platform. A group job's resource usage is computed by sorting its jobs topologically, summing resource usage per level and taking the maximum over all levels. For runtime it is the other way round: the maximum per level, summed over all levels.
concepts: maximize the number of used cores
partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs

## Performance Benchmarks

Performance benchmarks of Snakemake were conducted to estimate the runtime and memory usage required for dependency resolution (i.e., computing the job DAG), independent of actual job execution [5]. In these benchmarks, an example workflow from the manuscript (Figure 3) was artificially scaled by replicating input data to generate workflows with 10 to 90,000 jobs [5]. Benchmarks were run on a single core of an 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-1370P (up to 5.2 GHz), with 32 GB RAM and a Western Digital PC SN740 SSD [5]. Results showed that both runtime and memory usage scale linearly with the number of jobs [5]. For 11 jobs, Snakemake required 0.5 seconds and 90 MB of memory; for 90,000 jobs, it required 37 seconds and 1.1 GB of memory [5]. The authors note that this overhead is negligible compared to typical workflow execution times [3][5]. Future improvements to performance are planned, including leveraging PyPy, Mojo, or PyO3, and caching dependency resolution results between invocations [5].

### Meta-Conclusion: The Chain of Reliability

The relationship between technical artifact removal and statistical reliability in high-throughput sequencing analysis is **hierarchical and cumulative**; statistical validity is not an isolated outcome of a single statistical test but the result of a sequential "chain of reliability" where each stage of artifact removal serves as a prerequisite for the next [1][2][4].

**1. Physical Cleaning as the Foundation for Valid Quantification**
Statistical reliability begins with the elimination of physical artifacts. Raw sequencing data contains inherent noise, including adapter contamination, base content biases, and sequencing errors [2]. Tools like **fastp** are essential for generating "clean data" through quality control and adapter trimming. Without this initial physical cleaning, downstream quantification is compromised, leading to false positives and negatives, particularly in sensitive applications like detecting ultra-low mutation allele frequencies (MAF) in liquid biopsies where technical noise can obscure real biological signals [1][2].

**2. Bias Correction as the Prerequisite for Accurate Modeling**
Once physical artifacts are removed, statistical models must account for systematic biases inherent to the sequencing process, such as fragment GC content, sequence-specific biases at fragment ends, and positional coverage biases [4][6].
*   **Evidence:** The quantification tool **Salmon** addresses these by learning sample-specific parameters and re-estimating "effective lengths" [4][5].
*   **Impact:** Failure to correct for these biases leads to statistical artifacts, such as false "isoform switching" results. Conversely, bias-aware quantification eliminates these artifacts and significantly improves sensitivity (53% to 250% higher than competing tools) while reducing gene-level false positives by a factor of approximately 2.6 [1][10]. This demonstrates that statistical reliability in differential expression analysis is directly dependent on the prior removal of technical biases during quantification [4].

**3. Statistical Modeling as the Final Filter for Biological Signal**
The final stage involves distinguishing true biological signals from remaining technical variance and sampling noise using robust statistical frameworks like **DESeq2**.
*   **Mechanism:** DESeq2 employs empirical Bayes shrinkage to estimate gene-wise dispersion, fitting a parametric curve to capture the variance-mean dependence of the dataset [1][3][6]. It uses a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate to shrink noisy gene-wise estimates toward a trend line, preventing false positives caused by underestimating dispersion [2][6][7].
*   **Dependency:** This statistical modeling is only effective if the input data has already been purified of physical artifacts and systematic biases. If the input contains uncorrected technical noise, the statistical model cannot distinguish between biological variance and technical error, rendering the final inferences methodologically invalid [8][9].

**Conclusion**
The meta-conclusion is that **statistical reliability is contingent upon the successful execution of prior artifact removal stages**. Physical cleaning ensures that quantification is based on valid biological fragments; bias correction ensures that abundance estimates reflect true transcript levels rather than technical artifacts; and robust statistical modeling ensures that final inferences are not driven by sampling noise. As noted in the workflow, moving from raw data to discovery requires filtering noise at increasing levels of abstraction, where the failure of any single stage compromises the validity of the entire analysis [2][4][10].

The researchers defined and calculated the **Mortality Ratio (MR)** as a specific metric to identify the onset of the clinical period and assess early warning signals in poultry farms infected with HPAI H5Nx.

### Definition and Calculation
The MR is calculated by dividing the **daily mortality** on a specific day by the **baseline mortality**, which is defined as the **average daily mortality of the preceding week** (the week before mortality began to increase) [1].

The formula is expressed as:
**MR = Daily Mortality / Average Daily Mortality of the Preceding Week** [1].

### Threshold and Application
*   **Threshold:** The study utilized a threshold of **MR > 3**. This means the daily mortality had to be at least three times higher than the baseline average to be considered a significant early warning signal [1][2].
*   **Legal Basis:** This specific threshold was chosen to align with **current Dutch legislation**, which mandates that poultry farmers notify the competent authority if daily mortality exceeds three times the average of the preceding week for two consecutive days (applicable to layers, breeders, and broilers aged 10 days or older) [1].
*   **Clinical Period Onset:** The first day on which the MR met or exceeded this threshold (>3) was defined as the **first day of the clinical period** [1].

### Data Limitations
It is important to note that the MR could not be calculated for **36 out of 92 farms** included in the study due to missing or unreliable farm records [4][11]. Consequently, the analysis of MR associations (such as comparisons between poultry types or time periods) was conducted only on the subset of farms where reliable data was available.
items.question: How did the researchers define and calculate the Mortality Ratio (MR) metric used to assess early warning signals on the infected farms?
items.expected: The MR was calculated from NVWA farm production charts with daily mortality records, which were retrieved for 63 of 92 farms. The percentage of daily mortality was calculated per house. Then 0.1 was added to all percentages so that log10 could be taken, and log10(0.1) = −1 indicated no mortality (0%). For each flock, the MR of the day before notification was calculated using the method described by Gonzales and Elbers (2018). The MR compares mortality with the average mortality of the previous week. The method had also been used by Schreuder et al. (2021), but this study adjusted it slightly, using a threshold of >3 instead of >2.9. This threshold matches Dutch legislation, which requires notification when daily mortality is >3 times the average mortality of the preceding week for two consecutive days. Each farm was scored as increased (MR above the cut-off value of 3), not increased (MR < 3), or unknown/unclear (MR could not be calculated). The MR could not be calculated for 36 of 92 farms.
concepts: average mortality of the previous week

# Implementation Languages and Performance-Optimization Strategies

Based on the available research data, comprehensive details regarding implementation languages and optimization strategies are only available for **SeqKit**. Descriptions for **fastp** and **Cutadapt** were not found in the source material, preventing a complete comparative analysis of all three tools.

## SeqKit

**Implementation Language**
SeqKit is implemented in the **Go programming language** [1]. This choice facilitates cross-platform availability, allowing the software to run on Windows, Linux, Mac OS X, and FreeBSD [1].

**Performance-Optimization Strategies**
SeqKit employs several specific strategies to address computational bottlenecks in sequence data processing:

*   **Parallelization:** The toolkit utilizes "Goroutines," which are lighter than standard threads, to parallelize CPU-intensive tasks such as sequence validation, reverse complement computation, and file parsing [2][6]. The default thread count for multi-core computers is set to two [11].
*   **Custom Data Structures and Algorithms:**
    *   **File I/O:** Instead of the standard Go `bufio` library, SeqKit uses a custom buffered file reading algorithm to increase speed and lower memory usage for large sequences [4].
    *   **Reverse Complement Computation:** Optimization was achieved by using a slice data structure indexed by ASCII codes rather than a standard map/hash table, resulting in approximately a **20× speedup** [6].
    *   **Parsing:** The software uses a self-implemented, high-performance bioinformatics package called "bio" for parsing, which is 9–11 times faster than the biogo package [3][7].
*   **Memory Management:**
    *   Most subcommands are designed not to load all records into memory [7].
    *   Deduplication tasks use MD5 digests to represent sequence content, significantly reducing memory consumption [5].
    *   Subcommands like "sample," "split," "shuffle," and "sort" can utilize a "two-pass" mode leveraging a FASTA index to keep memory usage low [7].
    *   Peak memory usage is determined by the length of the longest sequence record rather than the total file size, staying constant (approx. 750–780 Mb) regardless of file size [14].

**Bottlenecks Addressed**
SeqKit specifically targets execution time, memory usage, file I/O efficiency, and scalability for large FASTA/Q files [Bottlenecks and Comparative Performance]. It outperforms tools like `seqtk` in processing time for FASTA file parsing and achieves approximately 85% of `seqtk`'s speed in FASTQ file parsing [7].

## Limitations on fastp and Cutadapt Data

The search results explicitly indicate that **descriptions for Cutadapt and fastp are not found in the source material** [Bottlenecks and Comparative Performance]. Consequently, their specific implementation languages and performance-optimization strategies could not be synthesized or compared against SeqKit in this analysis.

SeqKit achieves stable memory usage and high efficiency when processing datasets significantly larger than the human genome through specific architectural choices in memory management, parsing strategies, and parallelization.

### Memory Management Strategies
SeqKit ensures memory stability by decoupling memory consumption from the total file size. Instead, memory usage is primarily determined by the length of the longest sequence record [2]. To maintain this stability, most subcommands avoid loading entire files into memory [3]. For tasks that require tracking sequence content, such as deduplication, SeqKit uses MD5 digests to represent sequences, which significantly reduces memory overhead [3].

Additionally, specific subcommands including `sample`, `split`, `shuffle`, and `sort` utilize a "two-pass mode" that leverages a FASTA index for rapid access. This mode allows the program to avoid loading all FASTA/Q records into memory at once; when using the index for operations like shuffling and sorting, peak memory usage remains approximately 750 Mb regardless of the total file size [3][5].

### Efficiency Optimizations
SeqKit employs several technical implementations to maximize processing speed:
*   **Custom Parsing:** It uses a specialized buffered file reading algorithm instead of the standard Go `bufio` library, which is less efficient for large sequences. This custom implementation results in increased processing speeds and significantly lower memory usage [4].
*   **Parallelization:** CPU-intensive tasks, such as sequence validation, format conversion, and reverse complementation, are parallelized using Go Goroutines. While additional threads can improve performance, the tool defaults to two threads as tests indicated diminishing returns beyond this point [4][7].
*   **Optimized Data Structures:** For reverse complement calculations, SeqKit uses slices indexed by ASCII codes instead of standard hash maps. This specific implementation resulted in a 20-fold increase in speed [4].

### Performance on Large Datasets
Benchmarks validate SeqKit's efficiency on large-scale data. In tests involving a ~2.7 G file of DNA sequences and a ~2.9 G human genome file, SeqKit demonstrated superior or competitive speeds compared to other tools [2][8]. For instance, when parsing FASTA files, SeqKit outperformed the C-based tool `seqtk` in processing time while maintaining reasonable memory usage [2]. In contrast to tools like `seqmagick`, which consume much more memory by loading the entire file into system memory, SeqKit’s performance remained consistent and memory-efficient across different file formats [4][5].
items.question: How does SeqKit achieve stable memory usage and efficiency when processing datasets that are significantly larger than the human genome?
items.expected: Most SeqKit subcommands do not load all FASTA/Q records into memory. Removing duplicate sequences by content does need whole sequences in memory, so SeqKit uses an MD5 digest to represent sequence content, which greatly reduces memory usage. Some subcommands ("sample", "split", "shuffle" and "sort" on page 4; "subseq", "split", "sort" and "shuffle" on page 3) read the files twice in two-pass mode, which uses the FASTA index for rapid access of sequences and reduces memory usage (FASTA format only). The sequence parser uses a custom buffered file reading algorithm instead of Go's "bufio", which increased speed and significantly lowered memory usage. Most CPU-intensive processes are parallelized by multiple Goroutines. In tests on files made by repeating human chromosome 1 N times, memory stayed at approximately 780 Mb for reverse complement and duplicate removal, and peak memory stayed at approximately 750 Mb for shuffling and sorting with the FASTA index. The authors conclude that peak memory usage is determined by the length of the longest sequence record, so SeqKit can handle large FASTA and FASTQ files as data size grows.

# Bovine Tuberculosis (bTB) Prevalence Estimates

Based on the study conducted in the South and East regions of Cameroon involving 160 cattle, the specific bTB prevalence estimates varied significantly depending on the diagnostic test and the skin test reaction threshold applied. The primary findings from `14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf` are detailed below.

## Primary Diagnostic Test Estimates

The study utilized two main intradermal tuberculin tests with different cut-off thresholds to determine prevalence.

### Comparative Intradermal Tuberculin Test (CIDT)
*   **Threshold ≥3 mm:** The study calculated a prevalence of **6.8%** (11 out of 160 cattle). The 95% confidence interval (CI) for this estimate was 4.35%–9.41% [14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf].
*   **Threshold ≥4 mm:** The prevalence dropped significantly to **0.6%** (1 out of 160 cattle), with a 95% CI of 0%–1.2% [14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf].

### Simple Intradermal Tuberculin Test (SITT/IDT)
*   **Threshold 4 mm:** The prevalence was estimated at **1.8%** (3 out of 160 cattle), with a 95% CI of 0%–3.6% [14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf].
    *   *Note:* While some sections of the text initially referenced a 0.6% estimate for the simple IDT at the 4 mm threshold, the detailed breakdown clarifies that 1.8% corresponds to the SITT/IDT, whereas 0.6% corresponds to the CIDT at the same threshold.

## Sub-Group Prevalence Estimates (CIDT ≥3 mm)

Further analysis broke down the prevalence by specific animal characteristics using the CIDT ≥3 mm threshold [14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf]:

*   **Region:**
    *   **East Region:** 8.23% (95% CI: 5.1%–10.97%)
    *   **South Region:** 5.33% (95% CI: 4.2%–6.8%)
*   **Breed:**
    *   **Goudali:** 9.16% (95% CI: 7.21%–11.27%)
    *   **Bororo, Ndama, and Simmental:** 0%
*   **Age:**
    *   **Cattle under 3 years old:** 13.5% (95% CI: 10.55%–16.05%)
*   **Body Condition:**
    *   **Normal Body Score:** 19% (95% CI: 7.52%–11.3%) at the CIDT ≥3 mm threshold.
    *   **Normal Body Score:** 17.85% (95% CI: 10.5%–27.3%) at the CIDT ≥4 mm threshold.

## Impact of Diagnostic Thresholds

The researchers highlighted that the choice of threshold critically influenced the prevalence results. Applying a **3 mm threshold** significantly increased the sensitivity of bTB detection and the recorded prevalence compared to the **4 mm threshold** recommended by the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) [14_bovine_tb_cameroon.pdf]. While a threshold of >2 mm was noted in other research (e.g., in Ethiopia) as providing optimal diagnostic characteristics, it was not used to calculate prevalence rates in this specific Cameroon study.

# MultiQC's Approach to Data Presentation for Quality Identification

MultiQC assists researchers in identifying quality issues across large-scale projects primarily through the consolidation of data, interactive visualization, and scalable rendering techniques. These features collectively enable the rapid detection of outliers, batch effects, and global trends that are often missed in traditional per-sample reporting.

## Consolidated Reporting and Trend Identification
The core of MultiQC's approach is the integration of quality control (QC) metrics from multiple bioinformatics tools and large sample sets into a single, unified report [1][2]. This design addresses the limitations of traditional tools that generate reports on a per-sample basis, which are often time-consuming to compile and prone to human error [2]. By consolidating data into one report, MultiQC enables researchers to identify global trends, subtle biases, and batch effects that might otherwise be overlooked when switching between individual files [1][2]. This centralized presentation allows for the rapid assessment of analysis success and the identification of abnormal samples, which is particularly critical in large-scale population and single-cell studies [4].

## Interactive Visualization and Outlier Detection
To facilitate sample comparison, MultiQC utilizes interactive data visualization features [2][3]. Reports include resizable plots where researchers can use a toolbox to rename, hide, or highlight specific samples [3][4]. This functionality makes it easier to identify outliers or groups of samples behaving irregularly compared to the rest of the dataset. Additionally, the tool generates shared plots that allow for the direct and accurate comparison of metrics across all samples, making subtle differences much more apparent than when viewing individual files.

## Scalability and Performance Management
For projects involving hundreds or thousands of samples, MultiQC maintains performance and file consistency by automatically switching from interactive JavaScript plots to static images [3]. This ensures the report remains usable and the file size consistent even when parsing data for thousands of samples within minutes [3]. This adaptability is essential for large-scale projects like single-cell and population studies, where maintaining a manageable file size is crucial for usability [3].

## Integration and Metadata Tracing
MultiQC further assists in quality monitoring through extensibility and automation. It can be extended with plugins to incorporate metadata from internal systems like Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS) [4]. This allows researchers to overlay metadata, such as batch numbers or lab conditions, onto QC results to more effectively trace the source of batch effects. By automating metadata collection at the end of an analysis pipeline, MultiQC provides a central collection point that helps researchers spot failing samples and batch effects early in the data processing stage [4].
items.question: How does MultiQC's approach to data presentation assist researchers in identifying quality issues across large-scale projects?
items.expected: MultiQC scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and builds a single summary report that visualizes output from multiple tools across all samples, so global trends and biases can be identified quickly. Collecting the data in one report gives a fast way to scan key statistics, and a general statistics table gathers metrics from different tools for each sample. Shared plots allow accurate comparison between samples and detection of subtle differences not noticeable when switching between different files. Data visualization aids batch effect detection and minimizes the risk of confounding factors. Plots are resizeable and interactive, and a report toolbox lets samples be renamed, hidden and highlighted; highlighting helps identify groups of samples behaving in an irregular manner. For large projects MultiQC parses data for thousands of samples within minutes and adapts the report output. For reports with hundreds of samples it renders plots as images with MatPlotLib instead of HighCharts. The reports reveal overall analysis success, make abnormal samples easy to identify and give the overview required to spot failing samples. Routine use aids quality control early in data processing, reducing the risk of batch effects and other downstream analysis problems.

# Clinical Presentations and Frequency of H5N1 Clade 2.3.4.4b: Mammals vs. Humans

Based on the analysis of the provided documentation, there is a stark contrast between the clinical impact and frequency of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b infections in mammals compared to humans.

## Clinical Presentations

The primary symptoms and disease progression differ significantly between the two groups.

*   **Mammals:** The disease is characterized predominantly by **severe neurological signs**. Infected mammals typically die from **encephalitis or meningoencephalitis** [2]. Adaptive mutations, such as PB2-E627K, have been detected in the brains of various carnivores, indicating the virus's ability to target the central nervous system in these species [2]. While milder disease is suspected, surveillance bias currently favors the detection of severely ill or dead animals.
*   **Humans:** In contrast, the majority of human infections to date have been **mild or asymptomatic**. However, the virus retains the potential to cause **acute febrile respiratory disease** or **unexplained neurological disease** [1]. Other reported symptoms associated with H5 strains include conjunctivitis and gastrointestinal distress. Severe cases in humans have generally been linked to direct exposure to poultry.

## Relative Frequency and Scale

The scale of outbreaks and the number of detected cases vary drastically between species.

*   **Mammals:** The outbreak in mammals is described as having a "massive scope" and representing an "unprecedented global outbreak" [4]. Spillover has occurred across a wide range of species, including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, sea lions, and dolphins. Specific events include the culling of **thousands of animals** on mink farms in Spain and substantial die-offs in sea lions [3].
*   **Humans:** Infections remain extremely rare. For clade 2.3.4.4b specifically, **fewer than 10 human cases** have been identified globally [1]. These cases have been reported in the United Kingdom, United States, China, Vietnam, Ecuador, and Chile.

## Disease Severity and Mortality

*   **Mammals:** Mortality is very high in detected wildlife populations. The virus frequently reaches the brain, leading to fatal outcomes in many instances.
*   **Humans:** Mortality remains low for this specific clade so far. While historical H5N1 infections prior to 2020 had mortality rates of approximately 50%, current clade 2.3.4.4b cases have remained mostly mild [1].

## Summary Comparison

| Feature | Mammals (Clade 2.3.4.4b) | Humans (Clade 2.3.4.4b) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Primary Symptoms** | Severe neurological signs, encephalitis | Mild/asymptomatic, respiratory illness |
| **Detected Cases** | Thousands (mass die-offs/culls) | Fewer than 10 cases |
| **Mortality** | Very high in detected wildlife | Low (mostly mild to date) |
| **Species Affected** | Broad range (bears, seals, mink, etc.) | Limited to individuals with direct bird contact |
items.question: What are the common clinical presentations and relative frequency of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b infections when comparing mammals to humans?
items.expected: Mammals: clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 has infected multiple species, including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, porpoises, sea lions and dolphins. Most infected mammals presented with severe neurological signs and died from encephalitis or meningoencephalitis. Milder disease was likely also present (and likely more prevalent), because wildlife testing is biased towards severely infected or dead animals, and identified infections are assumed to represent only a minority of spillovers. Humans: this clade has been identified in less than 10 humans. Most cases have been mild or asymptomatic (the first case, in the United Kingdom, was mild; a second, in the United States in April 2022, was asymptomatic), but in recent months severe cases have occurred, all with direct exposure to poultry. The paper reports no symptom profile for the clade 2.3.4.4b human cases, but it advises clinicians to consider HPAI virus infection in any individual with acute febrile respiratory disease or unexplained neurological diseases after exposure to birds or sick wildlife in the previous 10 to 14 days; it notes that conjunctivitis and gastrointestinal symptoms have also been reported in humans infected with other avian H5 strains. Comparison: detected mammal infections span many species and are mostly severe neurological disease, while human infections are few (less than 10) and mostly mild or asymptomatic.

### Cattle Estimates
Quantitative estimates for preclinical transmission in cattle vary depending on the methodology used to define infectiousness:

*   **Based on Observed Transmission:** When relying on confirmed secondary transmission events, the proportion of preclinical transmission ($\theta$) is approximately **0.13** (Charleston et al. [92]).
*   **Based on Proxy Measures:** When estimates rely on proxy measures of viral presence (such as viral shedding) rather than confirmed secondary infections, the value increases significantly to approximately **0.44** (Charleston et al. [92]).

### Pig Estimates
For pigs, the research synthesis identifies a specific estimate derived from prospective experimental studies:

*   **Estimated Proportion:** The proportion of preclinical transmission ($\theta$) is estimated at **0.12** (95% CI: 0.00083–0.27) (Arzt et al. [27]).
*   **Implication:** This indicates that approximately 12% of Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus (FMDV) transmission in pigs occurs during the preclinical phase, prior to the onset of clinical signs.

### Methodological Context
The synthesis notes that while both Charleston et al. [92] and Arzt et al. [27] utilized Bayesian frameworks to estimate $\theta$, their approaches differed. Charleston et al. [92] compared transmission events against viral proxies in cattle, whereas Arzt et al. [27] conducted a prospective experimental study to confirm the existence and relevance of preclinical transmission in pigs. Additionally, infectiousness in pigs begins approximately 24–32 hours post-infection, preceding clinical symptoms (Stenfeldt et al. [28]).

With proxy measures (viral isolation from blood, nasal fluid or oropharyngeal fluid) their values were substantially higher: 0.43, 0.27 and 0.44 (up to ~0.44). Salmon achieves speed comparable to ultra-fast alignment-free tools while maintaining high accuracy through a combination of a lightweight "quasi-mapping" procedure, a dual-phase inference algorithm, and sophisticated bias correction models.

### 1. Quasi-Mapping: Lightweight and Direct Processing
The foundation of Salmon's speed is its **quasi-mapping** mode, which serves as a faster alternative to traditional alignment [1][6].
*   **Direct Quantification:** Unlike tools that generate intermediate alignment files (SAM/BAM), Salmon processes raw FASTA/Q files directly against a transcriptome index, eliminating the I/O overhead and disk space requirements associated with alignment files [1].
*   **Position and Orientation Tracking:** While similar to pseudoalignment in speed, Salmon's quasi-mapping is distinct because it tracks the **position and orientation** of all mapped fragments by default, providing more detailed data than standard alignment-free methods [8][10].
*   **Efficient Data Structures:** The algorithm utilizes a **concurrent cuckoo hash map** to construct equivalence classes. This data structure allows multiple threads to query and update the map with minimal contention, enabling efficient parallel processing [24].
*   **Performance:** This approach allows Salmon to scale efficiently with CPU cores; for instance, using 30 threads, it can process approximately 600 million reads in roughly 23 minutes, matching the speed of tools like kallisto [1].

### 2. Dual-Phase Inference Algorithm
Salmon employs a two-stage inference procedure to optimize transcript abundance estimates, balancing computational efficiency with statistical rigor [8].

*   **Online Phase (Streaming and Parallel):**
    *   This phase processes reads asynchronously in mini-batches.
    *   It uses a variant of **stochastic, collapsed variational Bayesian inference** to estimate initial expression levels and auxiliary parameters (such as fragment length distribution and orientation) [8][23].
    *   Simultaneously, it constructs **"rich" equivalence classes**, creating a reduced representation of the data [8][23].

*   **Offline Phase (Refinement):**
    *   This phase refines the abundance estimates using the reduced data from the online phase.
    *   It applies either a standard **Expectation-Maximization (EM)** or a **variational Bayesian EM (VBEM)** algorithm to the equivalence classes until convergence [8][12][25].
    *   By optimizing over equivalence classes rather than individual fragments, the algorithm significantly reduces the complexity of the likelihood function, accelerating convergence [25].

### 3. "Rich" Equivalence Classes
A key innovation for maintaining accuracy without sacrificing speed is the use of **"rich" equivalence classes**.
*   **Definition:** An equivalence class groups fragments that are compatible with the exact same set of transcripts ($M(f_x) = M(f_y)$) [Chunk 5].
*   **The "Rich" Component:** Unlike standard classes that only track transcript compatibility, "rich" classes store **weight vectors ($w_j$)**. These weights represent the **average conditional probability** of observing a fragment from a specific transcript, accounting for auxiliary factors like fragment length, alignment orientation, and position [Chunk 7][12].
*   **Impact:** This allows the offline phase to perform iterative optimization on a highly compressed dataset while retaining the statistical information necessary for accurate quantification [25].

### 4. Advanced Bias Correction Models
To ensure high accuracy, Salmon incorporates feature-rich, sample-specific bias models that are critical for reliable differential expression analysis [6][10].
*   **GC-Content Bias:** Salmon is the first transcriptome-wide quantifier to account for fragment **GC-content bias**, which significantly improves the reliability of abundance estimates [6].
*   **Sequence and Positional Biases:** The tool models sequence-specific biases at the **5′ and 3′ fragment ends** as well as positional coverage biases [10][11][19].
*   **Error Profiles:** When processing traditional alignments, Salmon uses a **spatially varying first-order Markov model** to account for error profiles that change across the length of a read [22].
*   **Bias-Corrected Effective Lengths:** These models are used to calculate bias-corrected effective lengths for transcripts, ensuring that abundance estimates are not skewed by technical artifacts [20].

### 5. Optimization Techniques for Speed
Several specific techniques are employed to maximize throughput:
*   **Multi-threading:** The software is fully multi-threaded, scaling efficiently with the number of available CPU cores [1].
*   **Sampling Options:** Users can utilize sampling options like `--biasSpeedSamp` to speed up the calculation of bias-corrected effective lengths by coarsening the model slightly, trading a negligible amount of precision for significant speed gains [22].
*   **Asynchronous Processing:** The online phase processes mini-batches asynchronously, ensuring that CPU cores remain utilized efficiently throughout the quantification process [23].
items.question: Describe the algorithmic components and optimization techniques Salmon uses to achieve speed comparable to ultra-fast alignment-free tools while maintaining accuracy.
items.expected:
The paper claims that Salmon achieves greater accuracy than tools such as kallisto and eXpress, employs sample-specific bias models (sequence-specific, fragment-GC and positional biases), and achieves the same order-of-magnitude speed benefits as kallisto and Sailfish. Salmon has three components: a lightweight-mapping model, an online phase that estimates initial expression levels and model parameters, and an offline phase that refines the expression estimates.

Speed: mapping uses a built-in, ultra-fast procedure called quasi-mapping. It quantifies raw FASTA/Q reads directly, without intermediate alignment files. This saves considerable time and space, because quasi-mapping is faster than traditional alignment. The online phase is a streaming variant of stochastic, collapsed variational Bayesian inference. It updates read-count estimates after each mini-batch (1,000 alignment groups by default), and mini-batches are processed asynchronously and in parallel. The only synchronization is an atomic compare-and-swap loop that updates the global transcript weights. The paper says that, because the updates are stochastic and additive, this has little-to-no detrimental effect. The updates are also sparse, so they can be performed efficiently. During the online phase Salmon also builds a highly-reduced representation: rich fragment-level equivalence classes, held in a concurrent cuckoo hash map that many threads can query and write with very little contention. The offline phase runs a standard EM algorithm or a variational Bayesian EM algorithm over the equivalence classes until a data-dependent convergence criterion is met. Equivalence classes have been shown to greatly reduce the time needed for this iterative optimization. The auxiliary models are learned from the first 5,000,000 observations by default and then applied to all later ones. Salmon is designed to take advantage of multiple CPU cores.

Accuracy: unlike pseudoalignment, the mapping tracks, by default, the position and orientation of all mapped fragments. The two-phase inference supports a model that includes terms not considered by Sailfish and kallisto. That model covers positional coverage biases, 5′ and 3′ sequence-specific biases, fragment-level GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution. The equivalence-class weights carry the full model's conditional probabilities without revisiting every fragment. The extra cost of bias correction is typically small (full bias modeling added 119 seconds with 16 threads on sample ERR188021), and its learning and application are parallelized. Its cost scales with the number of expressed transcripts rather than reads, and stored cumulative GC counts per transcript make GC computation efficient.

Result: Salmon quantified about 600 million 75 bp paired-end reads in about 23 minutes (1384 seconds) using 30 threads. On the same machine with the same number of threads, kallisto took about 20 minutes (1198 seconds).
concepts: quasi-mapping is faster than traditional alignment

### Purpose of the rlog Transformation

The specific purpose of the regularized logarithm (rlog) transformation is to make count data homoskedastic, ensuring that the variance does not depend strongly on the mean counts [1]. By providing variables with a similar dynamic range, it facilitates multivariate visualizations and ordinations, such as clustering or principal component analysis [1]. The transformation accounts for variations in sequencing depth (size factors) across samples [2]. It is important to note that the rlog transformation is intended for visualization and ordination purposes; it is distinct from the statistical inference procedure used for differential expression analysis, which utilizes raw counts [1][2].

### Performance Comparison: Variance Stabilization

In terms of performance regarding variance stabilization, the rlog transformation outperforms the ordinary logarithm (specifically the logarithm of normalized counts plus a pseudocount) [3]. Diagnostic plots show that while the ordinary logarithm results in gene-wise standard deviations that are variable across the range of mean counts, the rlog transformation keeps the variance relatively stable [3]. This stabilization helps reveal meaningful patterns in the data [3].

### Impact on Downstream Analysis

The impact of these transformations is evident in sample clustering [2]. Hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distances on rlog-transformed data successfully clusters samples into their appropriate treatment and time groups [2]. In contrast, using ordinary logarithm-transformed counts for the same clustering procedure produces more ambiguous results [2].

### Technical Mechanism

Technically, the rlog transformation is calculated by fitting a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) for each gene with a baseline expression and computing shrunken log fold changes (LFCs) [1]. It accounts for sequencing depth by representing the logarithm of $q_{ij}$ after accounting for size factors [1]. While the rlog value for large counts is approximately equal to the ordinary log of normalized counts, it offers the benefit of treating all samples equally without requiring sample covariate information [1].
items.question: What is the specific purpose of the regularized logarithm (rlog) transformation, and how does its performance compare to an ordinary log transformation in terms of variance stabilization?
items.expected: Purpose: the rlog transforms RNA-seq data to render them homoskedastic. On the original count scale, results would be dominated by highly expressed, highly variable genes. With logarithm-transformed data, undue weight goes to weakly expressed genes, which show exaggerated LFCs. The rlog thus facilitates multivariate visualization and ordinations such as clustering or principal component analysis, heat maps, and machine-learning techniques that require homoskedastic input data. It uses the shrinkage approach of DESeq2. For genes with high counts it behaves similarly to a log2 transformation, and for genes with low counts it shrinks together the values for different samples. This avoids the standard logarithm's spreading apart of data for genes with low counts. Comparison: after the rlog, gene variances are stabilized (approximately the same, or homoskedastic); otherwise they would strongly depend on the mean counts. On the Hammer et al. dataset (Figure 5), the gene-wise standard deviation is variable across the range of the mean of counts under the ordinary logarithm with a pseudocount of 1, log2(Kij/sj + 1), while relatively stable using the rlog. The comparison is qualitative, with no numeric measure in the text.

ordinary logarithm with a pseudocount of 1
variable across the range of the mean of counts

# Impact of Spatial Heterogeneity on Rabies Persistence

Spatial heterogeneity in vaccination coverage—the uneven distribution of vaccinated individuals across a landscape—is a critical driver of rabies persistence, often allowing the virus to continue circulating even when district-wide average coverage targets appear met. Research indicates that for the same average vaccination coverage, increased spatial variation leads to higher disease incidence because effective susceptibility is higher when unvaccinated dogs are concentrated in specific areas rather than distributed evenly [15_rabies_tanzania.pdf].

## Mechanisms of Persistence

The persistence of rabies despite meeting average targets is driven by several interconnected mechanisms:

*   **Reservoirs in Low-Coverage Pockets:** Pockets of low vaccination coverage act as reservoirs that allow the virus to maintain circulation. In Tanzania's Serengeti district, major rabies outbreaks followed multi-year periods where specific clusters of villages were left unvaccinated, despite broader district efforts [15_rabies_tanzania.pdf].
*   **Effective Susceptibility:** The impact of heterogeneity is analyzed through "effective susceptibility," modeled as "power mean susceptibility" (where susceptibility equals 1 minus coverage). This modeling demonstrates that variations in coverage across different scales significantly impact disease incidence [15_rabies_tanzania.pdf].
*   **Population Connectivity:** Rabies dynamics are driven by the interaction of local dog movements and vaccination efforts. Connectivity is quantified by calculating "bordering vaccination coverage" based on the proportion of borders a village shares with its neighbors. Villages typically share borders with a median of five neighboring villages, making them susceptible to incursions if vaccination in adjacent areas is insufficient [15_rabies_tanzania.pdf].
*   **Demographic Turnover:** High demographic turnover, with an estimated annual dog mortality rate of 44.8%, causes vaccine-induced immunity to wane rapidly at the population level. Consequently, even if a district shows high average coverage, the standard deviation in village-level "rolling coverage" reveals heterogeneities that allow the virus to persist [15_rabies_tanzania.pdf].

## Field Evidence and Data Limitations

Field studies highlight the limitations of relying solely on average coverage targets:

*   **The 70% Target vs. Heterogeneity:** While campaigns often aim for the internationally recommended 70% coverage target, research suggests that minimizing spatial gaps is more vital for interrupting endemic circulation than reaching high average targets alone. In the Serengeti, rabies was effectively controlled (incidence dropping to less than 0.4 cases per 1,000 dogs annually) when spatial heterogeneity was reduced through consistent district-wide campaigns, even though campaigns failed to reach the 70% target [15_rabies_tanzania.pdf].
*   **Masked Risks in Aggregated Data:** Coarse data aggregated at a district level often masks fine-scale gaps, making it difficult to identify the specific locations where transmission is maintained. For example, while "campaign completeness" reached 100% in the Serengeti in 2019, historical logistical constraints frequently caused specific regions to lapse, creating spatial gaps in immunity [15_rabies_tanzania.pdf].
*   **External Incursions:** Continued persistence is also driven by high population connectivity and frequent incursions from neighboring unvaccinated regions, which accounted for up to 50% of cases by 2022 [15_rabies_tanzania.pdf].

In summary, spatial heterogeneity allows rabies to persist by creating localized reservoirs of susceptible dogs that sustain transmission chains, a risk that is often invisible in district-level averages.
items.question: Explain how spatial heterogeneity in vaccination coverage impacts the persistence of rabies even when average coverage targets are met.
items.expected: The spatial distribution of coverage matters, not only its average. In the power mean susceptibility model, p was estimated to be substantially larger than one. With p>1, the same total number of unvaccinated dogs gives a higher effective susceptibility when those dogs are distributed unevenly. Against homogeneous 40% prior coverage, a 30%/50% split is predicted to raise focal incidence 1.4 (95% CrI: 1.3-1.6) times. A 20%/60% split raises it 2.6 (95% CrI: 1.9-3.4) times. Outbreaks followed multi-year periods when clusters of villages remained unvaccinated. High coverage in a small area has only limited impact if the rest of the population is poorly vaccinated. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell to <0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually, although mean district coverage stayed relatively low. Two caveats. The effect was seen only once the masking effects of prior non-focal incidence were removed. The estimated p lay beyond the range the authors expected a priori. The premise does not hold for this study: only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target, and vaccination controlled rabies without reaching it.

# DESeq2 Empirical Bayes Shrinkage for Low-Count Genes

DESeq2 utilizes Empirical Bayes shrinkage to improve the stability and reproducibility of results, specifically addressing the high uncertainty inherent in low-count genes [1], [3], [13]. This framework applies shrinkage to both dispersion and logarithmic fold change (LFC) estimation to mitigate noise and heteroskedasticity [1], [4].

## Dispersion Estimation
To handle the high variability of dispersion estimates in experiments with few replicates, DESeq2 shares information across genes [7], [15]. The process involves three key steps:
1.  **Gene-wise MLEs:** Initial dispersion estimates are obtained using maximum likelihood estimation for each gene independently [1], [7].
2.  **Trend Fitting:** A smooth curve is fit to these estimates to capture the dependence of dispersion on the average expression strength [1], [7].
3.  **Shrinkage to MAP:** The gene-wise estimates are shrunken toward the values predicted by the curve to produce final maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates [1], [7].

The "prior" for dispersion is assumed to follow a log-normal distribution centered around the fitted trend [10]. The strength of this shrinkage is automatically controlled by the width of the prior distribution and the degrees of freedom; as sample sizes increase, the shrinkage strength decreases [1], [7]. To avoid false positives, genes with extremely high gene-wise dispersion (more than two residual standard deviations above the curve) are identified as outliers and are not shrunken toward the prior [1], [2], [11].

## Logarithmic Fold Change (LFC) Estimation
Low read counts naturally result in high variance and exaggerated LFC estimates, a phenomenon known as heteroskedasticity [2], [26]. DESeq2 overcomes this by shrinking LFC estimates toward zero [4], [31].
*   **Prior Distribution:** DESeq2 fits a zero-centered normal distribution to the observed MLEs of all genes [4], [11], [31].
*   **MAP Estimation:** This distribution serves as a prior for a second round of GLM fits, resulting in MAP estimates [4], [31].

The shrinkage is strongest when the available information for a gene is low, such as when counts are low, dispersion is high, or there are few degrees of freedom [2], [4], [26]. Specifically, the shrinkage depends on the observed Fisher information; genes with flatter profile likelihoods (due to low means or high dispersion) see their MAP estimates pulled more strongly toward the zero-centered prior [5], [21]. This process effectively removes the problem of exaggerated LFCs for low-count genes, facilitating better gene ranking and visualization [5], [14], [16].
items.question: How does the DESeq2 framework utilize Empirical Bayes shrinkage to handle the high uncertainty associated with low-count genes in both dispersion and fold change estimation?
items.expected:
Both shrinkage steps follow one principle: empirical Bayes priors set the amount of shrinkage from the amount of information the data carry for the estimated quantity.

Dispersion: with two or three replicates, the dispersion estimates for each gene are highly variable. DESeq2 assumes that genes of similar average expression strength have similar dispersion. It first gets gene-wise maximum-likelihood estimates, then fits a smooth curve against average expression strength. It shrinks the gene-wise estimates toward the values predicted by the curve, combining the likelihood with the trended prior to give maximum a posteriori (MAP) dispersion estimates. The strength of shrinkage depends on how close true dispersion values tend to be to the fit, and on the degrees of freedom. It decreases as the sample size increases. The width of the prior is estimated from the data, and the fitted curve aids estimation in less information-rich settings. Estimates below the curve are raised, which helps avoid false positives from underestimated dispersion. A gene-wise estimate more than 2 residual standard deviations above the curve is used instead of the shrunken one. On low counts, the paper says that when μ ≲1/α the observed data provide little information on α, so the sampling variance of the estimator is large. Overestimating α in that low-count range has little effect on inference, because the Poisson component dominates the variance there.

Fold change: LFC estimates have strong variance for genes with low read count, because ratios are noisier when counts are low. DESeq2 fits ordinary GLMs to get maximum-likelihood estimates (MLEs) of the LFCs, then fits a zero-centered normal distribution to the MLEs over all genes. That distribution is the prior in a second round of GLM fits, and the MAP estimates are kept as the final LFCs. Shrinkage toward zero is stronger when a gene has little information, because counts are low, dispersion is high or there are few degrees of freedom. The amount of information is indicated by the observed Fisher information, not simply by the mean count. Such genes have flatter profile likelihoods, so the zero-centered prior pulls the high-uncertainty MLE closer to zero. This removes the problem of exaggerated LFCs for low counts. For genes with less than one read per sample on average, LFCs hardly deviate from zero. The paper describes this as a bias-variance trade-off: lower variance in exchange for a bias toward zero. As the degrees of freedom increase, the shrunken estimates converge to the unshrunken estimates.

# Anthropogenic Drivers of Disease Persistence in Transboundary Pathogen Control

Anthropogenic factors, specifically vaccination distribution strategies, animal management practices, and human-mediated movement, create distinct patterns of disease persistence in regions attempting to control transboundary pathogens. These factors often undermine control efforts by creating spatial vulnerabilities, facilitating transmission through trade, and introducing external pathogens.

## Vaccination Distribution and Spatial Heterogeneity
Vaccination coverage is a primary driver of disease persistence, particularly when distribution is uneven. Research indicates that **spatial heterogeneity**, characterized by pockets of low coverage or "spatial gaps," is a critical factor in continued circulation even when average district-level coverage appears sufficient [2], [9], [10].

*   **Clustering of Susceptibility:** For the same average vaccination coverage, increased heterogeneity among villages leads to higher focal incidence because effective susceptibility is higher when unvaccinated animals are clustered rather than distributed evenly [2], [30], [64].
*   **Data Masking:** Aggregating data at the district level often masks these fine-scale heterogeneities, leading to models that fail to detect the actual impact of vaccination on disease incidence [6], [9], [31].
*   **Coverage Thresholds:** While international guidelines often recommend a 70% coverage target, empirical evidence suggests rabies can be controlled with lower coverage levels (e.g., 20-40%) provided that persistent spatial gaps are minimized [4], [7].
*   **External Incursions:** Control is further challenged by frequent incursions from outside the district, which maintain transmission even when local endemic circulation is interrupted. In one district, these incursions averaged approximately seven per year and accounted for up to 50% of carnivore rabies cases by 2022 [2], [10], [14], [31].

## Animal Management and Biosecurity Protocols
Management practices significantly influence transmission dynamics and the ability to interrupt viral persistence.

*   **Wildlife-Livestock Interface:** Spatial variation in direct and indirect contact rates between domestic and wildlife populations is a critical factor used to inform disease management strategies [1].
*   **Housing and Transmission:** Within agricultural settings, animal housing management affects spread; specifically, the dynamics of within-pen versus between-pen transmission influence how viruses like Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD) spread among livestock [1].
*   **Vector and Movement Control:** For diseases like Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD), management relies on biosecurity through vector control (e.g., managing tick species) and movement management, including quarantining [1].
*   **Vaccination Efficacy:** The effectiveness of management is contingent on vaccine performance. For instance, attenuated sheeppox vaccines have shown only partial cross-protection against LSD field strains, complicating control efforts [2].

## Trade and Human-Mediated Movement
Human activities related to trade and movement are significant drivers of disease transmission and persistence across regions.

*   **Market Activities:** The purchase and sale of livestock in markets is a recurring risk factor. In Ethiopia, animals purchased or received as gifts had significantly higher odds of testing positive for Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR) compared to those born within the flock [4]. Similarly, buying cattle at markets is a factor related to bovine tuberculosis and Lumpy Skin Disease outbreaks [5], [8], [9].
*   **Human-Mediated Movement:** The physical movement of animals by humans facilitates the spread of pathogens, linking local outbreaks to broader regional transmission networks.
*   **International Trade:** The global impact of diseases like FMD is heavily tied to the regulation of international trade in animal-derived products, highlighting the transboundary nature of these risks [2].

In summary, disease persistence is not solely a function of pathogen biology but is heavily shaped by the spatial distribution of vaccination, the specifics of animal management, and the risks introduced through trade and movement.
items.question: How do anthropogenic factors, such as animal management and vaccination distribution, create patterns of disease persistence in regions attempting control of transboundary pathogens?
items.expected:
The four papers show two human-driven routes to persistence: moving and keeping animals, and uneven or insufficient vaccination.

(1) Moving and keeping animals.
- LSD in Nepal: the movement of animals from the Indian border area was a potential source of the outbreak, and the movement of animals between farms spread infection. Importing animals, sharing feed and water, and herd size were linked to outbreaks in univariable analysis only. Outbreaks have recurred over the past 3 years, and animals were not yet vaccinated against LSD.
- PPR in Borena, Ethiopia: seasonal movement of livestock across the borders with Kenya and Somalia, and uncontrolled animal movement, may contribute to spread. The probability of testing positive was four times higher for animals purchased from markets, and 8.3 times higher for gifted animals, than for animals born within the flocks. Outbreaks peak in the dry season, which cited studies attribute to animal movement in search of resources.
- LSD review: large-scale animal transfers from East Africa spread the disease to Syria, Iran and Iraq. Larger farms with intensive housing and shared feeding and watering facilities can contribute to transmission.
- Rabies in Serengeti: incursions in the district centre likely result from human-mediated transport.

(2) Uneven or insufficient vaccination.
- Rabies in Serengeti: campaigns ran less consistently away from the National Park, depending on local government resources, and only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target. Mean coverage over the district was relatively low, but the paper concludes that once heterogeneity was addressed, rabies was controlled nonetheless. Outbreaks followed multi-year periods when clusters of villages remained unvaccinated. At the same mean coverage, more heterogeneous coverage raised incidence (1.4 times for a 30%/50% split against a uniform 40%). Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell below 0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually. Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district then became a major source of residual transmission, reaching 50% of cases in 2022.
- PPR in Borena: there were 53 outbreaks from 2018 to 2022. 10,000 vaccine doses were deployed for an at-risk population of 397,189, and herd immunity was 68.8%, below the 80% FAO-WOAH threshold. The paper gives inadequate cold chain management, poor vaccine handling and distribution practices as possible causes. Outbreaks were concentrated in the hard-to-reach districts of Arero and Dhas, which risk becoming persistent focal points.
- LSD in Nepal: coverage of more than 80% is needed. The LSD review describes ring vaccination within a 5-km radius in border areas, and calls vaccination the singular means to prevent recurrence.

Moving and acquiring animals introduces and spreads these pathogens. In Nepal, LSD likely entered with animals moved from the Indian border area, then spread between farms [3, 4, 5, 7]. Importing animals, sharing feed and water, and herd size were linked to outbreaks only in univariable analysis [0, 6]. In Borena, seasonal cross-border livestock movement and uncontrolled animal movement may contribute to PPR spread, and purchased and gifted animals were more likely to test positive than animals born within the flocks [21, 22, 23]. Outbreaks there peak in the dry season, which cited studies attribute to animal movement in search of resources [29, 30]. The LSD review links spread to Syria, Iran and Iraq to large-scale animal transfers, and links transmission to larger farms with shared feeding and watering facilities [34, 35, 36, 37]. In Serengeti, rabies incursions in the district centre likely result from human-mediated transport [17].

Where vaccination is absent, insufficient or uneven, disease persists. In Nepal, LSD outbreaks recurred over 3 years while animals were not yet vaccinated, and the authors call for coverage of more than 80% [1, 2, 8]. In Serengeti, campaigns depended on local government resources, and only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target [12, 13], but the paper concludes that low mean coverage did not prevent control: once heterogeneity was addressed, rabies was controlled nonetheless [19]. Outbreaks followed multi-year periods when clusters of villages remained unvaccinated, and at the same mean coverage heterogeneity raised incidence (1.4 times in one modelled example) [9, 14, 15, 16]. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell below 0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually [10, 19]. Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district then became a major source of residual transmission (50% of cases in 2022), interacting with heterogeneous vaccination [11, 18, 19]. In Borena, 53 outbreaks in 2018 to 2022 coincided with 10,000 doses for 397,189 at-risk animals and 68.8% herd immunity, below the 80% threshold [20, 24, 25, 27, 28]. The paper attributes the shortfall to cold-chain, handling and distribution problems [26], and inaccessible districts with disproportionate outbreaks risk becoming persistent focal points [31, 32, 33]. The LSD review names movement management or limitations, quarantine and vaccination (including ring vaccination in border areas) as control measures, and vaccination as the singular means to prevent recurrence [38, 39, 40, 41].
