items.expected:
Spatial heterogeneity: in Serengeti district, increased heterogeneity in dog vaccination coverage among villages led to increased focal rabies incidence at the same average coverage. For example, a split of 30% and 50% coverage gave 1.4 (95% CrI: 1.3-1.6) times the incidence of homogeneous 40% coverage. Outbreaks followed years when campaigns missed many villages. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell to <0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually, and short vaccination lapses did not lead to resurgence. Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district, reaching 50% of cases in 2022, show regional connectivity driving residual transmission. For HPAI, infected farms clustered near the coast and the larger rivers, epidemics can escalate by farm-to-farm transmission in poultry-dense areas, and H5N1 spread through the four major migratory bird flyways.

Host-species heterogeneity: HPAI persisted in residential wild birds and was seen in an increasing number of wild bird species. H5N1 infected mammals including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, porpoises, sea lions and dolphins. Waterfowl-adapted clade 2.3.4.4b viruses had high infectivity and transmissibility in Anseriformes compared to Galliformes. Signs differ by host: exponential increasing mortality in layers and breeder chickens, but ducks reached MR > 3 less often, and drops in feed or water intake or egg production may be their only initial signs.

Surveillance implications: monitor fine-scale coverage, because models aggregating coverage to district level failed to show impacts on incidence. Make reporting criteria different for different poultry species and age groups (the Netherlands added thresholds such as MR > 3 in chickens and 0.15% per day for two days in ducks), with early notification. Monitor viral polymorphisms after transmission from Anseriformes to Galliformes. Focus strategic surveillance on the regions and populations at highest risk. Wildlife testing is biased towards severely infected or dead animals, so identified infections are only a minority of spillovers. Sentinel surveillance in mosquitoes, birds and horses, and animal die-offs (great apes with Ebola virus), can warn of risk to humans. Surveillance design should be standardised to strengthen its sensitivity for detecting new or unusual events.

Spatial heterogeneity sustains circulation. In Serengeti district, uneven dog vaccination coverage raised focal rabies incidence at the same mean coverage (1.4 times for a 30%/50% split against homogeneous 40%), and outbreaks followed years when campaigns missed many villages [12, 13, 16, 19]. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell below 0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually, and if persistent spatial gaps are minimal, sub-optimal coverage still has major benefits [13, 18]. Incursions linked to regional connectivity reached 50% of cases in 2022 and are now a major source of residual transmission [14, 19]. For HPAI, infected farms clustered near the coast and the larger rivers, introductions can escalate through farm-to-farm transmission in poultry-dense areas, and H5N1 dispersed through migratory flyways to all provinces and territories of Canada [5, 6, 20, 21].

Host heterogeneity also matters. HPAI persisted in residential wild birds and spread to an increasing number of wild bird species and to many mammals [0, 1, 21, 22]. Wild birds will continue to be a source of novel influenza viruses [25]. Waterfowl-adapted clade 2.3.4.4b viruses had high infectivity and transmissibility in Anseriformes compared to Galliformes [7]. Clinical signs and mortality differ by host and age: ducks reached MR > 3 less often than chickens and may show only drops in feed or water intake or egg production [2, 3, 9, 10].

For surveillance design, the papers point to the following. Monitor coverage at fine scale, since district-level aggregation hid the effects [15, 17, 19]. Set reporting criteria by species and age group, as the Netherlands did with new thresholds, together with early notification under passive surveillance [4, 6, 10, 11]. Monitor viral polymorphisms after transmission from Anseriformes to Galliformes [8]. Focus strategic surveillance on the highest-risk regions and populations [26]. Allow for the bias of wildlife testing towards severe or fatal cases, which means detected infections are a minority of spillovers [23, 24]. Use sentinel surveillance in mosquitoes, birds and horses, and animal die-offs, as early warning [27, 28]. Standardise surveillance design to strengthen its sensitivity for new or unusual events [29].

items.question: How does the choice of bioinformatic pipeline influence the interpretation of microbial community diversity and composition across different sample types?
items.expected:
Comparing an OTU-based and an ASV-based pipeline, the paper finds that both gave comparable results that would generally allow the same interpretations, and phylum-level composition was overall in good agreement. Still, community composition differed between 6.75% and 10.81% per treatment on phylum level, based purely on the pipeline. Biologically driven variability between samples affected the two pipelines differently.

- Thermophilic AD reactors: diversity trends were similar, and the OTU pipeline typically reported slightly higher diversity. Inverse Simpson values were almost identical. Both pipelines allow the same interpretation of alpha diversity. Some genera (Firmicutes, Chloroflexota, Patescibacteria, Hydrothermae) still differed, and several genera were not picked up by one or the other pipeline.

nf-core/sarek 3 (the pipeline in the paper filed as nf-core), at the workflow level:

- The paper states the cost effect four ways: a 70% cost reduction in commercial clouds (abstract), a 69% reduction in compute costs (Introduction), cloud computing costs reduced to approximately 30% (Results) and costs reduced to 50% compared with previous releases (Discussion).

fastp, inside one preprocessing tool:
- Avoids reading and loading data multiple times, which is slow and I/O inefficient, by doing quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering and per-read quality pruning in a single scan of the FASTQ data.

- Can split output into multiple files for parallel processing, by file lines or by file numbers.

Based on the retrieved passages, Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) are considered superior to Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) for modern microbiome comparative analyses for the following reasons:

*   **Direct Comparability:** Unlike OTUs, which are internally generated and analysis-specific, ASVs allow for direct comparisons across different studies [4][5].
*   **Database Independence:** ASVs offer database-independent biological veracity, meaning they are not constrained by the limitations of a specific reference database [7].
*   **Precision:** ASVs are generated via sequencing error correction algorithms, whereas OTUs rely on clustering at a similarity threshold (typically 97%) which can result in inconsistencies [2][5].
*   **Reliability:** ASVs provide a more reliable framework for data handling, helping to improve the consistency of ecological data interpretations [3].
items.question: Why are Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) considered superior to Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) for modern microbiome comparative analyses?
items.expected:
OTUs are clusters of reads that differ by less than a fixed dissimilarity threshold (usually 3%). The clustering is done either de novo or against a reference database (closed-reference). OTUs have no innate biological meaning: each is a "cloud" of similar sequences, not a single species or genus. They are artifacts of either a subjective threshold (de novo) or the reference database (closed-reference). As a result, de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies, and closed-reference clustering loses any biological information that is not in the database.

ASVs can differ by as little as one nucleotide and have no fixed threshold. They are produced by a model-based approach that separates sequencing errors from bona fide biological variation without constructing OTUs. The paper gives these advantages:
- ASVs significantly reduce clustering artifacts, so ASVs generated independently from different samples can be validly compared (cross-study tractability).
- They capture unique biological sequence variation from all phylogenetic lineages, without the limits of closed-reference databases (database-independent biological veracity).
- They avoid the computationally intensive clustering step. Their time and memory requirements are relatively light and scale linearly, which suits routine large-scale microbial monitoring.

For these reasons, replacing OTUs with ASVs has been proposed. The paper notes one concern: ASVs may inflate diversity, because a single bacterial genome can produce multiple ASVs (Schloss, 2021).

items.question: Describe the systematic methodology used to select the final 95 publications from the initial search results, including the databases and criteria involved.
items.expected:
The authors searched the PubMed, Web of Science and Science Direct databases. Only articles in English and from online databases were considered, and the time span was 2011–2022. The last search was on 11 March 2022. The search combined three groups of terms with AND: (i) animal terms (livestock, swine, pig, cattle, poultry, pets, dogs, cats, rats and others); (ii) the Southeast Asian countries or "Southeast Asia"; and (iii) "zoonoses OR zoonotic diseases". It retrieved 2,329 articles: PubMed n = 1043, Web of Science n = 994 and Science Direct n = 292. These were imported into Endnote (version X7), where duplicates were manually identified and removed. The authors also checked that known key articles were in the results.

First screening (titles and abstracts):
- Inclusion: original English research articles (peer-reviewed), published 2011–2022 (by 11th March), presenting prevalence or outbreak data on zoonotic/livestock diseases.
- Exclusion: study not conducted in Southeast Asia, articles about avian influenza, and review articles.
- 674 duplicates were removed and 1,302 publications were excluded: not conducted in Southeast Asia (n = 339), focusing on influenza (n = 145), review articles (n = 91), book chapters (n = 4) and not related to the targeted diseases (n = 723).
- 358 articles went to full-text assessment.

Second screening (full text):
- Inclusion: cross-sectional study, random selection of individuals, and clear description of methods and results.
- 263 articles were excluded: full text unavailable (n = 23), animal selection procedure unclear (n = 156) or results not presented clearly (n = 84). The stated reasons were missing information on how farms and individuals were selected, and poor random selection, such as targeted sampling of animals showing symptoms.
- Grey literature on the articles' reference lists was cross-checked against the search results.

All four authors (TTN, TNM, XSD and HSL) worked independently and classified each article 'Yes' or 'No' for inclusion. Conflicts were settled by discussion among the four reviewers. This left 95 publications in the final qualitative synthesis.

Based on the retrieved passages, the following information is provided regarding the biases of traditional relative microbiome profiling (RMP) and how quantitative microbiome profiling (QMP) addresses them:

*   **RMP Biases:** Relative abundance (RA) exaggerates the proportion of variation explained by factors such as individual, segment, and days post hatch (DPH) [3:0]. It also overestimates microbial community structure variations and the influencing factors [4:0]. Furthermore, RMP misses significant positive taxon–taxon interactions, particularly for the fungal community [4:0].
*   **QMP Solutions:** Quantitative microbiome profiling (QMP) minimizes the compositionality effects introduced by relative microbiome analyses [2:0]. It provides a more accurate representation of real quantitative changes in the chicken gut microbiota [4:0]. Additionally, QMP reveals microbial interactions that RMP misses, offering new clues to understand changes in the microbiota and interactions between microbes and the host [4:0].

**Note:** The retrieved passages do not contain information regarding "culturomics" or its specific role in addressing these biases.
items.question: In what ways do quantitative microbiome profiling (QMP) and culturomics address the biases of traditional relative microbiome profiling (RMP) in livestock research?
items.expected:
QMP (broiler chicken study): QMP combines high-throughput sequencing with a microbial load quantification assay. It turns the sequencing data into an absolute microbiome abundance matrix, so it follows changes in absolute abundance (AA), meaning whether a species thrives or withers over time. This minimizes the compositionality effects of relative analyses. Compared with QMP, RMP:
- ignored the absolute growth or decline of microbes and biased the developmental trajectory (by QMP, absolute numbers were relatively stable across segments and over time);
- exaggerated the variation explained by individual, segment and DPH;
- overestimated positive correlations in the bacteriome (e.g. 402 vs. 196 in the duodenum) and missed positive correlations in the mycobiome (e.g. 1048 vs. 2270 in the cecum).

Culturomics (swine study): the paper does not frame culture-dependent (CD) profiling as correcting RMP. It recovers taxa that culture-independent (CI) sequencing missed, and it gives the likely causes as low relative abundance below the detection limits of sequencing depth, incomplete lysis of bacterial cells during DNA extraction, or unfavorable PCR amplification. CD methods found 244, 411, 507 and 510 new ASVs at the four time points, including core ASVs and novel species. In one case Bacteroides relative abundance fell below CI detection, but culture suggested its absolute abundance might not decrease, because other taxa may have proliferated more.

Review: the livestock review says only that combining culturomics with shotgun metagenomics may give a more exhaustive picture of the gut in pigs.

QMP addresses RMP bias directly: it combines sequencing with a microbial load assay and produces an absolute abundance matrix [0, 3], so it follows whether taxa thrive or wither and shows real community dynamics [1, 2], minimizing compositionality effects [9]. Against QMP, RMP ignored absolute growth or decline and biased trajectories [4, 7, 8, 10], exaggerated the variation explained by individual, segment and DPH [5, 11], and overestimated or missed taxon–taxon correlations [6, 12]. Culturomics works on a different limitation of sequencing-based profiling: it recovers taxa missed for low relative abundance, shallow sequencing depth, incomplete lysis or unfavorable PCR amplification [14, 16], adding 244, 411, 507 and 510 ASVs across the four time points [15] and isolating core ASVs and novel species [20], which shows a more diverse microbiota [13]. Its Bacteroides example touches the compositional problem: relative abundance fell below detection while culture suggested absolute abundance might not decrease, as other taxa may have proliferated more [17, 18, 19]. The livestock review adds only that culturomics combined with shotgun metagenomics may give a more exhaustive picture of the gut [21].
concepts: RA exaggerated the proportion of variation
lower relative abundance and shallow sequencing depth
Bacteroides absolute abundance might not decrease

*   **Coverage:** **CoverM v. 0.6.1** was used to determine relative abundance with parameters including `--min-read-aligned-percent 75%`, `--min-read-percent-identity 95%`, and `--min-covered-fraction 0` [source_file:22_pig_mags.pdf:page_1].

items.expected: Reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic v. 0.38 (quality score threshold 15 over a sliding window of 4 bp, minimum length of 50 bp), which also removed sequencing adapters. Host reads were removed by alignment to the Sus scrofa genome (Sscrofa11.1) with Bowtie2 v. 2.4.2-1. MEGAHIT v. 1.29.0 co-assembled the metagenomes and also assembled each one individually. Before co-assembly, samples were normalized with BBNorm (BBTools v. 38.79). Reads were mapped back to the assemblies with Bowtie2, and contigs with a minimum length of 2,000 bp were binned with MetaBAT 2. CheckM v. 1.1.2 assessed the bins, and MAGs with greater than 90% completeness and less than 5% contamination were retained. This gave 2,327 MAGs from the individual assemblies and 85,145 from the co-assemblies, 87,472 in total, from 738 Gb of sequencing data. dRep v. 3.2.2 dereplicated these MAGs with primary clustering at 90% and secondary clustering at 99% ANI. The result was 1,150 non-redundant MAGs (potentially unique strains), which were used for all subsequent analyses. With 95% ANI for secondary clustering, 758 putative species were produced instead. Taxonomy was assigned with GTDB-tk 2.0.0 and GTDB release 207.

Based on the retrieved passages, the impact of using Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) versus Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) on microbial community interpretation is as follows:

**Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs)**
*   **Internal Generation and Lack of Comparability:** OTUs are internally generated and analysis-specific, meaning they lack direct comparability with other studies [5][8].
*   **Bias and Variability:** OTU-based approaches can be biased toward certain phyla and are susceptible to user- and input-defined biases or errors that may go unnoticed [7]. Additionally, clustering methods used to generate OTUs can introduce variability between pipelines, resulting in community composition differences ranging from 6.75% to 10.81% [1][6].
*   **Data Loss:** In closed-reference clustering, biological information outside of the database is lost from the sequencing data [8].

**Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs)**
*   **Accuracy and Error Correction:** ASVs are generated based on sequencing error correction algorithms, which allows for the identification of exact sequence variants [1].
*   **Thoroughness:** ASVs provide a more precise representation of the microbial community compared to OTUs [1][3].
*   **Contamination Control:** ASVs can be used in in silico contamination identification models to accurately discriminate contaminants and reduce batch effects [3].

**Comparability**
*   **General Agreement:** While the two approaches differ in their specific outputs, the outcomes of OTU and ASV-based pipelines generally provide comparable results that allow for the same ecological interpretations [1].
*   **Prerequisites:** However, the comparability between pipelines is excellent only if specific prerequisites regarding sequencing and sequence handling design are met; otherwise, pipeline-derived differences can affect interpretations [4].
items.question: Contrast the impact of using Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) versus Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) on microbial community interpretation as discussed in recent microbiome studies.
items.expected:
28_otu_vs_asv ran the same data through VSEARCH (clustering into OTUs) and DADA2 (error correction into exact ASVs). Both pipelines gave comparable results that generally allow the same interpretations. Even so, community composition differed by 6.75% to 10.81% at phylum level, based purely on the pipeline.

Findings in 28_otu_vs_asv:
- **Spurious OTUs.** OTU approaches overestimate diversity and produce spurious OTUs. The study saw this too, but relative abundance thresholds easily mitigated it: a cutoff as little as 0.001% removed enough spurious or rare taxa to fall within the ranges produced by the ASV pipeline. The ASV pipeline outputs fewer to no spurious variants and is precise to a single base.
- **Alpha diversity.** Trends were similar, and the OTU pipeline typically reported slightly higher diversity. The two pipelines diverged for the psychrophilic PWASS samples, where the inverse Simpson index differed at times by a factor greater than two.
- **Community composition.** Pipeline choice significantly influenced reported composition. Over more than 170 days, the dissimilarity between pipelines was greater than the dissimilarity between treatments. The ASV pipeline showed the influence of time and co-substrate more clearly.
- **Consequences.** These differences could lead to different conclusions and could interfere with downstream analyses such as network analysis. On the reduced dataset they would suggest that the pipeline affects composition more than any treatment, a conclusion with no foundation in experimental reality.
- **Comparability.** OTUs are analysis-specific and give no direct comparability with other studies. ASVs are directly comparable between studies.

Findings in 29_16s_best_practices (a review):
- OTUs are clustered at an arbitrary threshold (often 3%) and have no innate biological meaning.
- De novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies, and closed-reference clustering loses information that lies outside the database.
- ASVs significantly reduce clustering artifacts, allow valid comparison, are not restricted by reference databases and need relatively light computation.
- One concern with ASVs is possible diversity inflation from multiple ASVs generated from a single bacterial genome.

23_swine_cultivation does not compare the two approaches.

Both papers say OTUs come from clustering, are analysis-specific and cannot be compared directly between studies [0, 4, 5, 23, 26]. They also say ASVs come from error correction, resolve single-base differences and are directly comparable [0, 6, 13, 22, 27, 28]. 29 adds that OTUs have no innate biological meaning and that clustering affects biological interpretation [24, 25]. 28 measured the effect on interpretation. Overall, the two pipelines allow the same interpretations [1, 14], but phylum-level composition differed by 6.75% to 10.81% [2, 9]. Diversity estimates diverged for the PWASS samples [8, 15]. Pipeline choice significantly influenced composition, and the dissimilarity between pipelines exceeded the dissimilarity between treatments [17, 18, 20]. These differences could lead to different or unfounded conclusions [3, 21]. The papers place the diversity bias differently. 28 reports that OTU approaches overestimate diversity with spurious OTUs and that abundance thresholds mitigate this [7, 10, 11, 12]. 29 records the concern that ASVs may inflate diversity through multiple ASVs per genome [30]. 29 also says ASVs need lighter computation [31].
concepts: de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies

The retrieved passages provide evidence that both direct and indirect pathways link the host genome to animal phenotypes via the gut (or rumen) microbiome, but they focus primarily on dairy cattle.  

**Direct effects:** The host genome can influence microbial abundances through quantitative trait loci (QTL) or expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) that affect specific microbes such as *Rikenellaceae* RC9 and other families (Prevotellaceae, Lachnospiraceae). These genetic variants act on the microbiome directly, altering its composition and functional capacity.  

**Indirect effects:** The host genome also shapes phenotypes indirectly by modulating traits that in turn affect microbial communities—for example, dry‑matter intake (DMI), residual feed intake (RFI), or passage rate. Changes in these feeding or physiological parameters alter rumen retention time, digestibility, and microbial growth dynamics, thereby influencing microbiome composition and function.  

In dairy cows, integrating genomic scans with Bayesian network analyses revealed both direct genetic links to microbes and indirect pathways mediated by host‑controlled traits, supporting the use of specific microbes as correlated traits in breeding programs [1][4][5]. In pigs, similar mechanisms are suggested by studies showing that host genetics can affect gut microbial abundances and that these microbes may influence phenotypes such as growth or health [9] (though the passages do not detail indirect pathways for pigs).  

Thus, while direct genetic effects on microbiome composition have been demonstrated in dairy cows, indirect influences mediated through feeding behavior and other host traits also play a crucial role. The evidence for analogous mechanisms in pigs is less explicit but implied by the broader discussion of host‑microbiome genetics [9].

Galaxy is intended also for non-programmers but is mainly restricted to skilled bioinformaticians for complex tasks. Its pipeline output is not standardized, and expert users must add annotation libraries by modifying pipelines. At the other extreme, QuickNGS achieves high automation at the expense of flexibility, because parameters cannot be set.

The transition from nursing to weaning is associated with a pronounced shift in the pig gut microbiome.  During nursing the microbiota are dominated by lactobacilli, Prevotella, and other taxa that thrive on milk‑derived substrates; as pigs approach weaning these groups decline while members of families such as Enterobacteriaceae (e.g., Escherichia/Shigella) become more abundant [23_swine_cultivation.pdf:0].  Metagenome‑assembled genomes show that MAGs classified as *Bacteroides*, *Prevotellaceae* and related taxa are highly enriched in nursing piglets, whereas after weaning the relative abundance of these groups drops and other lineages—including *Clostridiaceae* and various unclassified genera—rise to higher levels [23_swine_cultivation.pdf:0; 22_pig_mags.pdf:0].  

In short, nursing is characterized by a high proportion of lactobacilli, Prevotella and related families, while weaning triggers a transition toward a more diverse community with increased representation of Enterobacteriaceae‑related taxa and other bacterial groups that were previously low‑abundance [23_swine_cultivation.pdf:0; 22_pig_mags.pdf:0].  

**Sources:**  
- [23_swine_cultivation.pdf:0] – “Bacillus, Mitsuokella, and Prevotella were also observed …” (relative abundances listed for lactation stage).  
- [22_pig_mags.pdf:0] – MAG abundance changes before vs. after weaning; specific taxa such as *Limousia pullorum*, *B. fragilis*, *E. coli* and others shift in relative abundance during the nursing‑to‑weaning transition.
items.question: Based on the study's findings, how does the transition from nursing to weaning impact the taxonomic composition and relative abundance of specific bacterial groups in pigs?
items.expected:
The diet changes abruptly at weaning, from liquid and milk-based to solid and based on cereal grains. By 7 days postweaning, the relative abundance of a large number of MAGs had shifted significantly (MaAsLin2, immediately before weaning versus 7 days postweaning).

Decreases: 69 MAGs fell in relative abundance. The most differentially abundant were Limousia pullorum, B. fragilis, E. coli, P. hyovaginalis and P. vulgatus. C. coli and S. pasteurianus MAGs were also enriched in preweaned piglets. Six MAGs above 0.1% in nursing piglets were not detected in the same pigs 7 d later: B. thetaiotaomicron, Bulleidia sp., Enterococcus faecalis, Mediterraneibacter torques, Parvimonas sp. and P. hyovaginalis. One E. faecalis MAG was relatively abundant in nursing samples (0.25 ± 0.07%, printed '0.25 6 0.07%') and was not detected in any postweaning sample. It may represent a strain unique to nursing piglets.

Increases: 140 MAGs rose in relative abundance, including Copromorpha sp., Clostridium sp000435835, Fusicatenibacter saccharivorans, Intestinibacter sp., Oliverpabstia intestinalis, Phascolarctobacterium sp004558595, Prevotella sp002251295, Prevotella sp004556065 and Ruminococcus sp003011855. They also included uncultured potential butyrate producers (CAG-83 sp., Aphodosoma sp900769035, Copromorpha sp., Egerieousia sp004561775, UMGS1668 sp004556975).

Genus level: earlier studies (38-40) report that weaning lowers Bacteroides and Escherichia and raises Blautia, Prevotella and Roseburia. Many of this study's differentially abundant MAGs were assigned to these genera, but several belonged to taxa not known to be associated with weaning.

On an NMDS plot of Bray-Curtis dissimilarities, the preweaned samples appear separate from the postweaned samples of other studies.

items.question: Assess the role of Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) in replacing or augmenting phenotypic testing for international antimicrobial resistance (AMR) monitoring.
items.expected:
Both contributing papers present WGS as augmenting phenotypic AMR testing, not replacing it. Paper 41 (Salmonella) says WGS detects AMR determinants with a high level of concordance with phenotypic tests while also assigning species, serovar and genotype. It reports a high correlation with phenotypic testing in this study and highly accurate prediction in earlier work on non-typhoidal Salmonella. It states that sequencing data complement phenotypic methods and that WGS is "not without limitations and cannot totally replace phenotypic methods". Applied to global surveillance, it can show the early emergence and spread of AMR and inform policy, and routine genomic sequencing will enable real-time monitoring of AMR genes entering the food chain. Paper 42 (Campylobacter, Thailand) calls WGS an essential tool for genotypic AMR surveillance from national to global scales (GLASS). It notes that several countries with established systems, for example the US NARMS, have started to integrate WGS. In its data, genotype matched phenotype for some drugs and not others. The gyrA T86I mutation was found in 96% of quinolone-resistant isolates and tet(O) matched tetracycline resistance at 100%. Macrolides showed a lower association: erm(B) was present in only 2 of 9 erythromycin-resistant isolates, possibly because of unexamined determinants such as L4 and L22 mutations. Paper 42 also warns that different computational pipelines may give considerably different results and that accuracy depends on how comprehensive the reference databases are. It recommends WGS-based AMR surveillance under One Health in Thailand and other low- and middle-income countries. Paper 43 does not address WGS.

Both papers present WGS as a tool for AMR surveillance beyond the national level. Paper 41 says its application to global surveillance can provide information on the early emergence and spread of AMR and inform policy [1]. Paper 42 calls it essential for genotypic AMR surveillance from national to global scales and notes that several countries, including the US through NARMS, have integrated it [7, 8, 9, 10]. Paper 41 reports high concordance and correlation between WGS-based AMR prediction and phenotypic tests [0, 4, 5]. Paper 42 finds that agreement depends on the drug class: 96% for the gyrA T86I mutation with quinolone resistance and 100% for tet(O) with tetracycline, but a lower association for macrolides, where erm(B) was present in only 2 of 9 erythromycin-resistant isolates [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. Paper 42 attributes the macrolide discordance possibly to unexamined determinants such as L4 and L22 mutations [17], and notes that predictions vary between computational pipelines and depend on the comprehensiveness of reference databases [18, 19]. Paper 41 accordingly describes WGS as complementing phenotypic methods and states that it cannot totally replace them [2, 3]. Both papers point to routine or new WGS-based monitoring: real-time monitoring of AMR genes entering the food chain [6], and WGS-based One Health surveillance in Thailand and other low- and middle-income countries [20].

The analysis of whole‑genome sequences showed that the AMR determinants detected in **imported raw chicken** isolates were largely confined to a few well‑known resistance genes (e.g., aminoglycoside, fluoroquinolone, tetracycline and sulphonamide resistance) and these isolates tended to cluster into distinct clades with limited genetic diversity [1][2].  

In contrast, the **imported edible leaves** isolates displayed a markedly broader AMR landscape: three percent of leaf‑derived Salmonella carried at least one resistance phenotype, including chloramphenicol resistance mediated by efflux pump genes (floR, cml1) and additional resistance determinants such as floR, cml1, and various plasmid‑borne genes [3][4]. Moreover, the leaf isolates represented a diverse set of serovars—most commonly S. Virchow, S. Newport and S. Bareilly—whereas chicken isolates were dominated by fewer serotypes (e.g., S. Heidelberg) and showed distinct temporal clades that emerged in the early 2000s [1][8].  

Thus, while raw‑chicken Salmonella exhibited a relatively uniform AMR gene repertoire and limited serovar diversity, edible‑leaf Salmonella displayed a wider variety of resistance genes (including specific efflux pumps) and a richer serovar distribution, reflecting differing contamination sources and import pathways.  

**Sources:** [1], [3], [4], [8]
items.question: Based on the findings, how do the antimicrobial resistance (AMR) profiles and serovar distributions differ between Salmonella found in imported raw chicken versus imported edible leaves?
items.expected: AMR: resistance was rare among Salmonella from imported edible leaves but common, including MDR, among those from imported raw chicken. Of the 115 leaf isolates, three (3%) had AMR determinants, all from three curry leaf samples, and two (2%) were MDR. 97% of leaf isolates had a genotypic profile in line with the typical intrinsic resistance to aminoglycosides. Of the 231 chicken isolates, 214 (93%) had at least one mutation or resistance gene determinant, most commonly to β-lactams, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines or sulphonamides, and only 17 (7%) had none. 164 (71%) were MDR, and these came from all four countries of origin. In chicken, 170 (74%) had β-lactam resistance determinants (blaCMY-2 the most common, 54%) and 222 (96%) had at least one QRDR mutation. Serovars: leaves showed a larger diversity of serovars than chicken. The paper gives the leaf count as 33, 29 or 30 in different places; chicken has 16 throughout. Curry leaves had the most diversity (23). The most common leaf serovars were S. Virchow (20.9%), S. Newport (11.3%) and S. Bareilly (7.8%). Chicken was dominated by S. Heidelberg (138, 60%), all from Brazil except one isolate of unrecorded origin, followed by S. Minnesota (9%) and S. Enteritidis (7%). All S. Heidelberg isolates had resistance genes for fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and sulphonamides, and the paper reports S. Heidelberg from Brazil as resistant to three or more antimicrobial classes. The authors say antimicrobials are less likely to be used in farming edible leaves, which may account for the larger serovar diversity in leaves.

items.question: What is the function of the 'motifPosperc' metric within the pipe4C data processing pipeline, and what value indicates high specificity?
items.expected: motifPosperc is a data quality metric in the pipe4C report file, used for quality assessment of individual 4C-seq experiments. It is the percentage of reads in the FASTQ file in which the first RE motif position is equal to the most occurring first RE enzyme motif position. To compute it, reads are scanned from the 5′ side for the first primary RE motif. The pipeline then trims all reads from their 5′-end to that fixed location, leaving the RE motif intact. In a good 4C experiment, with no a-specific amplification from undesired genomic locations, the value should typically be >90%. A lower percentage might indicate off target binding of the primer to the genome or low sequence quality reads.

The data show that the V394D mutation disrupts MYC’s ability to bind MIZ1 and that this loss directly impairs liver‑tumor formation.  In the tet‑MYC‑VD model, embryos develop MYC‑dependent hepatoblastomas at high penetrance, whereas mice bearing the V394D mutant exhibit markedly delayed tumor onset and reduced tumor burden compared with wild‑type MYC [5].  Moreover, when MYC‑ERWT and MYC‑ERVD cells are injected into the mouse liver, only the WT form generates rapidly expanding tumors; the VD mutant produces far fewer and smaller tumors [7].  Finally, knock‑down of MIZ1 in MYC‑ERWT cells reduces sphere‑forming efficiency to the level seen with the VD mutant, indicating that the transformation defect of the VD protein is fully attributable to loss of MIZ1 interaction [8].

Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the physical interaction between MYC and its cofactor MIZ1 is essential for:

* **Activation of a specific transcriptional program** required for rapid proliferation of hepatic tumor cells.  
* **Suppression of differentiation/apoptosis pathways** (e.g., TGF‑β–dependent autocrine signaling) that would otherwise limit tumor growth [4, 8].  
* **Maintenance of the undifferentiated, progenitor‑like state** of liver tumor cells; loss of MIZ1 binding leads to premature differentiation and a marked reduction in tumorigenic potential.

Thus, the MYC‑MIZ1 interaction functions as a critical molecular switch that drives the transcriptional circuitry underlying MYC‑dependent hepatoblastoma development.  

\[
\boxed{\text{The MYC–MIZ1 interaction is required for MYC to drive the transcriptional program that sustains rapid proliferation and blocks differentiation in liver tumor cells; disruption of this interaction (as in the V394D mutant) severely impairs liver tumor initiation and growth.}}
\]
items.question: Based on the findings regarding the V394D mutant, what is the functional significance of the MYC-MIZ1 interaction in the context of liver tumor development?
items.expected: The V394D mutant (MYC-VD), a MYC mutant defective in MIZ1 binding, shows that the MYC-MIZ1 interaction is required for MYC to transform liver cells and thus for initiation of liver tumorigenesis, and not for MYC-driven proliferation, for transcriptional activation, or for the aggressiveness of tumours once formed. (1) Tumour onset: tet-MYC-VD animals showed delayed tumorigenesis, with median survival 13 weeks against 5 weeks for tet-MYC-WT, and tet-MYC-VD in the liver showed significantly reduced tumorigenic potential relative to wild-type MYC; once formed, MYC-WT- and MYC-VD-induced tumours appeared equally aggressive, with comparable liver weights and tumour load. (2) Cellular level: MYC-WT and MYC-VD led to similar increases in the number of fetal hepatoblasts recovered per embryo, suggesting equivalent proliferative activities, but MYC-VD showed marked defects in cellular transformation, in vitro by sphere formation in methylcellulose and in vivo by subcutaneous tumour growth in CD1-nude mice, and MYC-ER VD cells showed a marked decrease in sphere-forming ability. Knockdown of MIZ1 with either of two different shRNAs (#8 and #9) decreased sphere-forming efficiency of MYC-ER WT to levels comparable with MYC-ER VD, so the deficit in cellular transformation of the VD mutant was entirely attributable to its interaction with MIZ1. The authors conclude that while retaining normal proliferative activity, MYC-VD is defective in cellular transformation, affecting most likely the frequency of tumour initiation in vivo. (3) Transcriptional mechanism: the defect is selective for repression. Secondary response genes were similarly deregulated in both genotypes, and MYC-VD is as effective as WT in transcriptional activation, whereas primary MYC-repressed genes showed weaker downregulation in MYC-VD tumours, with 285 genes repressed with a 2-fold lower efficiency in MYC-VD relative to MYC-WT tumours, enriching for functional categories including cell adhesion/response to wounding. Already at a pretumoral stage, in tet-MYC-WT and tet-MYC-VD fetal hepatoblasts purified by magnetic cell sorting, the two populations showed comparable activation of the MYC-induced gene Smpdl3b but defective repression of Cdkn1a by MYC-VD. Hence MIZ1-dependent repression plays an important role in MYC-induced liver tumorigenesis, and the requirement for the MYC-MIZ1 interaction differs among tumour types: suppression of TGFb-mediated senescence in T-cell lymphomas, maintenance of stemness in medulloblastoma, and tumour initiation in the liver in this work.

The retrieved passages indicate that the genomic distribution of sequencing reads is used to assess whether a 4C‑seq run has worked properly.  

* The protocol notes that “a successful 4C‑seq experiment should always show a strong enrichment of contacts with DNA fragments flanking the viewpoint on the linear chromosome (in particular, the DNA fragments co‑occupying the same TAD).” [source_file:50_4cseq_protocol.pdf:Page 0]  
* It further states that “Preferably >60% of the reads should map to the chromosome that contains the viewpoint (the cis chromosome), with most reads mapping within 1 Mb of the viewpoint.” [source_file:50_4cseq_protocol.pdf:Page 0]  

Thus, a proper distribution—characterized by a high proportion of reads mapping to the same chromosome as the viewpoint and concentrated near it—serves as an indicator that the experiment has been successful.
items.question: How does the distribution of sequencing reads across the genome serve as an indicator of a successful 4C-seq experiment?
items.expected: A successful 4C-seq experiment should always show a strong enrichment of contacts with DNA fragments flanking the viewpoint on the linear chromosome, in particular fragments co-occupying the same TAD. Preferably >60% of the reads map to the chromosome containing the viewpoint (the cis chromosome), with most reads mapping within 1 Mb of the viewpoint. Self-ligation of the viewpoint fragment and undigested DNA can heavily skew these metrics, so they should be assessed after exclusion of the top fragments (fragMappedCisCorr and cov1Mb). The viewpoint should also capture many different fragments: >40%, preferably >60%, of mappable fragment ends within 100 kb of the viewpoint should be captured at least once (capt100Kb > 40%). Low-complexity libraries (capt100Kb < 40%) often result from bad template quality rather than insufficient sequencing depth. With (previously frozen) primary tissue, the cis percentage frequently drops to ~50%. That drop indicates random ligations, but the local coverage around the viewpoint is often still good enough to draw reproducible conclusions.

The ISSE framework measures the **level of One Health (OH) integration** by applying a structured, multi‑level evaluation approach that asks specific questions at each tier of the surveillance system.  

1. **Evaluation Levels Defined in the Framework** – The authors describe five hierarchical levels (or “tiers”) that capture how deeply OH principles are embedded in a surveillance activity [2]. These levels range from basic coordination between human‑health and animal‑health sectors to full, cross‑sectoral integration where data, analyses, and decision‑making are jointly produced.  

2. **Key Evaluation Questions** – At each level the framework poses targeted questions that probe:  
   - *Collaboration mechanisms* (e.g., formal agreements, joint governance) [4]  
   - *Data sharing practices* across sectors [1]  
   - *Analytical integration* of human, animal, and environmental data [7]  
   - *Impact assessment* on health outcomes and economic costs [8]  

3. **Technical Scoring Mechanism** – Although the exact scoring algorithm is not spelled out in the excerpt, the framework’s design explicitly links each answer to a measurable indicator of integration (e.g., presence of joint data platforms, frequency of cross‑sectoral meetings, extent of shared analytical tools). These indicators are then aggregated to produce a composite score that reflects the overall OH integration level [9].  

4. **Application to Surveillance Systems** – By mapping these questions onto concrete surveillance components (e.g., data collection from humans, livestock, and environment; joint analysis; dissemination of integrated findings), evaluators can technically rate how well each system incorporates OH principles across its activities [1] [2].

In short, the ISSE framework quantifies One Health integration by systematically evaluating collaboration, data sharing, analytical integration, and impact assessment through defined levels and associated questions, producing a technical score that reflects the degree of cross‑sectoral embedding within surveillance systems.  

**Sources:** [1] Cécile Aenishaenslin et al., *Evaluating the Integration of One Health in Surveillance Systems for Antimicrobial Use and Resistance: A Conceptual Framework*, p.0; [2] same document, p.0; [4] same document, p.0; [7] same document, p.0; [8] same document, p.0; [9] same document, p.0.
items.question: How does the ISSE framework technically measure the level of One Health integration across different surveillance activities?
items.expected:
Integration is measured at the first evaluation level, which evaluates the integration of a OH approach across the different components of the surveillance system. The evaluator first answers three questions with a descriptive qualitative methodology: focus groups or individual interviews with key informants from the surveillance team, external end-users and AMR/AMU experts. That information is then used to assess the overall level of integration on a semi-quantitative scale (Table 3). Integration is treated as a continuum (multiple levels of integration), not a dichotomy. The scale defines six levels of OH integration, 0 to 5, for each of four surveillance activities: data collection, analyses, interpretation and dissemination. The levels are defined with respect to the type of information integrated, the integration into operations and processes (e.g., standardization of measures), and the integration of multiple institutions, disciplines and perspectives. Table 3 gives criteria for each level, for example the lowest and highest:
- Data collection: level 0 means the system does not collect data from sources other than humans. Level 5 means AMR data in >1 bacteria species from >1 animal source including retail food, AND from at least one collection point in the environment, AND AMU data in ≥1 animal species and humans.
- Data analysis: level 0 means separate, non-standardized analyses by different analysts in ≥2 organizations. Level 5 means conjoint analysis by a team of analysts, with formal statistical testing and multivariable statistical approaches or modeling.
- Data interpretation: level 0 means there are no formal integrated analyses. Level 5 means a team with multispecies/multidisciplinary/multiperspective expertise, including external collaborators/stakeholders from different sectors.
- Information dissemination: level 0 means animal and human information goes separately to animal and human health stakeholders. Level 5 means conjoint reporting by one organization, with means of dissemination adapted to different end-users.
concepts: data collection, analyses, interpretation, and dissemination

The One Health framework emphasizes that human health, animal (livestock and wildlife) health, and environmental health are tightly linked.  When these three domains interact, they create a continuous cycle in which antimicrobial‑resistant bacteria and genes can move back and forth among them:

* **Human ↔ Animal transmission** – Resistant pathogens or resistance genes from people can be shed into the environment (e.g., through feces, urine, or wastewater) and then contaminate water sources that are used by animals or reach farms.  Conversely, resistant microbes originating in livestock can be transferred to humans through direct contact, consumption of animal products, or environmental exposure [1] [2].

* **Animal ↔ Environmental transmission** – Antimicrobial use in agriculture selects for resistant bacteria in the gut microbiota of livestock and wildlife.  These resistant organisms are released into soils and waterways via manure, runoff, or spray‑irrigation, where they can persist, multiply, and spread to other environmental reservoirs [3] [4].

* **Environmental ↔ Human transmission** – Resistant bacteria and mobile resistance genes present in soil, surface water, or sediments can be taken up by crops, leach into drinking‑water supplies, or be aerosolized.  Humans exposed through ingestion, bathing, or occupational contact become colonised or infected with resistant strains, completing the loop back to the human domain [3] [5].

* **Feedback within each domain** – Inadequate sanitation, poor waste management, and uncontrolled antimicrobial use in any one sector amplify resistance pressures that spill over into the others.  For example, untreated hospital effluents can deposit resistant organisms into rivers that irrigate fields where animals graze, thereby re‑introducing resistance into the animal–environment interface [6] [7].

Together, these interconnections mean that a resistance event in one domain quickly propagates to the others, reinforcing and amplifying the overall cycle of antimicrobial‑resistance dissemination.  Effective mitigation therefore requires coordinated surveillance, regulation, and stewardship across all three One Health domains [2] [8].  

**Sources:**  
- [1] Pandey et al., “Antibiotics resistant genes…”, J. Anim Sci Technol. (2023) – discussion of inter‑domain spread.  
- [2] Pandey et al., Conclusion, J. Anim Sci Technol. (2023) – emphasis on One Health approach to curb AR.  
- [3] Velazquez‑Meza et al., “Antimicrobial resistance: One Health approach”, (2023) – description of transmission pathways among humans, animals, and environment.  
- [4] Delpy et al., “Integrated surveillance systems…”, BMC Public Health (2024) – Table on dissemination modalities across domains.  
- [5] Velazquez‑Meza et al., “One Health approach to combat AMR”, (2023) – highlights need for cross‑sectoral collaboration.  
- [6] Aenishaenslin et al., “Evaluating the Integration of One Health…”, (2024) – outlines environmental release pathways.

items.question: How do the interconnected domains of the One Health framework contribute to the cycle of antimicrobial resistance dissemination?
items.expected:
The review calls AR a One Health issue because livestock, humans and the environment are interconnected, which opens channels for transmission of antibiotic resistant bacteria (ARB). AR is linked to each domain through reckless and excessive antibiotic use in agriculture, livestock farming and human medicine. The interconnections create pathways for bacteria, mobile genetic elements (MGEs) and antibiotics themselves, and movement between compartments promotes the spread of AR. Each domain contributes:
- Humans: careless antibiotic use drives ARB and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), which pass to other humans through direct contact, food, water and environmental surfaces.
- Livestock: antibiotic use contributes to resistant bacteria, which reach humans through direct contact and food products. They reach the environment through livestock waste, and pathogens pass into the environment through air, slurry and feces from livestock, acting as a source of ARGs.
- Environment: environmental contamination is a major factor in dissemination. Residues from the pharmaceutical industry, livestock husbandry, hospitals, fecal waste from humans and animals, and agricultural runoff make it a hidden source of resistant organisms. ARB persist in soil and water and can potentially spread to animals and humans who contact contaminated sources.
The cycle closes when bacteria released in the feces of livestock and humans act as an environmental reservoir before reintroduction into the livestock-human cycle. At the human-animal-environment interface, AR bacterial clones, MGEs and ARGs carry the dissemination. MGEs (plasmids, transposons, integrons) act as vehicles, and together these components promote horizontal genetic exchange. Changes in one domain can have far-reaching effects on the others, and the Fig. 1 legend shows pathways running in every direction among the three domains. The review notes that it is not yet clear how much livestock-derived routes contribute compared with human-derived routes.
concepts: the use of antibiotics in livestock

Short‑chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are produced when gut microbes ferment dietary fiber.  These fermentation products can be absorbed by the host’s intestinal epithelium, enter the portal circulation, and travel systemically where they act as signaling molecules that influence lipid metabolism in peripheral tissues such as adipose tissue and skeletal muscle [1].  

In pigs, direct SCFA administration into the ileum has been shown to lower expression of fatty‑acid synthase (FAS) and acetyl‑CoA carboxylase—key enzymes for de novo lipogenesis—thereby reducing fat accumulation in the longissimus dorsi muscle [4].  This demonstrates that SCFAs can modulate host lipid synthesis pathways.  

SCFAs also affect energy balance by providing an additional caloric source (≈10–15 % of total energy) and by activating gut‑derived hormones such as peptide YY (PYY) and glucagon‑like peptide‑1 (GLP‑1), which promote satiety and improve insulin sensitivity, ultimately limiting excess fat storage [1].  

Moreover, SCFAs help maintain the integrity of the intestinal barrier and stimulate mucosal growth, which together support efficient nutrient absorption while preventing metabolic endotoxemia that can drive adiposity [4][7].  Together, these mechanisms link dietary fiber intake to reduced host fat accumulation through microbial production of SCFAs.  

**Citations:** [1], [4]
items.question: How do short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) bridge the gap between dietary fiber intake and the regulation of host fat accumulation and metabolism?
items.expected:
Gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber (host-indigestible carbohydrates) into SCFAs, chiefly acetate, propionate and butyrate. Dietary fiber intake therefore influences SCFA levels and composition. Colonic cells absorb SCFAs through monocarboxylate transporters, passive diffusion or bicarbonate exchange. Inside these cells, SCFAs are converted to acetyl-CoA or propynyl-CoA, which produces ATP. SCFAs the colonic cells do not metabolize travel through the portal circulation to the liver, where they serve as an energy substrate. Only small amounts reach the systemic circulation. There they increase insulin secretion, maintain energy homeostasis and improve the function of the liver, skeletal muscles and adipose tissue.

The review cites four links from SCFAs to fat:
- Acetate-dependent GPR43 stimulation in white adipose tissue improved glucose and lipid metabolism.
- In rabbits, acetate reduced intramuscular triglyceride levels by increasing fatty acid uptake and fatty acid oxidation, and PPARα was associated with this reduction in fat.
- Low-fat pigs had more butyrate-producing bacteria and more SCFA formation, especially butyrate, which alleviated fat deposition.
- SCFA administration into the ileum of growing pigs inhibited mRNA expression of fatty acid synthase (FAS) and acetyl-CoA carboxylase in the longissimus dorsi.

The review concludes that through these effects on muscle and fat tissue, SCFAs influence meat quality.

items.question: Compare the organizational models and economic benefits of integrated One Health surveillance systems as discussed in global reviews and regional case studies.
items.expected:
Organisational models.
- Global review (integrated antibiotic-resistance surveillance): 14 integrated antibiotic-resistance surveillance systems, all operating in high-income countries; the review found no operating integrated system in LMICs. It sets out integration along two dimensions, information integration and structural integration, and groups the systems into four distinct clusters:
  - Group 1 (six systems) mainly operates in silos, with data analysed separately by each sector.
  - Group 2 (four systems: DANMAP, NORM/NORM-VET, SWEDRES/SVARM, NARMS) has a high level of integration at both structural and informational levels.
  - Group 3 (CIPARS, SONAAR) is supervised solely by the human health sector.
  - Group 4 (ZoMo, FINRES-Vet) is supervised by the food safety sector, with the animal health sector for ZoMo.
  At governance level, four systems are supervised by a multi-sectoral body and five separately by each sector. Some authors consider governance more effective when there is an intersectoral committee (DANMAP) or a single supervising organisation (CIPARS). The level of resources and the regulatory framework appeared to play a major role in how integrated surveillance was set up and organised.
- The data-driven One Health paper describes:
  - an inter-agency technical working group set up after the 2008 Hendra virus outbreak in Australia;
  - multisectoral partnerships, in contrast to preparedness and surveillance plans that in most countries are often developed by a single sector;
  - data-driven coordinated surveillance with machine learning modelling capability.
- The One Health in Africa paper describes the African Union's interagency One Health Coordinating Group on Zoonotic Diseases, the Africa CDC Framework for One Health Practice in National Public Health Institutes (coordinated surveillance and data sharing), and a continental strategy at national, regional and continental levels. It notes gaps in political commitment, skilled workforce, domestic financing and legal frameworks, and that many countries lack formal and funded One Health programs.

Economic benefits.
- The review reports no monetary benefit. Integration is associated with a financial and social cost; intersectoral coordination remains costly and funding is usually lacking; integration outcomes are poorly described and rarely available. The outcomes it reports are non-monetary: less antibiotic use in animals and humans, and the poultry sector stopped using ceftiofur, after which resistance to it in salmonella fell.
- The data-driven One Health paper cites returns of over €1 million in savings from integrated West Nile virus surveillance and response, and 26% savings in operational cost from hosting human and animal health laboratories under one roof. It says coordination can save costs by preventing duplication and provides a positive return on investment, that analytically driven prediction costs much less than response, and that the Ebola economic losses in Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia could have been prevented by a more resilient and integrated health system. It also says data on financing and cost projections are limited.
- The One Health in Africa paper says zoonotic disease prevention costs less than 1/20th the value of lives lost each year (a business case), set against outbreak losses of billions of dollars.

The organisational models differ in scale and detail. The global review classifies 14 high-income-country antibiotic-resistance systems by information and structural integration into four clusters: siloed (Group 1), highly integrated (Group 2), and led by the human health sector (Group 3) or the food sector (Group 4) [0, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. It found no operating integrated system in LMICs [19]. Resources and the regulatory framework shape how systems are organised [1], and governance is seen as more effective with an intersectoral committee or a single supervising organisation [13]. Paper 37 describes an inter-agency working group, multisectoral partnerships set against single-sector planning, and data-driven surveillance with machine learning [20, 21, 25, 26]. Paper 38 describes a continental model: an AU coordinating group, an Africa CDC framework in national public health institutes, and a multi-level strategy [32, 36, 37, 38, 39]. It also notes gaps in financing and funded programmes [31, 35]. On economics, the review stresses the costs of integration (a financial and social cost; costly, underfunded coordination) and finds outcomes poorly documented, reporting only non-monetary benefits [3, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. Paper 37 cites over €1 million in West Nile virus savings and a 26% cut in laboratory operating cost, and argues for a positive return on investment, cheaper prediction and avoided losses [22, 23, 24, 28, 29, 30], while noting that cost data are limited [27]. Paper 38 makes a prevention business case (less than 1/20th the value of lives lost) against outbreak losses of billions of dollars [33, 34].

The study reported that the Earth (V4) primer pair generated markedly higher estimates of within‑sample diversity than the MiSeq (V3‑V4) primers.  

* **Alpha‑richness (ASV count):** In farm A, Earth yielded an average of **2166 ASVs** in biofilter water and **1934 ASVs** in tank water, whereas MiSeq recovered only **1504** and **1477** ASVs for the same samples. Across all sample types, Earth primers consistently produced richer ASV sets (e.g., 1070–2240 vs. 441–1962 for richness).  
* **Alpha‑diversity (Shannon index):** Correspondingly, Shannon diversity scores were higher with Earth primers (range 6.12–7.32) than with MiSeq primers (range 3.83–6.18).  

These quantitative differences meant that community‑structure ordinations based on the Earth amplicons captured a more expansive repertoire of taxa, leading to conclusions about higher overall diversity and distinct spatial patterns that were not evident when using the MiSeq V3‑V4 primers. In other words, primer choice directly altered the perceived magnitude and compositional nuances of microbial community structure in the aquaculture system [source_file:page_number].
items.question: Based on the comparative analysis of the Earth (V4) and MiSeq (V3-V4) primers, what were the quantitative differences in alpha richness and how did this impact the interpretation of community structure?
items.expected:
Earth (V4) primers gave higher alpha richness than MiSeq (V3-4) primers, even though the MiSeq primers identified more taxa. Richness ranged 1070–2240 with Earth and 441–1962 with MiSeq.

Average richness, Earth vs MiSeq:
- Farm A biofilter water: 2166 vs 1504.
- Farm A tank water: 1934 vs 1477.
- Farm A young biofilm: 1135 vs 465.
- Farm A mature biofilm: 1497 vs 829.
- Farm B tank biofilm: tank1 1793 vs 1665, tank2 1805 vs 1815.

Farm B tank 2 is the one place where MiSeq was slightly higher. The paper's figure legend nonetheless says Earth was higher across all sample types.

The authors call these minor differences in ASV richness. They did not impact the spatio-temporal patterns or the biological conclusion. Amplicon choice did not affect community composition at higher taxonomic levels. Composition and spatio-temporal patterns were very similar between the two amplicons. Subtle phylum biases remained: Chloroflexi was favored by Earth, and Myxococcota and Plantomycetota by MiSeq. These biases did not affect the inferred overall community structure, which was virtually identical for both amplicons according to MDS analyses. With Earth primers the pattern was identical but sat in a distinct area of the morphospace. The authors conclude that relative differences in community composition can safely be compared across primers, but they recommend against comparing absolute statistics from different primers.
concepts: Earth primers resulted in higher alpha diversity
did not impact the spatio-temporal patterns

The Generalized One Health Framework (GOHF) is presented as a step‑wise, systems‑based approach that seeks to strengthen and streamline programs for preventing, detecting, and controlling zoonotic diseases.  Its main aims are to:

1. **Build multisectoral collaborations** by engaging relevant stakeholders from human health, animal health, environmental sectors, and other partners [3].  
2. **Formalize roles and responsibilities** (e.g., through MOUs or letters of agreement) so that accountability is clear and progress can be tracked [6].  
3. **Conduct an initial assessment** of the strengths, weaknesses, and resource gaps within each sector to inform planning [8].  
4. **Develop a prioritized list of zoonotic diseases** of national concern and outline concrete next steps for addressing them using a One Health lens [8].  
5. **Integrate objectives across technical domains** such as surveillance, laboratory work, outbreak response, prevention & control, preparedness, communication, and policy [7].  
6. **Promote institutionalization of One Health** in governance and policy by shifting from sector‑specific units to overarching, coordinated systems [5].  

Together, these steps are intended to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of zoonotic disease programming by leveraging cross‑sectoral resources, enhancing coordination, and ensuring that interventions are aligned with a unified One Health strategy.  

**Sources**: [3], [5], [6], [7], [8].
items.question: How does the Generalized One Health Framework (GOHF) aim to improve zoonotic disease programming?
items.expected: The GOHF gives recommendations for using a One Health approach to improve multisectoral collaboration, and thereby enhance the prevention and control of zoonotic diseases. It is a five-step framework: engagement, assessment, planning, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation. A visualization (Fig. 2) sets out the steps and their corresponding activities, which give countries a structure for developing the capacity to coordinate zoonotic disease programming across sectors. Users may enter at any step based on their current capacity. A toolkit (Supplementary Tables S1–5) compiles available resources matched to each step and activity, so users can identify their progress on the visualization and then use the toolkit to advance. The GOHF is applied across technical domains: laboratory, surveillance, joint outbreak response, prevention and control, preparedness, communication, and government and policy. It is not intended to be prescriptive. It is meant to be broadly applicable to common zoonotic diseases, in high-income and low-middle income countries, from the local to the international level. Its intended outcome is improved capacity to control zoonotic diseases and other threats at the human–animal–environment interface. Instead of building independent programs for priority zoonotic diseases, it is intended to deepen One Health capacity throughout the system. Ideally this leads to a gradual transition towards a comprehensive One Health system that can combat a diversity of health threats.

iNAP provides four main approaches for network construction from non-temporal microbial data [source: 27_inap_pipeline.pdf, Page 0]:

For time-dependent microbial associations in time series data, iNAP recommends:

1. **eLSA** (Extended local similarity analysis) [source: 27_inap_pipeline.pdf, Page 0]
2. **LA** (Liquid association) [source: 27_inap_pipeline.pdf, Page 0]

These methods are specifically designed to "explore time-dependent microbial associations for time series data" [source: 27_inap_pipeline.pdf, Page 0].

# Current State of Knowledge on ABR Surveillance Integration Outcomes

Based on the study's findings, the current state of knowledge regarding outcomes and impacts of integrated ABR surveillance systems is characterized by significant gaps:

## Limited Evaluation

The research indicates that integrated surveillance systems are **not formally evaluated to assess their effectiveness and impacts**, which is "partly explained by the lack of adapted tools and methods to evaluate the added value of integrated surveillance" [source: 36_integrated_amr_surveillance.pdf, Page 0]. The study emphasizes "the need to enhance such methods and to conduct more evaluation of the impacts of integrated surveillance systems in order to better understand the mechanisms through which the integration process enhances surveillance effectiveness and value" [source: 36_integrated_amr_surveillance.pdf, Page 0].

## Documented Outcomes

Where outcomes have been identified, they include:

- **Policy development**: Integration of the One Health perspective into sectoral or intersectoral policies (DANMAP, NARMS) [source: 36_integrated_amr_surveillance.pdf, Page 0]
- **Behavioral change**: Encouraging prescribers to transition toward more responsible antibiotic use and decreasing antibiotic quantities in animals and humans (Swedres-Svarm, CIPARS, DANMAP, NethMap/MARAN) [source: 36_integrated_amr_surveillance.pdf, Page 0]
- **Research advancement**: New research projects on ABR conducted with a One Health perspective (NethMap/MARAN) [source: 36_integrated_amr_surveillance.pdf, Page 0]

## Overall Conclusion

The study concludes that operationalization of integrated surveillance for ABR "is still not well established at a global scale" and that "further studies are needed to better characterize the various integration models for surveillance with regard to their implementation context and evaluate the outcome of these models" [source: 36_integrated_amr_surveillance.pdf, Page 0].
items.question: Based on the study's findings, what is the current state of knowledge regarding the outcomes and impacts of integrating ABR surveillance systems?
items.expected: Knowledge is limited. The outcomes of integration are poorly described and evidenced, and information on them is rarely available in the literature. A few papers describe some outcomes. Immediate outcomes: improved knowledge about ABR, surveillance capacity to detect correlation in ABR across sectors and between ABU and ABR, and level of awareness on ABR and ABU. Intermediate outcomes: a more responsible use of antibiotics by prescribers (Swedres-Svarm), a decrease in the quantity of antibiotics used in animals and humans (CIPARS, DANMAP, NethMAp/MARAN), new research projects with a One Health perspective (NethMap/MARAN), and the One Health perspective in sectoral or intersectoral policies (DANMAP, NARMS). To a lesser extent, ultimate outcomes were identified as changes in ABR levels (CIPARS). In the example, CIPARS detected a strong correlation between ceftiofur-resistant Salmonella Heidelberg from retail chicken and human infections across Canada. As a result, the poultry sector stopped using ceftiofur, and resistance to this antibiotic in salmonella decreased. Where outcome information exists, the direct causal link with integration is difficult to establish. The information is usually provided by people in charge of the surveillance system, who may lack objectivity. Reliable information was found only for systems at an advanced stage of maturity that have undertaken external evaluations. For less performant and more recent systems, outcome claims seem more aspirational than based on observed facts. Few systems have been formally evaluated for effectiveness and impacts, partly because of a lack of adapted tools and methods. Better integration does not systematically bring greater surveillance performance. The authors call for more evaluation of the impacts of integrated surveillance systems, and of the outcome of the integration models.

items.question: How do the implementation strategies for NGS workflow management and reproducibility differ between Nextflow-based systems like Sarek, the Snakemake system, and the HTS-flow platform?
items.expected:
Sarek is implemented in Nextflow, a workflow language designed for bioinformatics. Nextflow supports Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF and Kubernetes, with native support for Google Cloud and AWS. To ensure reproducibility, all Sarek required tools are installed in Conda and then pushed to DockerHub, so Sarek and its dependencies are available from a Conda environment or as Docker or Singularity containers. Nextflow downloads the specified pipeline version from GitHub, together with its container and the reference files from AWS-iGenomes. Sarek follows the nf-core portability and documentation guidelines, restarts incomplete runs from any stage and ships with a suite of tests to verify the installation. A complete run was executed by a single command.

Snakemake specifies workflows as rules in a domain specific language (DSL). Its DSL extends Python, while Nextflow's extends Groovy. Dependencies between jobs are inferred automatically. Software stack management is integrated into Snakemake itself: each rule can declare a Conda environment, or a container image run with Singularity. Snakemake can also automatically generate a containerized version once a workflow is production ready. It tracks the input files, output files, parameters, software and code of each executed job and makes them available in self-contained, interactive, HTML based reports. Scaling to a specific platform needs only a change of command line parameters, using execution plugins (e.g. SLURM, LSF, Kubernetes, Amazon AWS Batch).

HTS-flow is designed to work together with a LIMS (SMITH), so raw NGS data become visible in it automatically. Analyses run through a web interface designed for users without bioinformatics skills (the typical wet-lab scientist). It works with predefined, easily customizable modular scripts, deposited to Github for versioning. It allows complete traceability of datasets, accompanying metadata and analysis scripts. Reproducibility rests on standard Bioconductor metadata libraries (TxDb and BSgenome), outputs in standard locations as Bioconductor R data objects, and identical workflows for data from various sources.

Sarek and Snakemake both define workflows in code. Sarek is implemented in the Nextflow workflow language [0], and Nextflow and Snakemake both specify workflows in a DSL, built on Groovy and Python respectively [8, 9]. Snakemake decomposes workflows into rules and infers dependencies between jobs automatically [10, 11]. HTS-flow instead couples a LIMS to a web interface for users without bioinformatics skills [20, 21, 24, 29]. The interface sits over predefined, easily customizable modular scripts [25]. Both code-based systems get reproducibility by packaging software, at different levels. Sarek encapsulates all its dependencies in Docker or Singularity containers or a Bioconda-built Conda environment [2], and pulls a specified pipeline version from GitHub with its container and reference files [5]. Snakemake builds software stack management into the engine, with a Conda environment or a Singularity-run container for each rule [12, 13, 14], and can generate a containerized version of a workflow [15]. HTS-flow instead bases reproducibility on standard Bioconductor annotation packages (TxDb, BSgenome) and Bioconductor R data objects [27, 28]. It versions its scripts on Github [26] and analyses data from various sources with identical workflows [23]. For traceability and robustness, Sarek relies on nf-core portability and documentation guidelines, error reporting with restart from any stage, and installation tests [3, 4, 6]. Snakemake tracks the files, parameters, software and code of every job and reports them in self-contained, interactive, HTML based reports [16, 17]. HTS-flow provides complete traceability of datasets, metadata and analysis scripts, with raw data made visible automatically from the LIMS [20, 22]. For execution, Nextflow supports Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF, Kubernetes, Google Cloud and AWS [1]. Snakemake scales through execution plugins and needs only a change of command line parameters [18, 19]. HTS-flow's automation comes mainly from integration with the SMITH LIMS [29].

The paper never calls it a cycle. Instead it describes a "transmission continuum" (Figure 1 legend), a "complex web" of transmission pathways that runs in both directions. All of it comes from cited studies.
1. Animals to the environment. # Differences Between the Three Sequencing Approaches

Based on the retrieved passages, the three sequencing approaches differ significantly in their scope and capabilities:

## 16S rRNA Short-Read Sequencing
Short-read 16S sequencing is described as "adequate for exploring the spatio-temporal dynamics and community composition at higher taxonomic levels" [30_aquaculture_metagenomics.pdf:0]. However, it has limitations: it "mainly target bacteria and omit other microbes, such as fungi and archaea" [30_aquaculture_metagenomics.pdf:0]. Additionally, "primer choice can introduce biases for or against certain taxonomic groups" [30_aquaculture_metagenomics.pdf:0].

## PacBio Long-Read Sequencing
Long-amplicon sequencing "targets all variable regions of the 16S gene, thus increasing resolution for species identification and eliminating primer choice biases" [30_aquaculture_metagenomics.pdf:0]. However, like short-read approaches, it "mainly target bacteria and omit other microbes, such as fungi and archaea" [30_aquaculture_metagenomics.pdf:0].

## Shotgun Metagenomics
Shotgun metagenomics is described as "a primer-free method" that "targets all sequences within a sample, allowing for the identification of all organisms present" [30_aquaculture_metagenomics.pdf:0]. Importantly, it "sequences all genetic information rather than just one taxon" and can identify "archaea, fungi, and viruses" [30_aquaculture_metagenomics.pdf:0]. The authors conclude that "shotgun metagenomics represents the most thorough approach for characterizing RAS microbial communities" [30_aquaculture_metagenomics.pdf:0].
items.question: How do the three sequencing approaches (16S rRNA, PacBio long-read, and shotgun metagenomics) differ in their contribution to the study's characterization of the microbial environment?
items.expected: 16S short-amplicon sequencing was adequate for community studies. It captured spatio-temporal dynamics and community composition at higher taxonomic levels. Primer choice and amplicon length changed some values, such as diversity measures and the number of assigned taxa, but had no impact on the spatio-temporal patterns between sample types, farms and time points. It cannot provide the resolution required for species or strain identification. PacBio long-read amplicons underperformed on the quantitative resolution of spatio-temporal patterns, because the low number of reads prohibited community statistics. Still, the 10,041 reads identified 204 species, and the approach was suited to identifying functional services (e.g. nitrification cycling) and detecting pathogens. Shotgun metagenomics corroborated the amplicon findings and extended the picture beyond prokaryotes (75.55%) to eukaryotes (23.97%), archaea (0.24%) and viruses (0.24%), including fungi and bacteriophages. The authors call it the most thorough approach. All datasets agreed on the major prokaryotic players (Actinobacteriota, Bacteroidota, Nitrospirota, Proteobacteria). The approaches gave overlapping and highly complementary results, and each contributed data the others could not provide.
