## Background: Zoonotic Disease Context in Africa

Zoonotic diseases—those transmissible between animals and humans—represent a major global health threat. Approximately 60% of existing infectious diseases and 75% of newly emerging infectious diseases in humans are zoonotic, with the majority originating from wildlife [1]. Six of the seven Public Health Emergencies of International Concern are zoonotic, including the H1N1 pandemic, Ebola outbreaks, Zika virus, COVID-19, and monkeypox [1]. These outbreaks have resulted in billions of dollars in economic losses across public health, tourism, agricultural, and financial sectors [1]. In low- and middle-income countries, zoonotic diseases cause an estimated 2.5 billion cases of human illness and 2.7 million deaths annually [1].

The emergence of zoonotic diseases is driven by human activities and environmental changes. Human actions have altered 75% of terrestrial environments and 66% of marine environments, with a 300% increase in crop agricultural production since 1970 [1]. As humans and livestock encroach into wildlife habitats through urbanization, tourism, and hunting, combined with agricultural intensification, the frequency and intimacy of contact between humans, domestic animals, and wild animals increases, contributing to zoonotic disease emergence [1]. The probability of zoonotic pathogen emergence is positively correlated with wildlife biodiversity and growing human population [2]. Additional drivers include urbanization, expanded agriculture, globalization, wildlife hunting, deforestation, and climate change [2]. As climate change progresses, emerging zoonotic events are estimated to increase, disproportionately impacting Asia and Africa [2].

## One Health Implementation and Institutional Framework

The One Health approach is a collaborative framework that involves coordination between human, animal, and environmental health sectors, along with other relevant stakeholders, to design and implement programs, policies, legislation, and research for better health outcomes [1]. This approach improves the ability to efficiently prevent, detect, and respond to emerging and re-emerging zoonotic diseases at the human–animal–environment interface [1].

The formalization of One Health collaboration began in 2010 when the World Health Organization (WHO), Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), and World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH)—collectively known as the Tripartite—established a multidisciplinary collaboration to address health threats at the human–animal–ecosystem interface [2]. This was expanded in 2022 when the Tripartite organizations and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) formed a Quadripartite Collaboration for One Health [2].

Despite documented progress in institutionalizing One Health mechanisms across African Union Member States, significant challenges remain, including gaps in political commitment, skilled workforce, domestic financing, and legal frameworks needed to strengthen coordination and collaboration among One Health stakeholders in Africa [1].

The African Union (AU) has established multiple institutions to implement One Health approaches, including the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), the Inter-African Bureau for Animal Resources (AU-IBAR), and the African Union Pan-African Veterinary Vaccine Centre (AU-PANVAC) [2]. The Africa CDC has developed a Framework for One Health Practice in National Public Health Institutes (NPHIs) that focuses on improving multisectoral coordination, strengthening surveillance systems, enhancing diagnostic capacity, and scaling up the multisectoral workforce [3]. AU-IBAR has spearheaded One Health institutionalization efforts and supported the development of integrated National Action Plans against highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) [4].

To strengthen coordination efforts, the AU has established an AU One Health Coordination Group on Zoonotic Diseases that will lead the development of an AU One Health Strategy for Zoonotic Disease Prevention and Control [4]. This strategy aims to leverage the AU's convening power to advocate for political support for One Health at national, regional, and continental levels [4].

## Challenges, Strategy Development, and Future Directions

**Challenges in Operationalizing One Health**

Operationalizing One Health remains a significant challenge, as One Health activities continue to exist in silos rather than being integrated [2]. This siloed approach has prevented One Health from gaining a firm institutional foothold at the national level [2]. To address this fragmentation, strong governance, political leadership, and community engagement are required to sustain multi-sectoral and interdisciplinary collaborations and formalize One Health coordinating mechanisms to improve data sharing and decision-making [1].

**AU One Health Strategy for Zoonotic Disease Prevention and Control**

Recognizing the need to improve and strengthen One Health activities, the African Union has developed an AU One Health Strategy for Zoonotic Disease Prevention and Control [1]. This continental strategy will leverage the AU's convening power and advocate for political support for One Health at national, regional, and continental levels to improve countries' ability to prevent, detect, and respond to emerging zoonotic disease threats [1]. The newly established AU One Health Coordination Group on Zoonotic Diseases will lead and facilitate the strategy development process together with Member States [1]. The strategy aims to support AU Member States in developing, establishing, coordinating, monitoring, and evaluating implementation of holistic zoonotic disease prevention and control programmes [2].

**Future Directions and Conclusions**

The African Union endorses the One Health approach as a critical solution to prevent and counter the emergence of zoonotic diseases and other shared public health threats [2]. A One Health approach is essential for accelerated implementation of the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) and to achieve the AU Agenda 2063: The Africa We Want [2]. The African Union envisions an integrated and prosperous Africa free of disease, disability, and premature death, aiming to promote the well-being of all in Africa through the One Health approach [2].

## Five Critical Issues in FMD Pathogenesis


The authors of "The pathogenesis of foot-and-mouth disease virus: current understandings and knowledge gaps" 
identify five critical issues that represent important knowledge gaps and challenges in FMD research:

1. **Long-term asymptomatic FMDV carriers and biological relevance**: It remains unclear if long-term 
asymptomatic FMDV carriers are biologically relevant and contagious, representing a significant gap in 
understanding disease transmission dynamics.

2. **Host genomics and transcriptomics effects on pathogenesis**: The manner in which host genomics and 
transcriptomics affect pathogenesis during different phases of infection remains poorly understood, limiting 
our ability to predict disease outcomes across different host species and individuals.

3. **Distinction between neoteric subclinical infection and persistent carrier state**: The characterization 
of neoteric subclinical infection as a distinct disease stage from the persistent FMDV carrier state has 
emphasized the importance of sampling clinically unaffected animals for surveillance purposes.

4. **Pre-clinical infectiousness in outbreak modeling**: Incorporating a phase of pre-clinical infectiousness 
in simulation modeling can dramatically improve prediction of FMD outbreaks in non-endemic regions, yet this 
remains inadequately addressed in current models.

5. **Host factors driving FMDV carrier state divergence**: The authors lack a satisfactory explanation of 
the host factors that drive FMDV carrier state divergence, noting that infection outcomes differ between 
host species and between individuals of the same species.

These five issues represent critical knowledge gaps that must be addressed to improve understanding of FMD 
pathogenesis and enhance disease control strategies.

## Technical Approach Comparison: Rarefaction vs Scaling Normalization


TECHNICAL APPROACH COMPARISON: RAREFACTION VS SCALING NORMALIZATION

1. FUNDAMENTAL MECHANISM:

Rarefaction (Subsampling):
- Operates through random subsampling WITHOUT REPLACEMENT to equalize sequencing depth
- All samples are reduced to the same predetermined depth (e.g., 1,000 reads per sample)
- Samples with fewer reads than the rarefaction threshold are completely removed
- Creates equal library sizes across all samples through data reduction

Scaling Normalization (TMM/DESeq2):
- Operates through statistical modeling and scaling factors applied to count data
- DESeq2 uses a negative binomial distribution model: μij = sij·qij, where sij is the normalization factor
- Preserves ALL original data while applying multiplicative scaling factors
- Accounts for library size differences through mathematical transformation rather than data removal

2. HANDLING OF SEQUENCING DEPTH VARIANCE:

Rarefaction:
- Eliminates depth-related variance by forcing all samples to identical sequencing depth
- Removes the source of variance entirely through equalization
- However, introduces STOCHASTIC VARIANCE through random subsampling process
- Each rarefaction run produces slightly different results due to random sampling

DESeq2/Scaling Methods:
- Explicitly MODELS variance through the dispersion parameter (αi)
- Variance is described as: Var(Kij) = μij + αi·μij²
- Accounts for both Poisson variance and overdispersion
- Uses empirical Bayes shrinkage to estimate dispersion parameters, especially important for small sample sizes
- Variance is estimated from the data itself rather than artificially equalized

3. DATA LOSS AND PRESERVATION:

Rarefaction:
- DISCARDS valuable data: sequences below the rarefaction threshold are removed
- Samples with insufficient reads are completely excluded from analysis
- Loss of statistical power due to reduced sample size and sequence count
- Researcher must balance rarefaction depth with number of samples retained
- Particularly problematic for valuable or difficult-to-obtain samples

Scaling Normalization:
- PRESERVES all original count data
- No samples are removed due to sequencing depth
- All sequences contribute to the analysis
- Normalization factors are applied mathematically without data loss
- Maintains full statistical power of the dataset

4. VARIANCE HANDLING IMPLICATIONS:

Rarefaction:
- Artificially equalizes sample variance by adding uncertainty
- Creates artificial homogeneity that may not reflect true biological variance
- Stochastic nature means results are not fully reproducible
- May mask or obscure true biological differences between samples
- Loss of statistical power to detect differences (McMurdie and Holmes, 2014)

DESeq2/Scaling Methods:
- Preserves true biological variance structure
- Variance is explicitly modeled and estimated from data
- Provides variance stabilization through transformations (rlog, VST) when needed
- rlog transformation accounts for size factors: rlog(Kij) ≈ log2(Kij/sj) for large counts
- Maintains statistical power and reproducibility
- Allows for proper statistical inference through GLM framework

5. STATISTICAL FRAMEWORK:

Rarefaction:
- Non-parametric approach
- No explicit statistical model
- Assumes equal variance after subsampling
- Limited ability to incorporate complex experimental designs
- Results depend on arbitrary rarefaction depth choice

DESeq2:
- Parametric approach using generalized linear models (GLM)
- Explicit negative binomial distribution model
- Flexible design matrix allows complex experimental designs
- Empirical Bayes shrinkage improves dispersion estimates for small sample sizes
- Provides formal statistical testing framework
- Can incorporate gene-specific normalization factors for technical biases (GC content, gene length, etc.)

6. APPROPRIATE USE CASES:

Rarefaction:
- May be appropriate for very low-abundance feature detection
- Useful when contamination concerns are high in low-biomass samples
- Simpler conceptually for exploratory analysis
- Appropriate when computational resources are severely limited

Scaling Normalization (DESeq2/TMM):
- Preferred for differential abundance/expression analysis
- Better for datasets with variable sequencing depth
- Appropriate when statistical power is important
- Better for complex experimental designs
- Recommended for publication-quality analysis
- Superior when sample size is small (common in controlled experiments)

items.question: How does the technical approach of rarefaction differ from scaling normalization methods like TMM or DESeq2 in handling sample variance?
items.expected: Rarefaction randomly subsamples ASVs or OTUs within each sample without replacement to a preselected depth that is the same across all samples. Every sample ends with the same number of ASVs, and samples below the rarefaction level are removed. This discards valuable data and loses statistical power by removing sequences, and rarefying equalizes sample variance by adding artificial uncertainty. Scaling normalization does not subsample. It multiplies the ASV numbers by a value or proportion. In DESeq2 (median of ratios), the scaling factor is the median ratio of an ASV's count over its geometric mean across all samples. TMM (Trimmed Mean of M-values) uses one sample as a reference and compares the weighted mean of log ratios of an ASV within a sample with that reference. These methods have been shown to be robust to differences between samples and to maintain the differences in relative abundance.

## RMP vs QMP: Effects on Microbial Interactions and Community Interpretation

Relative Microbiome Profiling (RMP) and Quantitative Microbiome Profiling (QMP) produce substantially different interpretations of microbial communities in livestock studies. RMP biased the real quantitative changes in the chicken gut microbiota, failing to accurately represent actual community dynamics [4]. Additionally, RMP overestimated the microbial community structure variations and the influencing factors [4].

A critical distinction between these approaches is their fundamental measurement approach. While RMP uses relative abundances to profile the proportions of different microbial taxa within a community across time and space, QMP concerns changes in absolute abundance and determines whether a species thrives or withers over time [6]. This difference is significant because QMP allows researchers to elucidate the real community dynamics, which facilitates the identification of biotic and abiotic forces that shape a microbial community and enables better correlation between gut microbiota features and host changes [6].

The choice of profiling method has direct consequences for understanding microbial interactions. RMP missed many significant positive taxon-taxon interactions that were found in QMP, especially for the fungal community [4]. This represents a substantial limitation, as absolute quantification-based microbe-microbe interactions can reveal that assembly dynamics are likely driven by context-dependent interactions between specific microbes [6].

The microbial load itself may serve as an identifier of ecosystem configuration, such as in health and disease statuses [6], making quantitative approaches particularly valuable for diagnostic purposes. These results suggest that quantitative approaches are necessary and will provide new clues to understand the changes in livestock gut microbiota and the interactions between microbes and the host [4].

## 1. Origins of ARB/ARGs in Food Animal Farms

Antibiotic resistance in food animal farms originates through several mechanisms. Unregulated or inappropriate antibiotic use in animal farms is a primary driver, with farmers in developing countries commonly using different types of antibiotics simultaneously [2]. In a survey of small-scale farms in Thailand, 57.1% of farmers reported using antibiotics for prevention purposes [2]. This practice increases the risk of resistance antibiotic development and its transfer in the community, which poses a major global public health threat [2].

Specific bacterial pathogens in food animals develop antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). For example, in aquaculture settings, ARGs including tetM, tetO, fexA, and ermB have been identified in tilapia farms, with Streptococcus agalactiae found in 60% of ponds and 46% of organ pools [2]. In shrimp, ARGs were identified from Vibrio (accounting for 2.8-51%) and Aeromonas (16-55%) plasmids [2].

Additionally, antibiotic resistance genes from livestock waste can occur and disseminate through the environment [3]. Bioaerosols have been identified as an important transmission route of antibiotic resistance genes in pig farms [5].

The lack of knowledge and poor practices related to antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance among farm workers, particularly in developing countries, further contributes to the development and spread of resistant bacteria [2].

STUDY DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY:

The paper by Jeske & Gallert (2022) compares two bioinformatic pipelines for analyzing 16S rRNA gene

anaerobic co-digestion (Co-AD) of primary and waste-activated sewage sludge (PWASS) with food waste 
as the experimental system.

EXPERIMENTAL SETUP:
- Six 1-liter reactors with 500 mL working volume operated at 55°C for 170 days
- Control reactors (n=3) received only PWASS daily
- Experimental reactors (n=3) received PWASS supplemented with food waste at increasing percentages (0-40%)
- 36 samples analyzed (5 timepoints × 6 reactors, plus 5 PWASS and 1 inoculum sample)

SEQUENCING METHODOLOGY:
- DNA extracted using Soil DNA Isolation Plus Kit
- V3–V4 region of 16S rRNA gene amplified using primers Pro341f/Pro805r
- Sequenced on Illumina MiSeq platform
- Two pipelines compared:
  1. OTU-based VSEARCH pipeline: clustered sequences at 97% similarity, classified using SINA classifier
  2. ASV-based DADA2 pipeline: used error correction algorithms
- Both used SILVA REF99 SSU reference database version 138.1 for taxonomy assignment
- Statistical analysis performed in R using phyloseq, vegan, and microbiome packages

KEY TECHNICAL CHALLENGE ADDRESSED:
The study addresses a fundamental challenge in microbiome research: NGS methods face significant 
technical challenges including short fragment lengths and sequencing-related artifacts. Traditional 
OTU approaches use clustering at 97% similarity threshold but lack direct comparability across studies. 
Newer ASV approaches use error correction but have limited capability with small overlap regions.


## SECTION 2: RESULTS SUMMARY


COMPARATIVE FINDINGS BETWEEN OTU AND ASV PIPELINES:

PHYLUM-LEVEL ANALYSIS:
- Both pipelines showed good overall agreement in thermophilic anaerobic digestion (AD) reactors
- Both detected similar decreasing relative abundances of Thermotogota, Coprothermobacterota, 
  Synergistota, Firmicutes, and Bacteroidota

  ranging from 6.75% to 10.81% of total community composition

GENUS-LEVEL ANALYSIS:

- In PWASS samples, some genera differed by as much as 400% between pipelines

DIVERSITY ANALYSIS:

- Identified slightly increased diversity in control reactors compared to co-substrate-fed experimental reactors
- Diversity indices diverged significantly for PWASS samples
- NMDS analysis revealed pipeline-derived differences were greater than differences between experimental 
  treatments over 170 days

  the statistical significance of environmental factors could no longer be detected in reduced AD-only dataset
- Pipeline choice affected community composition more than actual experimental treatments in some analyses

TECHNICAL EXPLANATION:
- ASV algorithm (DADA2) calculates error rates on subset of samples then applies individually to all samples
- This approach is problematic when analyzing samples from vastly different temperature environments simultaneously
- OTU-based approach (VSEARCH) uses k-mer clustering on entire dataset at once, avoiding this issue but 
  requiring greater computational power

METHODOLOGICAL IMPLICATIONS AND LIMITATIONS:

FUNDAMENTAL LIMITATIONS OF BOTH APPROACHES:

## Disease Burden Metrics: Zoonotic Infectious Diseases

# 

Approximately 60% of existing infectious diseases in humans are zoonotic [2][4], while 75% of newly emerging infectious diseases are considered zoonoses [2][3][4]. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), zoonotic diseases have a substantial impact: it is estimated that annually zoonotic diseases result in 2.5 billion cases of human illness and 2.7 million deaths [2]. Additionally, about one billion cases of zoonoses occur worldwide each year [4].

The economic burden is significant, with emerging zoonotic diseases posing "a significant and growing threat to global health, global security and the economy" [2]. Six of the seven Public Health Emergencies of International Concern (PHEICs) are zoonotic—including the H1N1 pandemic, Ebola outbreaks, Zika virus, COVID-19, and monkeypox—and these events have "resulted in billions of dollars lost and indirect losses affecting economies" [2]. The economic impacts extend beyond the public health sector to include tourism, agricultural, and financial sectors [2].

Livestock production is critical to human nutrition and health in LMICs [3], yet the intensification of animal agriculture practices has increased risks of zoonotic infection through animals kept in close quarters and global shipment of animal products [4]. Environmental degradation has also contributed to disease emergence, as human actions have altered 75% of terrestrial environments and 66% of marine environments [2].

## One Health Approach for Zoonotic Disease Programming

Brucellosis is a re-emerging bacterial zoonotic disease posing significant public and animal health problems in pastoral communities of sub-Saharan Africa [1]. The disease affects multiple livestock species and has documented seropositivity in humans, indicating the need for coordinated intervention [1]. 

The research demonstrates that evidence of brucellosis in various livestock species and associated human seropositivity indicates the necessity for "a coordinated One Health approach, considering sociocultural dynamics of pastoral communities in controlling brucellosis to safeguard public health and increase livestock productivity" [1]. This integrated approach is particularly important because pastoralists face the highest risk of contracting brucellosis due to close physical contact with animals and consumption of unpasteurized milk [1].

The One Health approach addresses multiple dimensions of the disease: it recognizes that risk factors for animal brucellosis are related to livestock management practices, animal movements, environmental factors, pastoralist behaviors and practices, lack of veterinary control measures, and socioeconomic factors [5]. For human disease, it acknowledges that risk factors include handling infected animals and ingestion of contaminated animal products [5]. By integrating these perspectives across animal health, human health, and environmental factors while respecting sociocultural dynamics, the One Health approach aims to provide comprehensive brucellosis control that protects both community health and livestock productivity [1].

items.expected: The GOHF gives recommendations for using a One Health approach to improve multisectoral collaboration, and thereby enhance the prevention and control of zoonotic diseases. It is a five-step framework: engagement, assessment, planning, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation. A visualization (Fig. 2) sets out the steps and their corresponding activities, which give countries a structure for developing the capacity to coordinate zoonotic disease programming across sectors. Users may enter at any step based on their current capacity. A toolkit (Supplementary Tables S1–5) compiles available resources matched to each step and activity, so users can identify their progress on the visualization and then use the toolkit to advance. The GOHF is applied across technical domains: laboratory, surveillance, joint outbreak response, prevention and control, preparedness, communication, and government and policy. It is not intended to be prescriptive. It is meant to be broadly applicable to common zoonotic diseases, in high-income and low-middle income countries, from the local to the international level. Its intended outcome is improved capacity to control zoonotic diseases and other threats at the human–animal–environment interface. Instead of building independent programs for priority zoonotic diseases, it is intended to deepen One Health capacity throughout the system. Ideally this leads to a gradual transition towards a comprehensive One Health system that can combat a diversity of health threats.

## Salmon's Bias Correction Mechanisms

# 

Salmon is a tool for quantifying transcript expression that corrects for multiple types of sequencing biases that can distort abundance estimates [1][7].

## Sequence-Specific Bias

Salmon corrects for sequence-specific biases at the 5' and 3' ends of RNA-seq fragments [7]. The sequences surrounding these fragment ends influence the likelihood that fragments are selected for sequencing, and if not accounted for, these biases can substantially affect abundance estimates and confound downstream analyses [7]. To learn and correct for these biases, Salmon trains variable-length Markov models (VLMMs) on sequence windows surrounding the 5' and 3' read start positions, comparing foreground models (trained on actual sequenced fragments) against background models (trained on sequence windows drawn uniformly across known transcripts, weighted by transcript abundance) [7][8].

## Fragment GC-Content Bias

Salmon accounts for GC-content bias, which occurs when the overall GC-content of an entire fragment affects the likelihood it will be selected for sequencing [8]. This bias is distinct from sequence-specific biases and requires separate correction [8]. The tool learns both foreground and background models of fragment GC-bias by maintaining distributions across 25 bins representing GC-content values ranging from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.04 [8]. The background model is trained on all possible fragments drawn uniformly across known transcripts, weighted by transcript abundance [8].

## Conditional Dependence Between Bias Types

Importantly, Salmon recognizes that sequence-specific and fragment GC biases display conditional dependence [9]. To account for this interaction, Salmon learns three different bias models by default, each conditioned on the average GC content of the 5' and 3' sequence context, with separate models for fragments with average GC content in the ranges [0, 0.33), [0.33, 0.66), and [0.66, 1] [9].

Not found in source material.

## Fragment Bias (General)

Fragment-transcript assignment scores incorporate multiple factors including: (1) the probability of observing a particular fragment length given a transcript, (2) the probability that a fragment starts at a particular position on the transcript, (3) the concordance of the fragment with the sequencing library format (e.g., paired-end, stranded), and (4) the alignment score [5]. The probability of a fragment starting at position p on a transcript is a function of the transcript's length [7].

## Implementation of Bias Correction

Bias models are incorporated by re-estimating the effective length of each transcript to account for the likelihood of sampling each possible fragment that transcript can produce [9]. The offline optimization algorithm runs for a small number of rounds (10 by default) to produce estimated abundances used when learning background distributions for the bias models [9]. Once bias-corrected effective lengths are computed, they are used in all subsequent rounds of the offline inference phase until estimates converge [9]. The computational cost of bias correction is relatively small and scales with the number of expressed transcripts rather than the number

These bias corrections are essential because uncorrected biases lead to systematic errors in transcript abundance estimates that propagate through downstream statistical analysis, potentially producing false conclusions about differential expression.

## Dual-Phase Inference Algorithm

# 

Salmon employs a dual-phase inference procedure to quantify transcript abundance while accounting for experimental biases [2][3]. 

**Phase 1 - Online Phase (Initial Quantification):**
The online phase uses a variant of stochastic, collapsed variational Bayesian inference to estimate initial expression levels, auxiliary parameters, and foreground bias models while constructing equivalence classes over input fragments [2][3]. During this streaming phase, parameters for auxiliary models are learned from the first 5,000,000 observations by default, which are then applied to all subsequent observations [10].

**Phase 2 - Offline Phase (Bias Learning and Refinement):**
The offline phase applies either a standard EM algorithm or a variational Bayesian EM algorithm over a reduced representation of data represented by equivalence classes until a data-dependent convergence criterion is satisfied [2][3]. Before learning bias-corrected effective lengths, the offline optimization algorithm runs for a small number of rounds (10 by default) to produce estimated abundances used when learning background distributions for various bias models [12].

**Bias Correction Integration:**
Salmon learns and corrects for multiple bias types including 5' and 3' sequence-specific biases (using variable-length Markov models) and fragment GC-bias [10][11][12]. These bias models are incorporated by re-estimating the effective length of each transcript to account for the likelihood of sampling each possible fragment [12].

**EM Algorithm Refinement:**
The EM algorithm iteratively refines transcript abundance estimates in the offline phase, optimizing the maximum likelihood objective by accounting for fragment-transcript assignment ambiguities [6]. All results reported in the manuscript used the maximum likelihood objective (EM algorithm) in the offline phase, which is the default in Salmon [6].

## Systematic Methodology for Selection of 95 Publications

The scoping review on integrated surveillance systems of antibiotic resistance in a One Health context employed a rigorous systematic methodology to select publications. The literature review was conducted using the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, ensuring transparency and reproducibility.

**Databases and Search Strategy:**
The search strategy was developed in collaboration with a research librarian and conducted using four major databases: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and EMBASE. The search was conducted between January 2020 and January 2022. The search strategy included keywords and MeSH terms related to integrated surveillance, antibiotic resistance, and One Health. The search strategy was adapted for each database to account for differences in indexing and search syntax. This comprehensive search resulted in a total of 1,330 initial records.

**Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria:**
The study applied specific inclusion criteria: (1) peer-reviewed publications, (2) published in English, French, Spanish, or Portuguese, (3) described an integrated surveillance system for antibiotic resistance, (4) described the system's organization and functioning, and (5) published between 2000 and 2022. Exclusion criteria included: (1) grey literature, (2) publications not in the specified languages, (3) publications that did not describe an integrated surveillance system, (4) publications that did not describe the system's organization and functioning, and (5) publications published before 2000.

**Screening and Selection Process:**
The screening process consisted of two distinct stages:
1. **Title and Abstract Screening:** Two independent reviewers screened all titles and abstracts using the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. After this initial screening stage, 95 references were retained for full-text review.
2. **Full-Text Review:** The 95 references were then subjected to full-text review, resulting in 59 references being kept, from which 14 integrated surveillance systems were ultimately identified and characterized.

**Data Analysis:**
The selected integrated surveillance systems were assessed according to 39 variables related to their organization and functioning, the socio-economic and political characteristics of their implementation context, and the levels of integration reached. Two distinct, complementary analyses were conducted: a descriptive analysis to summarize the characteristics of the integrated surveillance systems, and a multiple-correspondence analysis (MCA) followed by a hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA) to identify potential typology for surveillance systems.

This paper by Jeske and Gallert compares two bioinformatic pipelines for analyzing microbiome data from wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) systems [1]. ## Main Topic and Objectives

The research focuses on comparing two distinct approaches to processing 16S rRNA gene sequencing data [1]. One pipeline uses VSEARCH to generate operational taxonomic units (OTUs) through clustering at 97% similarity, while the other uses DADA2 to generate exact amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) through sequencing error correction [1][2]. ## Section 3: Conclusions and Discussion

# 

## Conclusions and Key Findings

Both OTU and ASV pipelines successfully identified shifts in microbial community composition over time that correlated with substrate addition, though the ASV pipeline demonstrated this relationship more clearly [1]. However, a critical finding emerged: dissimilarities between the two pipelines were greater than dissimilarities between experimental treatments over a 170+ day period [1]. This raises significant concerns for cross-study comparisons, as differences in pipeline choice could obscure or misrepresent actual biological differences [1].

## Implications for Pipeline Selection

Permanova analysis revealed that when pipeline choice was analyzed in interaction with experimental treatments, it became a statistically significant factor correlating with community composition [1][2]. This is problematic because it suggests that pipeline selection could affect conclusions more than actual environmental factors, which contradicts experimental reality [2]. The differences were particularly pronounced when analyzing psychrophilic (PWASS) versus thermophilic (AD reactor) environments [4].

## Mechanistic Explanation

The ASV algorithm calculates error rates on a subset of samples and applies these rates across the entire dataset, which can be problematic when samples originate from different temperature environments with different base transition rates [3]. In contrast, the OTU-based k-mer clustering approach processes the entire dataset simultaneously, avoiding this issue despite higher computational demands [3][4].

## Biological Significance and Future Directions

While ASV pipelines offer advantages in direct comparability between studies and reduced computational requirements, there remains a critical need for standardization in how ASV results are published and identified [5][6]. The authors emphasize that both approaches can only reveal "who is potentially present," and overall certainty about microbial community composition depends on statistics and algorithms requiring much more than sequence data analysis alone [6]. Greater unification in pipeline settings, quality metrics, and workflow accessibility is essential for reliable microbiome research [6].

items.question: Explain the role of 'Spatial Clustering' in the PDBinder methodology and the specific parameters used for this step.
items.expected: Spatial clustering filters PDBinder's predictions. On the training set the propensity value alone gave about 40% correct predictions. Binding sites are contiguous regions of the surface, so PDBinder discards spatially isolated predictions: any prediction without at least one other prediction within a defined radius is dropped. The authors tested radii from 1.0 Å to 20.0 Å in increments of 1 Å. The best clustering radius was 10.0 Å, close to the mean binding-site radius in the training set (8.97 ± 0.20 Å, 99% confidence interval). This threshold raised the positive predictive value by 5.4% and the MCC by 0.018, with a loss of 1.4% in sensitivity. The Table 1 results use a single propensity threshold for all amino acids together with spatial clustering at a 10 Angstrom threshold. With residue-specific thresholds, adding spatial clustering did not recover the slightly worse average performance (data not shown).

## Alpha Richness Differences: OTU vs ASV Pipelines

The study compared OTU and ASV pipelines for microbiome analysis in wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) systems, examining alpha diversity metrics including Shannon Wiener index, richness, evenness estimates, and the inverse Simpson index [6].

For thermophilic anaerobic digester (AD) reactors, both pipelines showed similar trends in alpha diversity development over time, though the OTU-based pipeline typically reported slightly higher diversity values than the ASV pipeline [6]. Both pipelines identified similar patterns, detecting slightly increased diversity in control reactors compared to co-substrate-fed experimental reactors as runtime increased [1].

However, significant differences emerged in psychrophilic PWASS (primary wastewater activated sludge) samples [6]. While some diversity indices like the Shannon Wiener index reported similar values between pipelines, other estimators "strongly differed between the two pipelines" [6]. Most notably, the inverse Simpson index showed dramatic divergence in PWASS samples, with OTU and ASV indices differing "at times by a factor greater two," whereas for AD communities these indices were "almost identical" [6].

These alpha diversity differences had important implications for community structure interpretation. The pipeline-dependent differences in PWASS samples raised "questions concerning the reliability of at least one of those pipelines, when such strongly differing habitats are investigated simultaneously" [4]. The researchers removed PWASS samples from further analysis to investigate whether pipelines would lead to different conclusions when comparing more closely related samples [4].

## Pipeline Differences and Community Composition Analysis

Jeske and Gallert compared two bioinformatic pipelines for analyzing 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from wastewater treatment systems: an OTU-based approach using VSEARCH clustering and an ASV-based approach using DADA2 error correction [8][9]. The OTU pipeline clusters sequences at 97% similarity to generate operational taxonomic units, while the ASV pipeline uses sequencing error correction algorithms to generate exact amplicon sequence variants [8][9].

## Magnitude of Pipeline-Dependent Differences

Despite both pipelines providing generally comparable results, significant discrepancies emerged in community composition. Community composition differed between 6.75% and 10.81% between pipelines across different treatments [1][9]. At the phylum level, differences ranged from ~1% to 4% for most taxa, though some phyla showed extreme deviations—for example, Acidobacteriota differed by 400% between pipelines (1.2% ASV vs. 0.3% OTU) [1]. Notably, differences between the two pipelines were often greater than differences observed between experimental treatments over 170 days [6].

## Environmental Context Effects

The pipelines showed markedly different performance depending on environmental conditions. In thermophilic anaerobic digestion (AD) reactors, both pipelines produced largely similar results for alpha diversity indices and community composition [14][17]. However, in psychrophilic wastewater-activated sludge (PWASS) samples, the pipelines diverged substantially, with some diversity estimators differing by a factor greater than two [14]. This discrepancy appears linked to how the ASV algorithm calculates error rates on a subset of samples (predominantly thermophilic) and then applies these rates to psychrophilic samples with different base transition rates [7].

## Taxonomic Resolution Issues

Pipeline-dependent differences manifested across taxonomic levels. At the genus level, taxa belonging to Firmicutes, Chloroflexota, Patescibacteria, and Hydrothermae showed significant differences between pipelines, with several genera not being detected by one or the other pipeline [5]. In PWASS samples, genera from Campylobacterota and Proteobacteria differed dramatically, with Aeromonas showing 400% deviation between pipelines (4% ASV vs. 1% OTU) [5].

The authors note that differences between pipelines were factually greater than dissimilarities between microbial populations in experimental treatments [2].

## SCFA Production from Dietary Fiber

Gut microbiota convert dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) through a fermentation process. Saccharolytic and anaerobic microbiota degrade host-indigestible carbohydrates such as cellulose and resistant polysaccharides into monomeric or dimeric sugars, which are subsequently fermented into SCFAs [5]. The levels and compositions of SCFAs are influenced by dietary fiber intake and consumption of SCFA-enriched foods [3].

The three main types of SCFAs produced are acetate, propionate, and butyrate [6]. These SCFAs are rapidly absorbed by colonic cells via monocarboxylate transporters, passive diffusion, or bicarbonate exchange [6]. SCFAs that are not metabolized by colonic cells travel via the portal circulation to the liver, where they provide an energy substrate for hepatocytes via oxidation [6]. The SCFAs that reach systemic circulation promote anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, increase insulin secretion, maintain energy homeostasis, and improve the function of the gut, liver, skeletal muscles, and adipose tissue [6].

Among these SCFAs, butyrate is the preferred energy source for colonocytes [5], while acetate can reduce appetite via a central homeostatic mechanism by crossing the blood-brain barrier [5]. High-fiber diets that produce high amounts of propionate protect against allergic airway inflammation through inducing hematopoiesis of dendritic cells that seed the lungs [5].

## SCFA-Mediated Appetite Regulation and Energy Expenditure

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) regulate appetite and energy metabolism through multiple mechanisms. Acetate, one of the primary SCFAs, can reduce appetite via a central homeostatic mechanism by crossing the blood-brain barrier [4]. Additionally, acetate-dependent GPR43 stimulation in white adipose tissue improved glucose and lipid metabolism [4].

SCFAs are absorbed by colonic cells through monocarboxylate transporters, passive diffusion, or bicarbonate exchange [7]. Once absorbed, SCFAs including acetate, butyrate, and propionate are converted to acetyl-CoA or propynyl-CoA through pathways involving acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACSSs) and beta oxidation, which produces ATP that contributes to cell homeostasis maintenance [7]. 

The SCFAs that reach systemic circulation through the portal vein promote anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects as well as increasing insulin secretion, maintaining energy homeostasis, and improving the function of the gut, liver, skeletal muscles, and adipose tissue [7]. In monogastric animals like pigs, up to 25% of daily energy requirements are met by SCFAs [3][5].

Butyrate is the preferred energy source for colonocytes and is the primary energy source for mammalian colonic epithelial cells; it can regulate apoptosis, enhance barrier function, and reduce inflammation in these cells [3].

## SCFA Effects on Insulin Sensitivity and Glucose Homeostasis

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) improve metabolic health through several mechanisms. SCFAs including acetate, butyrate, and propionate are produced when gut microbiota ferment indigestible carbohydrates and are rapidly absorbed by colonic cells [1][2]. Once absorbed, these fatty acids are converted to acetyl-CoA or propynyl-CoA through pathways involving acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACSSs) and beta oxidation, producing ATP that contributes to cell homeostasis [1].

Regarding insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis specifically, the colon-derived SCFAs that reach systemic circulation promote anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects as well as increasing insulin secretion, maintaining energy homeostasis [1]. Additionally, acetate-dependent GPR43 stimulation in white adipose tissue improved glucose and lipid metabolism [2]. SCFAs also play important roles in maintaining the morphology of the small intestine wall, offering energy to host cells [4].

However, the provided source material does not contain detailed mechanistic information about how SCFAs specifically enhance metabolic flexibility beyond these general metabolic improvements.

## SCFA Effects on Lipid Metabolism and Fat Accumulation

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) play a critical role in regulating lipid accumulation and fat deposition in livestock. SCFAs, particularly butyrate, are microbial fermentation products that significantly impact fatty acid metabolism and body composition [2]. In rabbits, acetate, a major SCFA, reduces intramuscular triglyceride levels by increasing fatty acid uptake and fatty acid oxidation, with PPARα associated with acetate-reduced intracellular fat content [2]. Low-fat content pigs demonstrate higher abundances of butyrate-producing bacteria species that improve SCFA formation, especially butyrate, thereby alleviating fat deposition [2].

At the molecular level, SCFA administration into the ileum improves meat quality in growing pigs by inhibiting the mRNA expressions of fatty acid synthase (FAS) and acetyl-CoA carboxylase in the longissimus dorsi muscle [5]. Beyond lipid regulation, SCFAs maintain the morphology of the small intestine wall and provide energy to host cells and gut microflora [5]. The levels and compositions of SCFAs are influenced by dietary fiber intake and consumption of SCFA-enriched foods [5].

In contrast, high fat-content pigs show higher abundance of Archaeal species with increased methanogenesis functions, leading to more efficient fat deposition [2]. The gut microbiome can explain nearly 11% of the variation in finishing weight in rabbits, demonstrating the substantial impact of SCFA-producing microbiota on growth performance [2].

## Microbiota Composition and SCFA Production Efficiency

Gut microbiota composition and diversity play critical roles in short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production and metabolic outcomes in livestock. Short-chain fatty acids, particularly butyrate, are microbial fermentation products that have received increasing attention due to their important role in disease prevention and recovery [7]. The microbiota residing in the gastrointestinal tract digest and ferment food consumed by animals into nutrients utilized by the host to produce meat and milk [7].

Specific bacterial taxa directly influence SCFA production and metabolic efficiency. Low fat content pigs had higher abundances of butyrate-producing bacteria species that improved the formation of SCFAs, especially butyrate, thus alleviating fat deposition [7]. Conversely, high fat-content pigs had a higher abundance of Archaeal species along with higher methanogenesis functions, leading to more efficient fat deposition [7]. items.expected:
Gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber (host-indigestible carbohydrates) into SCFAs, chiefly acetate, propionate and butyrate. Dietary fiber intake therefore influences SCFA levels and composition. Colonic cells absorb SCFAs through monocarboxylate transporters, passive diffusion or bicarbonate exchange. Inside these cells, SCFAs are converted to acetyl-CoA or propynyl-CoA, which produces ATP. SCFAs the colonic cells do not metabolize travel through the portal circulation to the liver, where they serve as an energy substrate. Only small amounts reach the systemic circulation. - SCFA administration into the ileum of growing pigs inhibited mRNA expression of fatty acid synthase (FAS) and acetyl-CoA carboxylase in the longissimus dorsi.

The review concludes that through these effects on muscle and fat tissue, SCFAs influence meat quality.

## How Animal Agriculture Facilitates AMR Development and Transmission

# 

Animal agriculture facilitates the development and transmission of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) to humans through multiple interconnected mechanisms. The volume of antimicrobials used in animals worldwide is estimated to be greater than in humans, with most classes of antimicrobials used in humans also prescribed for animals, including classes vital to human medicine such as broad-spectrum beta-lactams and quinolones [7].

## Key Mechanisms of AMR Development in Agriculture:

**Growth Promotion and Prophylactic Use:**
Antimicrobials are widely used as growth promoters in animal food production, which is the main reason for the large volumes of antimicrobials used in the animal industry [7][8]. The use of antimicrobials as prophylaxis and growth promoters should be considered dangerous and unnecessary [13].

**Environmental Contamination:**
Animals excrete a significant percentage (75%-90%) of antimicrobials without being metabolized, dispersing them into the environment [13]. In aquaculture specifically, antimicrobial doses may be higher than those prescribed for livestock, with residues remaining in fish products and aquatic environments for extended periods through animal excreta, exerting selective pressure [7].

## Transmission Pathways to Humans:

**Food Chain Contamination:**
Resistant zoonotic bacteria can be found in soil and from there can infect plants, vegetables, and fruits [7]. The use of antimicrobials in agriculture induces antibiotic-resistant fungi transmitted from the environment to humans [7].

**Direct Pathogen Transmission:**
Scientific evidence demonstrates that indiscriminate use of antimicrobials in the veterinary field has led to the emergence of resistant bacteria that cause infections in humans, particularly in Enterococcus spp., Campylobacter spp., Salmonella spp., and E. coli strains [12]. Migration of people and animals infected with resistant bacteria facilitates the spread of resistance [1][2].

## Specific Examples:

**Cephalosporin Resistance:**
Ceftiofur, the most widely used veterinary cephalosporin, is approved in many countries to treat bacterial infections in animals for human consumption [9]. Its use has been shown to select strains of Salmonella resistant to cephalosporins, a bacterium that causes serious diseases in humans and is associated with consumption of contaminated poultry products [11]. Monitoring revealed a temporal correlation between ceftiofur and ceftriaxone resistance in Salmonella Heidelberg strains isolated from both poultry and humans [11].

**Fluoroquinolone Resistance:**
Fluoroquinolones are another class of important antimicrobials where resistance has emerged among Campylobacter jejuni isolates in poultry [11]. In Australia, where fluoroquinolones have never been approved for use in animal feed, strain resistance to fluoroquinolones is rare, demonstrating the direct link between agricultural use and resistance development [11].

The drivers named are: group antimicrobial treatment, which causes overuse and inconsistent dosing; use for disease prevention and growth promotion; metaphylactic and prophylactic use; and delivery in feed and water, which gives suboptimal dosing and environmental residues. ### 1. SEQUENCING AND PREPROCESSING

**Sequencing Platform and Parameters:**
Fecal samples were collected from piglets (n = 15) at seven timepoints (days 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 70, and 140 of age) for a total of 179 samples [26]. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 instrument with a SP flowcell using 2 × 250 bp paired-end reads [26].

**Quality Trimming:**
Metagenomic sequences were trimmed using Trimmomatic v. 0.38 with a quality score threshold of less than 15 over a sliding window of 4 bp and a minimum sequence length of 50 bp [27]. Sequencing adapters were removed during this same step [27].

**Host Sequence Removal:**
Host sequences were removed by alignment to the Sus scrofa genome (Sscrofa11.1) using Bowtie2 v. 2.4.2-1 [27].

### 2. ASSEMBLY WORKFLOW

**Assembly Tool and Algorithm:**
MEGAHIT v. 1.29.0 was used for both co-assembly and individual assembly of metagenomes [27].

**Normalization Procedure:**
Prior to co-assembly, all metagenomic samples were normalized using BBNorm in BBTools v. 38.79 [27].

**Assembly Approaches:**
The study employed two complementary assembly strategies: co-assembly of all metagenomic samples and individual assembly of each sample separately [27].

**Mapping Strategy:**
For the co-assembled metagenome, metagenomic sequences from each sample were mapped to the co-assembly using Bowtie2 [27]. For individual assemblies, each sample was aligned to its own metagenomic assembly [27].

**Sequencing Data Volume:**
The study generated 738 Gb of shotgun metagenomic sequencing data [4].

### 3. BINNING

MetaBAT 2 was used to bin contigs from each sample into metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) [27].

Contigs with a minimum length of 2,000 bp were binned [27].

The binning process resulted in 2,327 MAGs from individually assembled metagenomes and 85,145 MAGs from co-assembled metagenomes, for a total of 87,472 MAGs with greater than 90% completeness and less than 5% contamination [4][27].

The identification of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) across diverse food animal environments (e.g., manure, wastewater, soil, and animal gut) relies on a shared suite of molecular methods and bioinformatic strategies. These methods are often integrated to provide a comprehensive view of the "resistome."

### 1. Shared Identification Methods
*   **Metagenomic Shotgun Sequencing:** This is a primary method for determining the diversity and abundance of ARGs in complex samples like duck waste, pig feces, and manured soil [source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0, source_file:40_animal_agriculture_one_health.pdf:0]. It allows for the discovery of novel ARGs (e.g., *blaDWA* and *fosA-like* genes) and the characterization of the entire resistome without prior knowledge of specific sequences [source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0].
*   **Quantitative PCR (qPCR):** Used for the targeted quantification of known ARGs, such as *tetW*, *tetA*, *sulI*, *sulII*, and *blaTEM* [source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0]. It is particularly effective for monitoring the reduction of ARGs during waste treatment processes like composting or anaerobic digestion [source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0].
*   **16S rRNA Gene Sequencing:** While not directly identifying ARGs, 16S rRNA sequencing is a standard method used in tandem with ARG analysis to profile the microbial community structure [source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0, source_file:arxiv_1305.2323v1.pdf:0]. This helps researchers understand the correlation between bacterial taxa and specific ARG profiles [source_file:40_animal_agriculture_one_health.pdf:0].

### 2. Technical Considerations and Bioinformatics
*   **Normalization Strategies:** To compare ARG abundance across different environments (e.g., comparing manure to soil), researchers typically normalize ARG counts to the number of **16S rRNA gene copies**. This provides a "relative abundance" (e.g., gene copies per 16S rRNA copy), accounting for variations in total bacterial biomass [source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0].
*   **Bioinformatic Pipelines and Databases:**
    *   **Functional Profiling:** Tools like the **HUMAnN2** pipeline are used to profile metabolic pathways and functions, often annotated using the **KEGG** database [source_file:arxiv_2407.05055v1.pdf:0].
    *   **Taxonomic Classification:** 16S rRNA reads are clustered and mapped against databases of characterized sequences to identify the phylogenetic composition of the sample [source_file:arxiv_1305.2323v1.pdf:0].
*   **Mobile Genetic Elements (MGEs):** A critical technical consideration is the identification of MGEs, such as **integrons (intI1, intI2)** and plasmids. These are often analyzed alongside ARGs because they facilitate the horizontal gene transfer (HGT) of resistance between environmental bacteria and pathogens [source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0].
*   **Matrix-Specific Challenges:** Different environments present unique challenges. For instance, animal manure and wastewater are high-density sources of both antibiotics and ARGs, requiring robust DNA extraction methods to handle high organic matter and potential PCR inhibitors [source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0, source_file:32_amr_livestock_environment.pdf:0].

### 3. Environmental Contexts for Identification
*   **Waste and Manure:** High abundance of tetracycline (*tetC, tetG, tetW*) and sulfonamide (*sul*) genes are frequently reported in pig and cattle manure [source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0].
*   **Soil and Crops:** Studies focus on the transmission of ARGs from manured soil to the endosphere and phyllosphere of crops (e.g., lettuce), where ARG profiles are significantly correlated with the bacterial community [source_file:40_animal_agriculture_one_health.pdf:0, source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0].
*   **Wastewater:** Monitoring focuses on the detection frequency of genes like *tet* and *van* (vancomycin resistance) in farm effluent and surrounding water sources [source_file:32_amr_livestock_environment.pdf:0, source_file:33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0].

Shared methods: all three papers detect resistance genes by sequencing.

Reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic and assembled into MAGs, and the MAGs were screened against the comprehensive antibiotic resistance database (CARD) with CARD-RGI v. 5.2.0. Technical considerations:
(a) Binning ARGs into MAGs from short reads is extremely challenging, because ARGs are often flanked by repeat sequences and located on mobile genetic elements such as plasmids. MAG-detected ARGs are therefore assumed to be chromosomal. Only 115 ARGs were found, against 250 in a previous study of the same short reads and 897 in the co-assembly. (b) WGS detects AMR determinants with a high level of concordance with phenotypic tests, but it is not without limitations and cannot totally replace phenotypic methods.
(c) Insertions, integrations and transposons drive horizontal transfer of ARGs. Plasmid metagenomics focusing on mobile genetic elements (MGEs) may have great potential to identify ARGs in complex environments.

These resistance elements reach the human population through two main routes: **environmental pathways**, including the application of manure to soil (which can increase ARG levels 28,000-fold), the subsequent contamination of crops (e.g., lettuce) and water sources, and the airborne dispersal of bioaerosols up to 10 km from farms [33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0, 40_animal_agriculture_one_health.pdf:0]; and **occupational pathways**, where farm and slaughterhouse workers are directly exposed to ARB/ARGs through contact with manure, wastewater, and contaminated air [33_amr_food_animals.pdf:0]. This interconnectedness is a core focus of the One Health approach [32_amr_livestock_environment.pdf:0].
items.question: How do antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) and genes (ARGs) originate in food animal farms and eventually reach the human population through different environmental and occupational pathways?
items.expected:
Origin: the misuse or overuse of antibiotics in animal production has led to ARB and ARGs. The animal gut microbiota is a reservoir of ARB and ARGs, and antibiotic use is the main cause of ARG prevalence. Insertions, integrations and transposons lead to horizontal transfer of ARGs among microbes, and spread between farm animals and humans is mostly attributed to the transfer of mobile ARGs. About 75% of antibiotics (70% in another passage) are not absorbed and are excreted via feces and urine, contaminating the surrounding environment. Manure used as fertilizer increases resistant bacteria and resistance genes in the environment.

Pathways to humans (three groups):
(1) Direct contact with farm animals. Farm workers have an increased risk and can transfer ARB and ARGs between persons; ESBL-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae were found in 9.8% of workers versus 5% of the Dutch population.
(2) Exposure to animal manure, wastewater or aerosol. Manure and wastewater are hotspots for animal-to-human transmission. Animal waste and slaughterhouses are an occupational risk to workers (MDR E. coli in up to 50% of butchers). Bioaerosols from swine confinement buildings carry zoonotic pathogens and ARGs from feces and may cause respiratory infections in pig farmers. Natural wind carries ARB and ARGs from farms to environmental dust, ARGs disperse up to 10 km, and MDR bacteria and ARGs reach workers and residents in the surrounding environment via inhalation into the respiratory tract.
(3) Consumption of uncooked or contaminated animal products (meat, eggs, milk), a key route of extraintestinal MDR pathogens, especially E. coli and Salmonella; the food chain is one of the important sources of transmission between animals and humans.

items.question: How does the choice between Relative Microbiome Profiling (RMP) and Quantitative Microbiome Profiling (QMP) affect the interpretation of microbial interactions and community variations?
items.expected:
RMP profiles the proportions of taxa, while QMP tracks changes in absolute abundance (AA) and shows the real community dynamics. Microbial loads changed over time and space in the gut. RMP ignored the absolute growth or decline of microbes, failed to detect real microbial changes, and biased both the developmental trajectory and the microbial interactions.

Community variation: AA was relatively stable over time compared with the RMP results. Firmicutes AA was relatively stable in the four gut segments, but its RA varied more, especially in the duodenum and cecum. Ascomycota showed the opposite development trend under QMP and RMP. QMP showed similar Lactobacillus numbers across segments after 7 DHP, whereas RMP showed its abundance as extremely low in the cecum. The same held for Candida. The correlation coefficients (Figure 2B) were only 0.622 (bacteriome) and 0.459 (mycobiome). RA exaggerated the proportion of variation explained by individual, segment and DPH, so RMP overestimated community structure variations and the influencing factors.

Microbial interactions: the comparison used genus-level Spearman's correlation. The QMP and RMP correlations were consistent in 82.1%, 66.0%, 78.7% and 86.8% of cases for the bacteriome (duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum) and in 81.1%, 73.8%, 78.6% and 56.0% for the mycobiome. RMP missed fungal positive correlations: 400 vs. 775, 997 vs. 1338, 865 vs. 1044 and 1048 vs. 2270. Overall, RMP missed many significant positive taxon–taxon interactions found in QMP, especially for the fungal community. The authors conclude that quantitative approaches are necessary.

items.expected:

It reports a high correlation with phenotypic testing in this study and highly accurate prediction in earlier work on non-typhoidal Salmonella. It states that sequencing data complement phenotypic methods and that WGS is "not without limitations and cannot totally replace phenotypic methods". Applied to global surveillance, it can show the early emergence and spread of AMR and inform policy, and routine genomic sequencing will enable real-time monitoring of AMR genes entering the food chain. Paper 42 (Campylobacter, Thailand) calls WGS an essential tool for genotypic AMR surveillance from national to global scales (GLASS). The gyrA T86I mutation was found in 96% of quinolone-resistant isolates and tet(O) matched tetracycline resistance at 100%. Macrolides showed a lower association: erm(B) was present in only 2 of 9 erythromycin-resistant isolates, possibly because of unexamined determinants such as L4 and L22 mutations. Paper 42 also warns that different computational pipelines may give considerably different results and that accuracy depends on how comprehensive the reference databases are. items.answer: The shift from Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) to Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) marks a transition from clustering sequences by similarity to using error-correction algorithms (denoising) to identify exact biological sequences [source_file:28_otu_vs_asv.pdf:0]. This shift is critical for cross-study meta-analyses because de novo OTUs are dataset-dependent and cannot be directly compared across different studies without re-clustering raw data [source_file:29_16s_best_practices.pdf:0]. ASVs, being exact sequences, are consistent across any study using the same genomic region, allowing for direct comparison and integration of data from diverse ecological sources like wastewater systems and animal microbiomes [source_file:28_otu_vs_asv.pdf:0, 11]. Furthermore, ASVs provide higher resolution (down to single-nucleotide differences) and avoid the loss of information inherent in closed-reference OTU picking, making them a more reliable standard for large-scale ecological synthesis [source_file:29_16s_best_practices.pdf:0, source_file:28_otu_vs_asv.pdf:11].
items.question: Analyze the shift from Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) to Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) across diverse ecological studies and explain why this shift is critical for cross-study meta-analyses.
items.expected:
The shift: OTUs as the standard 16S reporting unit have been challenged, and ASVs have been proposed as an alternative and as a replacement (29). DADA2, an ASV pipeline, is increasingly used, and aquaculture studies using ASVs are on the rise against a large OTU-based literature (30). In swine gut work, the paper cites other studies that reported 1,261 and 1,281 OTUs. The authors' previous study reported an average of 1,178 ASVs, and this study assigned 1,850 ASVs at single-nucleotide resolution with Deblur (23). Why it matters across studies: OTUs are internally generated and analysis-specific, with no innate biological meaning. They are artifacts of a subjective dissimilarity threshold or of the reference database. So de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies, and comparisons go indirectly through databases such as Greengenes or SILVA, typically at genus level at best (28, 29). ASVs are actual sequences that represent true sample sequence variants, accurate to a single base, and directly comparable across studies. They give valid comparison of independently generated data, cross-study tractability and database-independent biological veracity, with savings in computation time and memory. They give direct comparability between studies without the need to reanalyze original data (28, 29, 30). Switching to ASVs has the potential to allow the direct comparisons across studies that are needed (28), and ASV studies could provide relevant data for meta-analysis studies (30). Caveats: OTU and ASV pipelines gave community compositions differing by 6.75% to 10.81%, more than the treatments differed, which brings doubt to comparisons across studies that used different pipelines (28). ASVs may inflate diversity (29). ASVs are less widely accepted, partly because their names are hard to use in text (28).

The papers describe a move from OTUs to ASVs. The use of OTUs as the standard unit of 16S reporting has been challenged, and ASVs have been proposed as an alternative to OTUs and as their replacement [11, 15, 17]. The ASV pipeline DADA2 is increasingly used [21], and aquaculture studies using ASVs are on the rise against a large body of OTU-based literature [23, 24]. In swine gut work, cited studies reported 1,261 and 1,281 OTUs [25, 26], while the authors' previous study reported an average of 1,178 ASVs and this study 1,850 Deblur ASVs at single-nucleotide resolution [27, 28]. The shift matters for comparisons across studies because OTUs are internally generated and analysis-specific [0], have no innate biological meaning [13], and are artifacts of a subjective dissimilarity threshold or of the reference database [12], with biases from the algorithm or the fixed identity threshold [22]. De novo OTUs therefore cannot be compared between studies, and comparisons go indirectly through databases such as Greengenes or SILVA, typically at genus level at best [1, 2, 14]. ASVs are actual sequences that represent true sample sequence variants and are directly comparable across studies [3, 22]. They enable valid comparison of independently generated ASVs [16], cross-study tractability and database-independent biological veracity [19], and direct comparability between studies without reanalysing original data [7]. Improving comparability between studies is the stated goal, and switching to ASVs has the potential to allow the direct comparisons across studies that this requires [5, 6]. ASV studies could provide relevant data for meta-analysis studies [24], where non-standardised protocols otherwise make inter-study comparisons problematic [20]. The papers also give limits. OTU and ASV pipelines yielded compositions differing by 6.75% to 10.81% [8], greater than the differences between treatments [9], which brings doubt to comparisons across studies that used different pipelines [10]. ASVs may inflate diversity [18], and ASVs are less widely accepted, partly because their names are hard to use in text [4].

items.answer: In a successful 4C-seq experiment, the distribution of sequencing reads across the genome is characterized by a strong enrichment on the chromosome containing the viewpoint (the cis chromosome), with **>60% of reads** ideally mapping to it [source_file:50_4cseq_protocol.pdf:0]. Within this chromosome, the majority of reads should be concentrated within **1 Mb of the viewpoint**, particularly within the same **Topologically Associating Domain (TAD)** [source_file:50_4cseq_protocol.pdf:0]. A successful profile typically requires **50,000–100,000 cis-mapped reads** to ensure reproducibility [source_file:50_4cseq_protocol.pdf:0]. Deviations from this pattern, such as high trans-mapping or low enrichment near the viewpoint, often indicate technical issues like non-specific amplification or low-quality libraries [source_file:50_4cseq_protocol.pdf:0].
items.question: How does the distribution of sequencing reads across the genome serve as an indicator of a successful 4C-seq experiment?
items.expected: A successful 4C-seq experiment should always show a strong enrichment of contacts with DNA fragments flanking the viewpoint on the linear chromosome, in particular fragments co-occupying the same TAD. Preferably >60% of the reads map to the chromosome containing the viewpoint (the cis chromosome), with most reads mapping within 1 Mb of the viewpoint. Self-ligation of the viewpoint fragment and undigested DNA can heavily skew these metrics, so they should be assessed after exclusion of the top fragments (fragMappedCisCorr and cov1Mb). The viewpoint should also capture many different fragments: >40%, preferably >60%, of mappable fragment ends within 100 kb of the viewpoint should be captured at least once (capt100Kb > 40%). Low-complexity libraries (capt100Kb < 40%) often result from bad template quality rather than insufficient sequencing depth. With (previously frozen) primary tissue, the cis percentage frequently drops to ~50%. That drop indicates random ligations, but the local coverage around the viewpoint is often still good enough to draw reproducible conclusions.

Both pipelines gave comparable results that generally allow the same interpretations. Even so, community composition differed by 6.75% to 10.81% at phylum level, based purely on the pipeline.

Findings in 28_otu_vs_asv:
- **Spurious OTUs.** OTU approaches overestimate diversity and produce spurious OTUs. The study saw this too, but relative abundance thresholds easily mitigated it: a cutoff as little as 0.001% removed enough spurious or rare taxa to fall within the ranges produced by the ASV pipeline. The ASV pipeline outputs fewer to no spurious variants and is precise to a single base.
- **Alpha diversity.** Trends were similar, and the OTU pipeline typically reported slightly higher diversity. The two pipelines diverged for the psychrophilic PWASS samples, where the inverse Simpson index differed at times by a factor greater than two.
- **Community composition.** Pipeline choice significantly influenced reported composition. Over more than 170 days, the dissimilarity between pipelines was greater than the dissimilarity between treatments. The ASV pipeline showed the influence of time and co-substrate more clearly.
- **Consequences.** These differences could lead to different conclusions and could interfere with downstream analyses such as network analysis. On the reduced dataset they would suggest that the pipeline affects composition more than any treatment, a conclusion with no foundation in experimental reality.
- **Comparability.** OTUs are analysis-specific and give no direct comparability with other studies. ASVs are directly comparable between studies.

Findings in 29_16s_best_practices (a review):
- OTUs are clustered at an arbitrary threshold (often 3%) and have no innate biological meaning.
- De novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies, and closed-reference clustering loses information that lies outside the database.
- ASVs significantly reduce clustering artifacts, allow valid comparison, are not restricted by reference databases and need relatively light computation.
- One concern with ASVs is possible diversity inflation from multiple ASVs generated from a single bacterial genome.

23_swine_cultivation does not compare the two approaches.

Both papers say OTUs come from clustering, are analysis-specific and cannot be compared directly between studies [0, 4, 5, 23, 26]. They also say ASVs come from error correction, resolve single-base differences and are directly comparable [0, 6, 13, 22, 27, 28]. 29 adds that OTUs have no innate biological meaning and that clustering affects biological interpretation [24, 25]. 28 measured the effect on interpretation. Overall, the two pipelines allow the same interpretations [1, 14], but phylum-level composition differed by 6.75% to 10.81% [2, 9]. Diversity estimates diverged for the PWASS samples [8, 15]. Pipeline choice significantly influenced composition, and the dissimilarity between pipelines exceeded the dissimilarity between treatments [17, 18, 20]. These differences could lead to different or unfounded conclusions [3, 21]. The papers place the diversity bias differently. 28 reports that OTU approaches overestimate diversity with spurious OTUs and that abundance thresholds mitigate this [7, 10, 11, 12]. 29 records the concern that ASVs may inflate diversity through multiple ASVs per genome [30]. 29 also says ASVs need lighter computation [31].
concepts: de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies

items.answer: [Max turns reached] SEARCH: OTU vs ASV microbial diversity comparison soil human gut marine samples interpretation differences alpha beta diversity accuracy taxonomical resolution meta-analysis
items.question: How does the choice of bioinformatic pipeline influence the interpretation of microbial community diversity and composition across different sample types?
items.expected:
Comparing an OTU-based and an ASV-based pipeline, the paper finds that both gave comparable results that would generally allow the same interpretations, and phylum-level composition was overall in good agreement. Still, community composition differed between 6.75% and 10.81% per treatment on phylum level, based purely on the pipeline. Biologically driven variability between samples affected the two pipelines differently.

- Thermophilic AD reactors: diversity trends were similar, and the OTU pipeline typically reported slightly higher diversity. Inverse Simpson values were almost identical. Both pipelines allow the same interpretation of alpha diversity. Some genera (Firmicutes, Chloroflexota, Patescibacteria, Hydrothermae) still differed, and several genera were not picked up by one or the other pipeline.
- Psychrophilic PWASS: diversity indices diverged. The Shannon Wiener index was similar, but other estimators strongly differed, with a partial trend reversal for some (especially evenness). Inverse Simpson differed at times by a factor greater than two. Between-pipeline variability in composition was much greater than in the other treatments. Aeromonas differed by as much as 3% of the total community, or by 400% (4% ASV, 1% OTU).
- Statistics: on the AD-only dataset, NMDS and Permanova showed that the choice of pipeline significantly influences the reported composition. Pipeline differences were greater than treatment differences, even over more than 170 days. The ASV pipeline showed the time and co-substrate drift more clearly. On the whole dataset, pipeline alone was not significant, but it became significant once its interaction with treatment was included. With factors nested within pipeline, the null hypothesis could no longer be rejected. On the reduced dataset, this would suggest that pipeline affects composition more than any treatment, which has no foundation in experimental reality.
- Cause the authors propose: temperature was the prominent factor. The ASV algorithm calculates error rates on a subset of samples, mostly thermophilic AD samples, and applies them to every sample, including psychrophilic ones, where the results diverged.
- Consequence: pipeline-dependent differences in taxonomic assignment could lead to different conclusions and interfere with downstream analysis such as network analysis or predictions of ecosystem service. The differences were not limited to the PWASS.
