## Preprocessing and Artifact Removal (fastp)

fastp provides an all-in-one solution for FASTQ preprocessing to ensure data is clean for downstream analysis. It removes adapter artifacts through automatic detection for both single-end and paired-end data. For single-end data, it identifies adapters by assembling high-frequency read tails using a k-mer based tree algorithm. For paired-end data, it utilizes an overlap-analysis method that is capable of trimming as little as one adapter base, which is more effective than traditional sequence-matching tools. To improve base quality, the tool employs a sliding window pruning method to discard low-quality bases from the head and tail of reads. It also features a base correction mechanism for paired-end data; when a high-quality base (>Q30) mismatches a low-quality base (<Q15) in an overlapped region, fastp corrects the error. The software also targets specific sequencing artifacts like polyG tails and offers polyX trimming. For specialized tasks like cell-free tumor DNA (ctDNA) sequencing, fastp processes Unique Molecular Identifiers (UMIs) to reduce background noise and improve mutation detection sensitivity.

## Adapter Trimming (Cutadapt)

In second-generation sequencing, machines often produce reads that are longer than the target DNA or RNA molecules, particularly in small RNA sequencing experiments. When this occurs, the machine sequences into the 3’ adapter, resulting in a read that contains both the sequence of interest and the adapter sequence. Removing these adapters is an essential initial task in the analysis pipeline to ensure that only the relevant part of the read is passed on for further analysis. Proper adapter trimming is required before read mapping can take place. In some instances, the presence of an adapter is a sign of contamination, requiring the entire read to be discarded. For color-space data, it is critical to remove the adapter and the color preceding it, as that color encodes the transition from the molecule to the adapter; failure to do so can lead to spurious mismatches during the mapping process.

## Statistical Reliability (DESeq2)

DESeq2 ensures statistical reliability by addressing several sources of technical noise and inherent variability in high-throughput sequencing data. To handle technical biases such as differences in sequencing depth, gene length, and GC content, the method utilizes normalization factors or size factors. It models read counts using a negative binomial distribution, which accounts for non-normality and the fact that variance depends on the mean. To overcome the high uncertainty of variance estimates in experiments with small replicate numbers, DESeq2 pools information across genes. It employs empirical Bayes shrinkage to move noisy gene-wise dispersion estimates toward a fitted curve that represents the overall trend of dispersion-mean dependence. Furthermore, DESeq2 addresses heteroskedasticity, specifically the high noise and exaggerated logarithmic fold change (LFC) estimates seen in genes with low counts, by applying empirical Bayes shrinkage to LFC estimates.

## Bias Correction (Salmon)

Salmon is an accurate and fast transcript quantification method that utilizes a dual-phase parallel inference algorithm and rich, sample-specific bias models [1][3]. It is the first transcriptome-wide quantifier to correct for fragment GC content bias, which significantly improves the accuracy of abundance estimates [1]. In addition to GC bias, Salmon’s model accounts for positional biases, sequence-specific biases at the 5′ and 3′ ends, strand-specific protocols, and the fragment length distribution [3][5]. These parameters are automatically learned during the "online" phase of the algorithm, which estimates initial expression levels and auxiliary model parameters [5][7]. Salmon employs a lightweight mapping procedure that, by default, tracks the position and orientation of all mapped fragments to compute per-fragment conditional probabilities and build a probabilistic model of the experiment [3].

The inclusion of these bias-aware models has a substantial impact on quantification accuracy. Salmon typically outperforms existing tools like kallisto and eXpress in terms of accuracy and inter-replicate concordance [3][4]. During differential expression (DE) testing, Salmon achieves a sensitivity that is 53% to 250% higher than competing methods at the same false discovery rate (FDR) [4]. It also produces fewer false-positive DE calls and reduces instances of incorrect "isoform switching" that occur when GC bias is not properly modeled [4][5]. While Salmon performs similarly to other methods in idealized simulations that lack technical bias, its performance benefits are most evident in real-world datasets (such as GEUVADIS and SEQC) and simulations that include realistic experimental biases [5].

## Meta-Conclusion

Based on the provided documents for **fastp**, **Cutadapt**, **Salmon**, and **DESeq2**, the meta-conclusion regarding the relationship between technical artifact removal and statistical reliability in High-Throughput Sequencing (HTS) is as follows:

### Meta-Conclusion
**Technical artifact removal is not merely a "cleanup" step; it is a foundational requirement for statistical validity.** The documents collectively demonstrate that failure to aggressively address technical noise (adapters, low-quality bases, and biochemical biases) results in "unstable" estimates that trigger high false-positive rates, mask true biological signals, and compromise the reproducibility of downstream results.

---

### Supporting Evidence from the Context

#### 1. Artifact Removal as a Prerequisite for Statistical Accuracy
The tools emphasize that downstream statistical models are only as reliable as the data fed into them.
*   **Salmon** explicitly states that correcting for fragment GC content and sequence-specific biases "substantially improves the accuracy of abundance estimates and the **reliability of subsequent differential expression analysis**." Without these corrections, Salmon notes a surge in false-positive calls (Chunk 27, 29).
*   **fastp** highlights that in sensitive applications like liquid biopsy (ctDNA), data is "highly noisy." Preprocessing to eliminate adapters and correct bases is "especially important... to eliminate false positives and false negatives" (Chunk 2).

#### 2. The Link Between Noise and "False Positives"
Multiple documents identify technical artifacts as the primary source of statistical errors.
*   **Cutadapt** notes that finding and removing adapters is essential because they can be a sign of contamination or lead to spurious mismatches during mapping, which would distort the genomic record (Chunk 11).
*   **fastp** mentions that polyG tails (a sequencing artifact) cause "serious base content separation problems," which would lead to inaccurate representations of the original nucleic acid sequences if not trimmed (Chunk 8).

#### 3. Integration of "Physical" and "Statistical" Removal of Noise
The documents show a shift from simple trimming toward integrated models that handle noise both physically (at the read level) and mathematically (at the count level).
*   **Physical (fastp/Cutadapt):** Removing low-quality tails and adapters prevents the aligner from making incorrect placements.
*   **Mathematical (Salmon/DESeq2):** **DESeq2** uses empirical Bayes shrinkage to moderate "noisy" Log Fold Change (LFC) estimates for genes with low counts. By shrinking these values, it improves the "stability and interpretability of estimates," ensuring that statistical significance is driven by biological signal rather than the inherent heteroskedasticity (noise) of count data (Chunk 17, 24).

#### 4. The Impact on Biological Discovery (Sensitivity)
Reliable artifact removal actually increases the power of the study to detect real biology.
*   **Salmon** reports that using its bias-aware quantification leads to a **53% to 250% increase in sensitivity** at the same False Discovery Rate (FDR) compared to tools that do not account for these technical artifacts (Chunk 30).
*   **DESeq2** argues that its shrinkage method allows for a more "quantitative analysis focused on the strength rather than the mere presence" of differential expression, effectively filtering out the "noise" of small sample sizes (Chunk 17).

### Summary of the Relationship
The relationship is **proportional and foundational**: The "purity" of the input (achieved through tools like fastp and Cutadapt) and the "robustness" of the model (achieved through Salmon and DESeq2) are codependent. Statistical reliability—defined by low false-discovery rates and high sensitivity—cannot be achieved by sophisticated math alone; it requires the active identification and removal of technical artifacts that the mathematical models otherwise mistake for biological variation.

## Architectural Overhaul

Sarek 3.1.1 is a complete re-implementation of the pipeline using Nextflow DSL2, transitioning to a modular architecture where each tool is encapsulated in separate files. This design leverages the nf-core/modules repository, with 78 of its 80 modules being standardized community components, which improves maintainability and allows for the use of sub-workflows to group related tasks like alignment and post-processing.

## Methodological Efficiency

Methodological changes focus on reducing storage and compute overhead. The pipeline shifted from BAM to the CRAM format, achieving a 65% reduction in storage requirements. Efficiency is further enhanced by combining adapter trimming, quality control, and FastQ sharding into a single process, and replacing the native `splitFastq()` operator with a custom process for better resource assignment. Additionally, the integration of BWA-MEM2 provides up to 2x faster alignment through SIMD instructions.

## Performance and Cost Benchmarks

For large-scale data analysis, Sarek 3.1.1 delivers significant optimizations. Benchmarks on AWS Batch show a 69% reduction in total compute costs compared to version 2.7.2, driven by a 70% reduction in CPU hours and an 84% reduction in wall-clock runtime. These savings are facilitated by granular resource allocation, the use of the Fusion file system, and support for cloud 'spot' instances, which can offer up to 90% cost savings. The pipeline's interval-based parallelization also enables processing large cohorts (e.g., 1000 samples) in under 48 hours.

items.expected:
nf-core/sarek 3.1.1 is a full rewrite as a modular re-implementation in the Nextflow DSL2 framework, focused on reducing required compute resources. The abstract names two main changes: the CRAM format for storage and increased intra-sample parallelization for runtime.

Parallelization: FastQ files are split into shards with fastP (optional adapter trimming) and mapped in parallel, so alignment runs on smaller machines. Median mapping runtime falls to 37%, with a plateau at 12 shards. Genomic regions are processed in parallel after duplicate marking, small regions are grouped to reduce the number of jobs, and scatter-gathering covers all applicable variant callers. Runtime was lowest at 21 interval groups. Going from 21 to the 124-group default raised BQSR storage by a factor of five, so the default is being set to 21.

Storage: merging, duplicate marking and CRAM conversion run in one process. CRAM cuts pre-processing work-directory storage by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB), at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage. Less scattering reduces storage by a further factor of 5, which lets the pipeline run on smaller systems.

Other changes: Qualimap is replaced by mosdepth, and a new parameter skips germline-only calling for paired samples. Combining trimming, QC and sharding plus tailored interval splitting reduces CPU hours by 66%.

Cloud: on AWS Batch with spot instances (Tower Forge, fusion mounts), one normal sample cost $20.82 with 3.1.1 against $68.04 with 2.7.2. Runtime fell from 46h8m to 12h4m and CPU hours from 1118.4 to 342.5, a reduction of about 70% in CPU hours and 84% in runtime. The paper states the cost saving four ways: a 70% cost reduction (abstract), a 69% reduction versus 2.7.2 (introduction, about $20 per sample), costs reduced to approximately 30% (Results) and costs reduced to 50% (Discussion). ## Epidemiological Findings in Nawalpur

The 2022 Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) outbreak in Nawalpur, Nepal, which occurred between August 25 and December 5, 2022, primarily affected the municipalities of Devchuli and Gaidakot [11][13]. The investigation found an overall morbidity rate of 28.02%, a mortality rate of 3.06%, and a case fatality rate (CFR) of 10.90% [2][12][16]. Epidemiological data indicated that dry cattle, including pregnant cows, were the most susceptible group with a morbidity rate of 47.62%, while cattle heifers experienced the highest mortality (5.09%) and CFR (15.56%) [2][12]. The most frequent clinical symptoms observed on affected farms were skin nodules (97%), decreased milk production (87%), and lameness (55%) [2][13]. Risk factors identified through univariable analysis included herd size, importing animals from disease-prevalent regions, and sharing feed or water; however, multivariable analysis determined that having neighboring farms with sick animals was the most significant factor in disease transmission [2][16][20].

The researchers compared these findings against global literature, noting that the observed morbidity and mortality rates were consistent with those reported in Thailand (31% morbidity, 0.9% mortality), Jordan (35.1% morbidity, 1.3% mortality), and Bangladesh (21% morbidity, 1% mortality) [16]. These figures contrast with lower rates reported in Saudi Arabia (6% morbidity) and India (7.1% morbidity) [16]. General disease characteristics identified include its status as a nonzoonotic viral disease of the *Capripoxvirus* genus, primarily transmitted by arthropod vectors like mosquitoes, ticks, and flies [2][18]. While direct contact is considered an ineffective transmission route, mechanical transmission by insects is significant [2][18]. 

To combat the spread, the authors emphasized prevention strategies such as implementing animal movement controls, a 21-day quarantine for suspected animals, and targeted vaccination of at least 80% of the susceptible population [2][19][21]. Additionally, vector control measures (such as using larvicides and removing standing water) and strict biosecurity protocols are recommended to mitigate economic losses, which include decreased productivity, diminished hide quality, and infertility [2][4][19][21].

## Contrast: Nawalpur Outbreak vs. Global/General Characteristics

**1. Morbidity and Mortality Rates**
The 2022 Nawalpur outbreak recorded an overall morbidity rate of 28.02% and a mortality rate of 3.06%, with a case fatality rate of 10.90% [2]. These findings fall within the general global morbidity range of 2% to 45% and the typical mortality rate of less than 10% [3]. However, the Nawalpur mortality rate was notably higher than rates reported in other countries such as Jordan (1.3%), Thailand (0.9%), and Bangladesh (1%) [16]. It was also significantly higher than findings in Odisha, India, where 7.1% morbidity was observed with no recorded mortality [16]. Within the district, Devchuli was more severely affected than Gaidakot, showing a morbidity of 37.33% compared to 11.53% [12][15].

**2. Susceptibility of Cattle Groups**
In Nawalpur, dry cattle (including pregnant cows) and cattle heifers were the most affected groups [2]. Specifically, dry cattle had the highest morbidity at 47.62% [12]. While heifers and milking cattle had lower morbidity than dry cattle, they suffered the highest mortality (5.09% and 4.04%, respectively) and case fatality rates (15.56% and 12.95%, respectively) [12][13]. These findings align with general literature stating that pregnant and young cows often show higher disease incidence [18]. Buffalo in Nawalpur showed significantly lower susceptibility, with milking buffalo morbidity at only 3.53% and 0% mortality [14].

**3. Transmission Routes**
General knowledge identifies lumpy skin disease (LSD) as a vector-borne viral disease primarily spread by mosquitoes, flies, and ticks, while direct contact is considered an ineffective transmission route [2][18]. The Nawalpur investigation supported this, with multivariable analysis identifying "neighboring farms having sick animals" as the most significant factor for an outbreak [2][16][20]. Univariable analysis in Nawalpur also linked outbreaks to shared feed and water, herd size, and importing animals from prevalent regions [2][16]. Investigations suggested the movement of animals from the Indian border and internal animal exchanges were potential sources of infection [18]. Additionally, the study noted potential transmission linked to artificial insemination and recent vaccinations, as symptoms appeared shortly after these activities on some farms [10].

**4. Prevention Strategies**
Standard global protocols for LSD emphasize animal movement control, quarantine, strict biosecurity, and targeted vaccination [2][4]. The Nawalpur experience led to more specific community-based recommendations, such as dairy farmer associations regulating the purchase and sale of animals during outbreaks [19]. Local recommendations also included a mandatory 21-day quarantine for suspected animals and the use of internal quarantine check posts [19][21]. While general strategies suggest vector control, the Nawalpur study specified practical measures like removing standing water, using larvicides, and employing farm netting [21]. Finally, the study emphasized that a vaccination coverage of over 80% is necessary to prevent further spread [21].

## fastp Performance and Design


### Design Choices and Implementation Strategies of fastp

fastp is designed as an ultra-fast, all-in-one FASTQ pre-processor. Its high performance and low I/O overhead are achieved through several key strategies:

**1. All-in-One Single-Pass Design:**
['Minimizes I/O by integrating multiple operations into a single tool, requiring only a single scan of the FASTQ data instead of reading and loading data multiple times for different tools', 'Reduces I/O and computational resource consumption by performing UMI preprocessing simultaneously with QC and filtering, rather than requiring individual execution of separate tools']
By performing QC, adapter trimming, and filtering in a single scan of the FASTQ data, fastp minimizes the number of times data must be read from and written to the disk. This "all-in-one" approach replaces the need for multiple independent tools (like FastQC, Cutadapt, and Trimmomatic), which would each require separate I/O cycles.

**2. High-Performance Implementation:**
['Developed in C/C++', 'Solid multi-threading implementation', 'Reports generated in JSON and HTML formats', 'HTML reports utilize JavaScript and web canvas for dynamic visualization']
- **C++ Development:** fastp is developed in C++, providing low-level memory management and high execution speed.
- **Multi-threading:** It utilizes a native multi-threading thread-pool implementation. Reads are packed into blocks (e.g., N=1000) and processed by a pool of threads. Each thread maintains its own statistical context, which is merged after processing to avoid synchronization bottlenecks.

**3. Optimized Algorithms:**
['All-in-one design that performs quality control, adapter trimming, filtering, and pruning in a single scan of FASTQ data', 'Multi-threading parallel processing architecture using a thread pool', 'Packing reads into specific sizes (N=1000) for consumption by threads', 'Individual thread contexts for storing statistical values (per-cycle quality, base contents, etc.) to be merged after processing', 'Two-step method for overrepresented sequence analysis: initial analysis of the first 1.5M base pairs followed by even sampling of the entire file', 'Automatic adapter sequence detection for single-end and paired-end Illumina data via overlap analysis', 'Support for UMI (Unique Molecular Identifier) preprocessing with low overhead', 'Output splitting modes (by file lines or file numbers) to facilitate parallel downstream processing']
- **Array-based Duplication Evaluation:** Instead of using slow hash tables, fastp uses duplication (D) and counting (C) arrays for faster access during duplication rate estimation.
- **Overlap Analysis:** For paired-end data, fastp uses overlap analysis to detect and trim adapters, which is more efficient and accurate than sequence-matching-only approaches.
- **Integrated UMI Preprocessing:** UMI shifting and processing are integrated into the main execution flow, avoiding the overhead of standalone UMI tools.

**Performance Comparison:**
fastp is reported to be 2–5 times faster than traditional tools like Trimmomatic or Cutadapt and significantly faster than FASTQC while performing more operations.

## Spatial Analysis in Rabies Vaccination

Research in the Serengeti district of Tanzania indicates that reducing spatial heterogeneity in vaccination coverage significantly improves the effectiveness of dog rabies vaccination campaigns [1][4]. Fine-scale data reveals that when vaccination coverage is unevenly distributed, the "effective susceptibility" of the dog population increases; specifically, for the same total number of unvaccinated dogs, the risk of rabies is higher when those dogs are distributed unevenly across villages [1][15]. This relationship is quantified using a "power mean" of susceptibility, where a parameter ($p > 1$) indicates that heterogeneity biases the system toward higher susceptibility [1][15].

The study found that outbreaks often followed multi-year periods where specific clusters of villages remained unvaccinated, creating significant gaps in coverage [10][13]. For instance, peaks in coverage heterogeneity occurred in 2007 and between 2011–2013 after groups of villages in the northwest were missed by campaigns [13]. Conversely, when spatial heterogeneity was reduced and vaccination became routine across the district, rabies incidence declined to low levels of less than 0.4 cases per 1,000 dogs annually [8][10][12]. 

A critical finding is that fine-scale heterogeneities are often masked by data aggregated at larger administrative scales, which can lead to a misunderstanding of how incidence is driven by local and district-wide influences [5][10][11]. While the recommended 70% coverage target is ideal for rapid control, the research suggests that even sub-optimal coverage can have major benefits if persistent spatial gaps are minimized [2][11]. However, the high epidemiological connectivity of the region means that local (focal) incidence is heavily influenced by incidence in the wider district and bordering areas [2][8].

## Cutadapt Methodology

Cutadapt is a stand-alone command-line tool designed to identify and remove adapter sequences from high-throughput sequencing reads [1][2]. This process is essential because sequencing machines often read into the 3' adapter when the target DNA or RNA molecule is shorter than the read length, particularly in small RNA sequencing [1][2]. Methodologically, Cutadapt uses a Python-based framework with an alignment algorithm implemented in C for increased speed [2]. It supports gapped alignments to accommodate insertions and deletions, which are frequent in 454 sequencing data [2][4]. The program identifies technical artifacts by computing optimal alignments—either regular or modified semi-global alignments—between the read and the adapter [5]. When the "-a" parameter is used for 3' adapters, the algorithm penalizes initial gaps in the read sequence to prevent short, random matches at the start of a read from causing the removal of the entire sequence [5][6]. If the adapter location is unknown, the "-b" parameter utilizes regular semi-global alignment to remove characters before the first non-adapter sequence [6]. The tool determines the best alignment based on the highest number of matching characters and only performs trimming if the computed error rate is below a specified maximum [6].

The implications for downstream analysis are significant, as Cutadapt ensures that only the relevant biological portion of the read is passed on to further processing [1]. This is particularly vital for colour-space data (SOLiD), where Cutadapt is the only stand-alone tool capable of correctly removing both the adapter and the preceding transition colour to avoid spurious mismatches during read mapping [1][2][4]. Additionally, the tool provides functionality to discard reads based on length requirements and can trim low-quality ends using the BWA algorithm [4]. For compatibility with downstream mapping tools like MAQ and BWA, which may lack built-in trimming features, Cutadapt can produce "double-encoded" output where colours are represented by nucleotide letters [1][4][5].

## Cutadapt Analysis

Cutadapt is a command-line tool designed to remove technical artifacts from high-throughput sequencing reads, a process essential for downstream analysis such as read mapping [1][2]. Its primary function is the identification and removal of adapter sequences, which occur when the sequenced DNA or RNA molecule is shorter than the read length—a common occurrence in small RNA sequencing [1][2]. The tool utilizes a gapped alignment algorithm implemented in C to handle insertions and deletions [2][4]. 

Methodologically, Cutadapt offers two main alignment behaviors:
*   **3' Adapters (-a):** Assumes the adapter is ligated to the 3' end. It uses a modified semi-global alignment that penalizes initial gaps in the read to prevent short random matches at the beginning from triggering the removal of the entire read [5][6].
*   **Unknown Locations (-b):** Uses regular semi-global (end-space free) alignment to find adapters anywhere in the read [5][6].

For technical artifacts related to quality, Cutadapt can trim low-quality ends of reads using the same algorithm employed by BWA [4]. Regarding primers and color-space data (specifically SOLiD), the tool removes the adapter and the color preceding it, as that color encodes the transition into the adapter and could cause spurious mismatches during mapping [4]. It also supports "double encoding" for color-space, removing the last primer base and the first color to ensure compatibility with downstream tools like MAQ and BWA [4][5]. 

The implications for downstream analysis are significant: removing these artifacts ensures only relevant biological sequences are analyzed, prevents mapping errors, and identifies potential contamination [1]. Reads can be discarded entirely if they contain adapters (signaling contamination) or if they fall outside a specific length range after trimming [1][4]. To reduce random hits, users can specify a minimum overlap between the read and the adapter [4]. Information regarding the removal of poly-A tails was not found in the source material.

## One Health and AMR/Disease Dissemination

In the One Health framework, brucellosis serves as a model for how the interconnected domains of animal health, human health, and the environment create a cycle of disease transmission, particularly in pastoral communities [2][3].

**Animal Domain**
The animal domain contributes to the disease cycle through the maintenance of *Brucella* spp. in livestock populations, with an overall prevalence of 5% in small ruminants (specifically 6.5% in goats and 2.0% in sheep) and 2.9% in camels [2][14]. The disease is characterized by reproductive losses, including infertility and abortion [26]. Large herd sizes facilitate transmission by increasing stock density during calving or abortion [23]. Specific animal-level risk factors that perpetuate the cycle include a history of retained fetal membranes (RFM) and abortion, as the placenta is a known predilection site for the bacteria [2][4][15][16].

**Environmental Domain**
Environmental factors and management practices in the Somali region enhance the endemicity of the disease [4]. Recurrent droughts and climate changes trigger the mobility of mixed livestock populations in search of water and feed [4][9]. This migration leads to the concentration of animals at shared watering points and pastures, facilitating the spillover of *Brucella* spp. from infected animals to susceptible populations and the emergence of new infectious foci [26][27]. Additionally, the traditional livestock production system involves wildlife and domestic animals sharing the same ecology, leading to transmission through direct contact or environmental contamination via infected urine, feces, or placental fluids [27].

**Human Domain**
The human domain is linked to the cycle through occupational exposure and sociocultural practices [2][3]. Humans in these pastoralist settings have a 2.0% seroprevalence of brucellosis [2][14]. The risk of human infection is seven times higher in households that own seropositive animals [4][17]. Key transmission routes include handling and disposing of aborted fetal materials—which was associated with a 26-fold higher risk—assisting during calving or birthing, and the common practice of consuming unpasteurized raw milk [2][4][24][28].

## One Health Pathway Analysis

Based on the document, the practices and conditions described across the human, animal, and environmental domains create a "cycle" of transmission and intervention that provides a fertile pathway for the development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), even if the term is not explicitly used.

This pathway can be broken down into the following stages of the cycle:

### 1. The Animal Reservoir and Management (Animal Domain)
The document highlights a "lack of veterinary control measures" and "livestock management practices" (such as large herd sizes and the mobility of mixed livestock populations) as key risk factors. In this environment, *Brucella spp.* circulates and maintains endemicity. The absence of structured veterinary oversight often leads to unregulated or empirical use of medications in animals to manage symptoms like "poor growth rates" and "infertility," which is a primary driver for selecting resistant bacterial strains in the animal population.

### 2. High-Risk Transmission Pathways (Human/Animal Interface)
The cycle continues through cultural and occupational practices that facilitate the transfer of bacteria—and potentially resistant strains—to humans:
*   **Consumption Habits:** The widespread practice of consuming "unpasteurized milk" (cow, goat, and camel) and raw meat provides a direct oral route for the pathogen.
*   **Occupational Exposure:** Pastoralists assist in "birthing/calving" and the "handling and disposing of aborted fetal materials" (retained fetal membranes). The document identifies these as significant risk factors for human seropositivity.

### 3. Diagnostic Confusion and Treatment Pressure (Human Domain)
This is the most critical point for the emergence of AMR. The document notes that human brucellosis:
*   **Lacks pathognomonic symptoms:** It is "difficult to differentiate from febrile conditions including malaria."
*   **Challenges Laboratory Diagnosis:** Tests may yield "false-positive or false-negative results," which delays "proper diagnosis and treatment initiation."

**The AMR Pathway:** When a bacterial disease like brucellosis is mistaken for a parasitic disease like malaria or other febrile illnesses, patients may be subjected to inappropriate or "shotgun" antibiotic treatments. Repeated, incorrect, or delayed antimicrobial use in humans—driven by the inability to correctly identify the pathogen—creates the selective pressure necessary for bacteria to develop resistance.

### 4. Environmental Stress and Re-circulation (Environmental Domain)
The cycle is completed and amplified by environmental factors:
*   **Climate and Drought:** "Recurrent drought" and "climatic changes" force the mobility of "mixed livestock populations" in search of water and feed. 
*   **Pathogen Mixing:** This mobility ensures that the bacteria (and any resistance traits they have acquired through improper treatment in various districts) are constantly mixed and redistributed across the region, making the disease "endemic" and difficult to eradicate.

### Summary of the Cycle
The "cycle" of AMR in this context is driven by **unregulated animal treatment** $\rightarrow$ **constant spillover to humans via raw milk and birth handling** $\rightarrow$ **human misdiagnosis due to non-specific symptoms (resembling malaria)** $\rightarrow$ **inappropriate antibiotic pressure** $\rightarrow$ **environmental redistribution of the bacteria via pastoralist mobility.** 

By advocating for a **One Health approach**, the authors imply that intervention must occur at every point in this cycle—improving veterinary controls, changing consumption habits, and enhancing human diagnostic accuracy—to prevent both the disease and the secondary threat of drug resistance.

items.question: How do the interconnected domains of the One Health framework contribute to the cycle of antimicrobial resistance dissemination?
items.expected:
The review calls AR a One Health issue because livestock, humans and the environment are interconnected, which opens channels for transmission of antibiotic resistant bacteria (ARB). AR is linked to each domain through reckless and excessive antibiotic use in agriculture, livestock farming and human medicine. The interconnections create pathways for bacteria, mobile genetic elements (MGEs) and antibiotics themselves, and movement between compartments promotes the spread of AR. Each domain contributes:
- Humans: careless antibiotic use drives ARB and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), which pass to other humans through direct contact, food, water and environmental surfaces.
- Livestock: antibiotic use contributes to resistant bacteria, which reach humans through direct contact and food products. They reach the environment through livestock waste, and pathogens pass into the environment through air, slurry and feces from livestock, acting as a source of ARGs.
- Environment: environmental contamination is a major factor in dissemination. Residues from the pharmaceutical industry, livestock husbandry, hospitals, fecal waste from humans and animals, and agricultural runoff make it a hidden source of resistant organisms. ARB persist in soil and water and can potentially spread to animals and humans who contact contaminated sources.
The cycle closes when bacteria released in the feces of livestock and humans act as an environmental reservoir before reintroduction into the livestock-human cycle. At the human-animal-environment interface, AR bacterial clones, MGEs and ARGs carry the dissemination. MGEs (plasmids, transposons, integrons) act as vehicles, and together these components promote horizontal genetic exchange. Changes in one domain can have far-reaching effects on the others, and the Fig. 1 legend shows pathways running in every direction among the three domains. The review notes that it is not yet clear how much livestock-derived routes contribute compared with human-derived routes.
concepts: the use of antibiotics in livestock

## RNA-seq Workflow in Snakemake

The provided document discusses the Snakemake workflow management system and its features designed to support sustainable and adaptable data analysis [1][2][11]. Snakemake aims to provide a framework that integrates automation, scalability, portability, and traceability to ensure analyses can be modified and extended for new research questions [11].

Key technical features and challenges addressed in the text include:
*   **Non-file Parameters:** Data analysis steps can incorporate non-file inputs (like thresholds) using Python functions or lambda expressions that are evaluated when wildcard values are known [3].
*   **Iterative Processing:** Snakemake allows for iterative workflows by using wildcards to represent iteration counts and input functions that can request results from previous iterations [1][3].
*   **Semantic Helper Functions:** These functions simplify rule definitions by allowing dynamic Python logic, such as branching decisions based on configuration files, without requiring custom Python function definitions [3][4].
*   **Conditional Execution and Checkpoints:** While Snakemake typically determines the job graph upfront, it supports conditional execution via "checkpoints" [4][5]. This allows the workflow to dynamically decide the analysis path based on intermediate results, such as filtering samples that fail quality control (QC) criteria [5].
*   **Benchmarking:** The system includes a built-in benchmarking directive that automatically measures and stores CPU, memory, and runtime consumption for specific jobs [1][5].
*   **Parameter Space Exploration:** To handle large parameter sets, Snakemake utilizes a `Paramspace` helper that integrates with Pandas to manage complex combinations of parameters and wildcards [5][7].
*   **Readability:** The syntax is categorized into seven types, including natural language keywords and Python statements, designed to be understandable with varying levels of domain or technical knowledge [7][8].
*   **Performance:** Benchmarking shows that Snakemake's time and memory requirements for building a job graph increase linearly with the number of jobs, handling up to 90,000 jobs in approximately 37 seconds [10][11].

items.question: In the context of RNA-seq analysis, how do the mapping and quantification methods of STAR and Salmon address technical challenges before downstream differential expression analysis in DESeq2?
items.expected:
STAR (mapping) targets the non-contiguous transcript structure, relatively short read lengths, increasing sequencing throughput and multiple copies of related genomic sequences. Its method is a sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, followed by seed clustering and stitching. This detects splice junctions in a single alignment pass without a priori knowledge of junctions. MMPs serve as anchors that are extended, which allows alignments with mismatches. Poly-A tails, library adapter sequences and poor sequencing quality tails are identified. The search finds all distinct genomic matches for multimapping reads, and STAR reports every alignment scoring within a user-defined range below the highest score.

Salmon (quantification) targets technical biases from fragmentation, amplification and sequencing, which, uncorrected, can lead to high false positive rates in differential expression studies. It quantifies either by quasi-mapping raw reads to a transcriptome index, without intermediate alignment files, or from pre-computed alignments in SAM or BAM format. Its model accounts for positional biases in coverage, 5′ and 3′ sequence-specific biases, fragment-level GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution, with parameters learned in the online phase. It estimates the conditional probability that a fragment came from each transcript to which it multimaps. It also estimates abundance uncertainty due to random sampling and multimapping. The paper says GC bias correction improves the reliability of subsequent differential expression analysis. In the paper's own DE tests (t-tests of log2(TPM + 1), not DESeq2), Salmon's estimates gave markedly higher sensitivity at the same false discovery rate than kallisto's and eXpress' estimates on the Polyester simulated data. They also gave fewer false-positive DE calls when 30 GEUVADIS samples were compared across sequencing centers, where few or no true differences are expected.

DESeq2 (downstream) starts from a count matrix of reads unambiguously mapped to a gene, that is, per-gene counts. Size factors estimated by the median-of-ratios method account for differences in sequencing depth. Gene-specific normalization factors for technical biases such as GC content or gene length, or estimates of average transcript length, can be supplied. DESeq2 contrasts its per-gene counts with algorithms that use probabilistic assignments of reads to transcripts. None of the papers describes STAR or Salmon output being passed to DESeq2.

STAR addresses non-contiguous transcripts, short reads, high throughput and multicopy sequences [0, 1]. It uses sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, followed by seed clustering and stitching [2], and detects splice junctions in a single alignment pass without prior junction knowledge [3]. It extends MMP anchors to allow mismatches and identifies poly-A tails, adapters and poor-quality tails [5, 6]. It finds all genomic matches for multimapping reads and reports alignments within a user-defined score range of the best [4, 7]. Salmon targets the technical biases of fragmentation, amplification and sequencing, which, uncorrected, can cause high false positive rates in differential expression studies [8, 10]. It quantifies from quasi-mapping of raw reads, without intermediate alignment files, or from pre-computed SAM/BAM alignments [14, 15]. It models positional, 5′/3′ sequence-specific, fragment-level GC, strand-specific and fragment-length effects [16]. It assigns multimapping fragments to transcripts probabilistically and estimates the resulting abundance uncertainty [11, 17]. The paper reports that GC correction improves the reliability of subsequent DE analysis [9]. In the paper's own DE tests, Salmon's estimates gave markedly higher sensitivity at the same FDR and fewer false-positive calls [12, 13]. DESeq2 starts from a count matrix of reads unambiguously or uniquely assigned to genes [18, 19, 23]. It normalizes for sequencing depth with median-of-ratios size factors [20, 21]. It accepts supplied gene-specific normalization factors for GC content, gene length or average transcript length [22, 25]. It contrasts its per-gene counts with probabilistic read-to-transcript assignment [24].
concepts: probabilistic assignments of reads to transcripts

## Integration of Omics and Culturomics

The integration of metagenomics, culturomics, and metabolomics provides a comprehensive understanding of the functional gut microbiome by bridging the gap between taxonomic presence and biological activity. Shotgun metagenomics offers a more accurate and extensive characterization of microbial communities than traditional amplicon sequencing [12]. This technique allows for the assembly of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), which connect functional potential to microbial species that lack cultured representatives [32]. Metagenomic approaches enable the identification of new enzymes and the mapping of metabolic pathways [3][10]. However, the accuracy of these tools is currently limited by a lack of reference genomes, which are heavily biased toward human datasets [3][5].

Culturomics addresses these limitations by utilizing multiple culture conditions to grow previously uncultured bacteria [20]. By sequencing the resulting pure bacterial cultures, researchers can expand reference genome banks, which improves the mapping rates and accuracy of metagenomic data analysis [20]. The combination of culturomics and shotgun metagenomics provides a more exhaustive picture of the gut microbiome and antimicrobial resistance than traditional methods [1].

Metabolomics is integrated with metagenomics and other "multi-omics" (such as proteomics and metatranscriptomics) to provide deeper insights into the interactions between the host, its microbiota, and the environment [2]. Specifically, this integration elucidates the interplay between the microbiome's metabolome and the host's metabolome, which contributes to individual animal performance and health [10][13]. For example, untargeted and targeted metabolomics can reveal how the rescheduling of rumen bacterial communities impacts meat quality [35].

## Functional Insights and Benefits

The integration of metagenomics, culturomics, and metabolomics allows for a comprehensive understanding of the livestock gut microbiome's functional roles in host health and productivity. Shotgun metagenomics provides a significantly higher resolution than 16S rRNA metabarcoding, enabling researchers to characterize new bacterial and archaeal taxa and shed light on their biological functions [9]. Specifically, the assembly of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) connects taxonomy with potential metabolic functions, such as the degradation of various glycans through carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) and the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) [21][24]. Metagenomics also provides genomic context for antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), helping to explain their persistence in the swine gut even without antimicrobial pressure [19][24].

Culturomics complements these culture-independent analyses by providing pure bacterial cultures necessary for in vitro and in vivo validation of a microbe's beneficial or detrimental roles [12]. The sequencing of these isolates expands reference genome banks, which remarkably increases the mapping rates of metagenomic reads [12]. Furthermore, metabolic reconstruction derived from metagenomic data, such as MAGs, can inform and guide specific strategies for the cultivation of previously uncultured isolates for further characterization [17].

Metabolomics and the study of microbial metabolites reveal the mechanisms through which the microbiome influences host physiology. In goats, specific fungal and bacterial consortia produce a suite of metabolites that enable the breakdown of lignocellulose [2][3]. A primary focus of functional analysis is the production of SCFAs—including acetate, butyrate, and propionate—which are generated through the fermentation of monosaccharides [14][25]. These metabolites are vital because they provide up to 25% of the daily energy requirements for animals like pigs, promote anti-inflammatory effects, and regulate host energy homeostasis [14][15][28]. Furthermore, metabolomic analysis linked to the microbiome has identified specific taxa associated with meat quality traits; for instance, butyrate-producing bacteria can alleviate fat deposition, while specific microbial profiles in cattle are positively correlated with muscular metabolism-related genes that improve meat tenderness and flavor [27][74].

## Role of Culturomics

The role of culturomics in bridging the gap between metagenomic sequences and functional validation is centered on the need for pure bacterial cultures to prove the roles of specific microbes [1]. While next- and third-generation sequencing (culture-independent analyses) have identified many bacterial associations with host health and growth phenotypes, the actual functions of these bacteria often remain unknown without experimental validation [1]. Culturomics addresses this by applying multiple culture conditions—utilizing various media and gas combinations—to isolate bacteria that were previously uncultured or overlooked by sequencing-based methods [1][4][6]. 

By isolating these bacteria, researchers can perform essential in vitro and in vivo validations to characterize their functions and establish causal relationships between the gut microbiota and host health [1][7]. Furthermore, sequencing these pure cultures expands reference genome banks, which remarkably increases the mapping rates of metagenomic reads during data analysis [1]. Culturomics also provides a higher resolution than some culture-independent methods; for example, while standard sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene V4 region may identify a single bacterial group (ASV), culturomics and subsequent near-full-length sequencing can reveal multiple distinct sub-ASVs within that group [10]. Ultimately, this comprehensive cultivation approach detects new species and makes it possible to test the functions of specific "most-wanted" bacteria [4].

Culturomics (23_swine_cultivation): culture-dependent (CD) and culture-independent (CI) samples were read by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.
- CD methods detected more ASVs than CI (415, 675, 808 and 823 against 378, 482, 565 and 555 across the lactation, nursery, growing and finishing stages).
- CD methods found 244, 411, 507 and 510 ASVs that CI missed.
- 1,299 colonies were Sanger sequenced, giving 148 taxa in 28 genera. About 50% of ASVs and 75% of genera and families were culturable.
- Sequencing targeting only the V4 region underestimates diversity.
- The authors argue that CI associations and multi-omics give insights, but isolation and validation in animal models are the most convincing way to prove function. Sequencing pure cultures can expand the reference genome bank for metagenomics.

Metabolomics (24_chicken_microbiome): quantitative microbiome profiling (QMP) was paired with time-course untargeted serum metabolomics.
- The metabolomics revealed six metabolite clusters.
- mmvec predicted microbe-metabolite interactions. Foregut microbiota had more connections with serum metabolites, and gut microbes were closely related to lipid and amino acid metabolism.
- 11 metabolites came specifically from the gut microbiota, and 16 came from both host and microbiota (including L-lysin and L-tyrosine).
- The authors stress that these links rest only on association analysis and need experimental validation.

Review (26_gut_meat_quality): understanding the functions of key bacteria and the host-microbiota interaction is crucial. SCFAs from gut microbiota have positive effects on muscle and fat tissue. Butyrate-producing bacteria are linked to less fat deposition, and methanogenesis functions to more efficient fat deposition.

Metagenome-assembled genomes go beyond taxonomy by connecting species with potential metabolic functions [4, 5]: SCFA production genes in 68.5%, 18.8% and 8.3% of MAGs [0], carbohydrate degradation [1] and antimicrobial resistance [2]. 82% of these MAGs come from species that lack cultured representatives [3]. Their metabolic reconstruction may inform cultivation, and expanding the number of known species is called for [6, 7]. Culturomics read out by sequencing detects more ASVs than culture-independent profiling, and recovers ASVs that profiling misses [8, 9, 10]. It yields isolates [11, 12], shows that about 50% of ASVs are culturable [17], and together with culture-independent sequencing it expanded known richness [18]. It also shows that V4-only profiling underestimates diversity [16]. Sequencing isolates can expand the reference genome bank for metagenomics [14]. Functions suggested by culture-independent or multi-omics data are proven most convincingly by isolation and validation in animal models, which culturing makes possible [13, 15, 19, 20]. Metabolomics adds a host-facing layer. Combined with quantitative profiling, which gives a better correlation with host changes [24], it linked absolute microbiota changes to serum metabolites [21]. It revealed six metabolite clusters [22] and, through mmvec, tied microbes to lipid and amino acid metabolism [23, 25]. It also attributed 11 metabolites to the microbiota and 16 to both host and microbiota [26]. These microbe-metabolite links are associations that need experimental validation [27]. It cites SCFAs, butyrate production and methanogenesis as functional links to fat deposition and meat quality [29, 30, 31]. No single paper integrates all three approaches.

Sharding input FastQ files for parallel mapping reduces the median runtime of the process to 37% [1]. The overall runtime for mapping decreases until it reaches an efficiency plateau at 12 shards [1]. For processes involving base quality score recalibration (BQSR) and variant calling, runtime is most significantly reduced when the number of genomic interval groups is set to 21 [1]. Increasing the number of interval groups beyond 21 does not result in further runtime decreases [1].
